# Overview


This page introduces **CALVADOS** — a Python package for coarse-grained, implicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations of biomolecules — and maps its repository, architecture, and workflow at a level suitable for first-time developers. By the end you will understand what the package does, how its modules fit together, and where to go next in this documentation. Deeper treatment of each subsystem is delegated to the pages referenced along the way; this page stays at the boundary between *what it is* and *how it works*.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L5-L7)

## What Is CALVADOS?

CALVADOS describes itself precisely: *"Coarse-grained implicit-solvent simulations of biomolecules in the OpenMM framework."* Each amino acid (or nucleotide) is represented by a **single bead**, which reduces a protein that would need tens of thousands of atoms in an all-atom model to a chain of a few hundred particles. This makes it possible to simulate slow, collective processes — such as the **liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS)** of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) — that are out of reach for all-atom force fields. The package was developed at the KULL-Centre (University of Copenhagen) and is distributed under GPL-3.0, supporting Python 3.11–3.13 on Linux.

The scientific credentials come from a peer-reviewed lineage: the CALVADOS model was introduced and refined in PNAS (2021), Open Research Europe (2022), and Protein Science (2024), with the software architecture itself documented in an arXiv paper (2025). If you use the package, these are the citations to include.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L6-L27), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L4-L33)

## The Core Idea: One Bead, One Residue

The entire package revolves around a **residue parameter database** — `residues.csv` — which assigns each residue type its physical identity:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `three` / `one` | Amino acid identifier (3-letter and 1-letter codes) |
| `MW` | Molecular weight |
| `lambdas` | Hydrophobicity scale used by the Ashbaugh-Hatch interaction |
| `sigmas` | Bead size for Lennard-Jones-type interactions |
| `q` | Formal charge (drives electrostatics) |
| `bondlength` | Distance between consecutive bonded beads |

For example, arginine (ARG/R) carries charge `+1` with hydrophobicity `λ ≈ 0.73`, while glutamic acid (GLU/E) carries `-1` with `λ ≈ 0.0007`. Because this database is a **CSV file rather than hard-coded values**, you can supply custom parameter sets — the `single_RNA` example ships its own `residues_C2RNA.csv` for RNA coarse-graining. The physics that consumes these parameters (Ashbaugh-Hatch hydrophobic attraction, Debye-Hückel electrostatics) is covered in [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions) and [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics); the database itself in [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database).

Sources: [calvados/data/residues.csv](calvados/data/residues.csv#L1-L8), [examples/single_RNA/residues_C2RNA.csv](examples/single_RNA/residues_C2RNA.csv#L1)

## Repository at a Glance

The repository separates the installable package (`calvados/`), runnable demonstrations (`examples/`), and the test suite (`tests/`):

```
CALVADOS/
├── calvados/                  ← the Python package
│   ├── cfg.py                 ← declarative, validated configuration
│   ├── components.py          ← molecule abstraction + registry
│   ├── sequence.py            ← FASTA/PDB parsing, charge assignment
│   ├── interactions.py        ← force field physics (AH + DH)
│   ├── build.py               ← OpenMM system construction
│   ├── sim.py                 ← simulation engine (Sim class)
│   ├── analysis.py            ← trajectory analysis toolkit
│   ├── utilities.py           ← shared helpers
│   ├── BLOCKING/              ← blocking error estimation
│   └── data/
│       ├── residues.csv       ← residue parameter database
│       └── templates/         ← Jinja2 cluster-script templates
├── examples/                  ← 17 end-to-end use cases (see table below)
├── tests/                     ← pytest suite incl. energy validation
└── residues.csv               ← top-level residue database copy
```

Note the symmetry: nearly every module name maps to a documentation page in the **Deep Dive** section of this catalog. The public API is deliberately flat — the package `__init__.py` simply re-exports all eight core modules (`analysis`, `build`, `cfg`, `components`, `interactions`, `sequence`, `sim`, `utilities`), so `from calvados.cfg import Config` is the canonical import style.

Sources: [calvados/__init__.py](calvados/__init__.py#L1-L19), [calvados/data/templates/computerome.jinja](calvados/data/templates/computerome.jinja#L1)

## Architecture: The Build → Simulate → Analyze Pipeline

CALVADOS follows a classic three-stage MD pipeline, but with a distinctive **declarative front end**. You never construct OpenMM objects directly; instead you describe *what* to simulate in validated configuration objects, and the package generates *how* to run it. The diagram below shows how data flows from your inputs to analyzed trajectories:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph inputs["1 · Declarative Inputs (your prepare.py)"]
        CFG["Config — validated by pydantic"]
        COMPS["Components — molecule definitions"]
        RES["residues.csv — parameter DB"]
    end
    subgraph stage2["2 · Generated Artifacts"]
        YAML["config.yaml<br/>+ components.yaml"]
        SCRIPT["run script<br/>(Jinja2 templates)"]
    end
    subgraph stage3["3 · Simulation Engine"]
        SIM["Sim — orchestrator"]
        BUILD["build.py — OpenMM System"]
        FF["interactions.py — forces"]
    end
    subgraph stage4["4 · Output"]
        TRAJ["trajectory.dcd + checkpoint"]
        ANA["analysis.py"]
        BLK["BLOCKING"]
    end

    CFG --> YAML
    COMPS --> YAML
    RES --> COMPS
    YAML --> SCRIPT
    SCRIPT --> SIM
    SIM --> BUILD
    FF --> BUILD
    SIM --> TRAJ
    TRAJ --> ANA
    TRAJ --> BLK
```

The key architectural insight is the split between **configuration** and **execution**. `Config` (in `cfg.py`) validates every simulation parameter through a pydantic model (`SimulationInput`) and, when written, produces two artifacts: a `config.yaml` and a companion Python run script — the templates in `data/templates/` even generate cluster-submission wrappers for specific HPC facilities (Computerome, DEIC). On the execution side, the `Sim` class (in `sim.py`) re-validates those YAML inputs, constructs the OpenMM system via `build.py`, applies forces from `interactions.py`, and runs or resumes the trajectory.

> [!TIP]
> This two-file pattern separates *what to simulate* (editable, version-controllable YAML) from *how to run it* (a generated script). When debugging, always check whether the problem lies in your YAML inputs or in the generated script's runtime settings — they evolve independently.

Sources: [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L28-L60), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L35-L61), [calvados/data/templates/computerome.jinja](calvados/data/templates/computerome.jinja#L1)

### Module Responsibility Map

| Module | Responsibility | Key Public Interface |
|---|---|---|
| `cfg` | Declarative configuration, validation, script generation | `Config`, `Components`, `Job` |
| `components` | Molecule abstraction and type registry | `Component`, `Protein`, `RNA`, `Lipid`, … |
| `sequence` | FASTA/PDB reading, charge and termini patching | `read_fasta`, `seq_from_pdb`, `get_qs` |
| `interactions` | Force field physics — AH and DH parameters, custom forces | `genParamsDH`, force builders |
| `build` | OpenMM `System`, topology, and placement | consumed via `Sim` |
| `sim` | Simulation lifecycle: build → run → resume | `Sim` |
| `analysis` | Trajectory observables and property tables | `save_conf_prop`, `self_distances` |
| `BLOCKING` | Statistical error estimation for correlated time series | blocking analysis tools |
| `utilities` | Shared low-level helpers | — |

Sources: [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L28-L43), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L24-L40), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L35-L44), [calvados/interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L17-L23)

## The Component System: Eight Molecule Types

Everything simulated is a `Component`. A single registry — `COMPONENT_REGISTRY` — maps string keys to classes, and your `components.yaml` selects from it via `molecule_type`. This design means adding a new biomolecule class requires only subclassing `Component` and registering it, not modifying the simulation engine.

| Registry Key | Class | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `protein` | `Protein` | Standard IDP / multi-domain chains |
| `ptm_protein` | `PTMProtein` | Protein with post-translational modifications grafted as branches |
| `rna` | `RNA` | RNA molecules |
| `lipid` / `cooke_lipid` | `Lipid` | Membrane lipids (two parameterizations) |
| `crowder` | `Crowder` | Crowding agents (e.g., globular proteins) |
| `cyclic` | `Cyclic` | Chains with cyclic backbone topology |
| `seastar` | `Seastar` | Star-branched topology (hub + arms) |

Each component subclass customizes how its *sequence* is computed and which beads are *bonded* — for instance, `PTMProtein` overrides both `calc_comp_seq` (appending PTM bead sequences) and `bond_check` (creating protein-to-PTM bonds at configured locations). The component machinery is detailed in [Component Registry & Molecule Types](9-component-registry-and-molecule-types), with sequence and charge handling in [Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment](10-sequence-handling-and-charge-assignment).

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L1002-L1015), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L956-L999)

## A Simulation in Practice: The Two-File Workflow

The shortest path to understanding CALVADOS is to read one example. Every example in `examples/` follows the same skeleton — a `prepare.py` script that (1) declares a `Config`, (2) declares `Components`, and (3) writes both to disk. From `examples/single_IDR/prepare.py`:

```python
config = Config(
  sysname = sysname,
  box = [L, L, L],        # nm
  temp = 293.15,          # K
  ionic = 0.19,           # M
  pH = 7.5,
  wfreq = N_save,         # trajectory writing interval
  steps = N_frames*N_save,
  platform = 'CPU',       # or CUDA
)

components = Components(
  molecule_type = 'protein',
  nmol = 1,
  fresidues = residues_file,
  ffasta = f'{cwd}/input/idr.fasta',
)
```

Calling `config.write(path, analyses=...)` produces `config.yaml` **plus** a run script whose analysis section is embedded verbatim — here, a call to `calvados.analysis.save_conf_prop` that computes conformational properties after the trajectory completes. Running that generated script invokes `Sim`, which builds the OpenMM system and executes the dynamics. This embed-the-analysis pattern means each simulation folder is self-contained and reproducible.

> [!TIP]
> Mind the units: configuration values follow kcal/mol conventions (e.g., `eps_lj`), but CALVADOS converts them internally to OpenMM's kJ/mol (`self.eps_lj = float(self.config.eps_lj) * 4.184` in `sim.py`). Never mix unit systems when supplying custom parameters.

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L72), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L53-L54)

## The Examples Gallery: A Map of Capabilities

The seventeen examples double as a capability catalog. They are grouped below by what they demonstrate — each has a `README.md` and a self-contained `prepare.py`:

| Category | Examples | Demonstrates |
|---|---|---|
| Single chain | `single_IDR`, `single_pIDR` | Basic box simulation; phosphorylated (pIDR) variant |
| Structure guidance | `single_AF_CALVADOS`, `custom_restraints` | AlphaFold-guided restraints; user-defined forces |
| Multi-chain | `two_IDR`, `ten_IDR_cyl`, `single_MDP`, `two_IDR_MDP` | Inter-molecular contacts; cylindrical confinement; crowders |
| Phase separation | `slab_IDR`, `slab_IDR_MDP`, `slab_IDR_PEG`, `slab_mixed` | Slab geometry for coexisting dilute/dense phases |
| Geometry equilibration | `single_IDR_box_eq` | Box-size equilibration protocol |
| Nucleic acids | `single_RNA`, `single_dsRNA` | RNA with custom residue parameters; double-stranded RNA |

The slab examples are the entry point to LLPS studies — the scientific core of CALVADOS — and ship with Jupyter analysis notebooks (`example_slab_analysis.ipynb`). Browse them interactively in [Example Gallery](4-example-gallery), and follow the full lifecycle in [Simulation Workflow Primer](3-simulation-workflow-primer).

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L1-L73), [examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb#L1)

## Verification Culture: Tests That Check Physics

The test suite goes beyond API smoke tests — it validates **energy correctness**. The flagship test, `test_potentials`, simulates two free amino acids, recomputes potential energies from the saved trajectory, and compares them against OpenMM's own log output; other tests verify RNA bond order and custom restraint application. Run everything with `python -m pytest`. This matters for extension developers: when you add a custom force (see [Extension & Custom Forces](18-extension-and-custom-forces)), energy-conservation tests are the safety net that catches unit and factor errors before they corrupt your science.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L45-L57), [tests/test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L1)

## Installation in One Breath

The supported path is conda + pip: create a Python 3.13 environment, install `openmm` (≥ 8.2, < 8.5) with `cudatoolkit` if using CUDA GPUs — or without it for CPU/OpenCL — plus `mdanalysis` and `mdtraj`, then `pip install .` from a clone of this repository. Core dependencies include numpy, pandas, biopython, pydantic (configuration validation), Jinja2 (script templates), numba, scipy, and statsmodels (blocking statistics). Full platform details, including GPU selection and performance tuning, are covered in [Hardware Platforms & Performance](20-hardware-platforms-and-performance).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L29-L43), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L20-L33)

7. *Configuration & Simulation* — [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation), [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry), [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing).

Advanced topics — custom forces, energy validation, and hardware — conclude the catalog in [Extension & Custom Forces](18-extension-and-custom-forces), [Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation), and [Hardware Platforms & Performance](20-hardware-platforms-and-performance).


# Quick Start



CALVADOS is a Python package for **coarse-grained, implicit-solvent simulations of biomolecules built on the OpenMM framework**. This page gets you from an empty conda environment to a finished simulation with computed conformational observables in a few minutes of setup. You will install the package, run its test suite, and execute the smallest complete workflow in the repository — a single intrinsically disordered region (IDR) in a cubic box — while learning the file conventions every CALVADOS project shares. For a conceptual explanation of what the model represents physically, start with the [Overview](1-overview).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L9-L13)

## Prerequisites and Installation

CALVADOS requires a conda environment with **Python 3.13**, the OpenMM engine, and two trajectory libraries (MDAnalysis and MDTraj). The recommended setup is:

```bash
conda create -n calvados python=3.13
conda activate calvados
```

The only decision you must make at install time is your compute target, because it determines whether CUDA support is bundled:

| Compute target | Installation command |
|---|---|
| **GPU (CUDA)** | `conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.2.0 cudatoolkit=11.8 mdanalysis=2.9 mdtraj=1.11` |
| **CPU / OpenCL** | `conda install -c conda-forge openmm=8.2.0 mdanalysis=2.9 mdtraj=1.11` |

Then clone the repository and install the package itself with pip:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/KULL-Centre/CALVADOS.git
cd CALVADOS
pip install .
```

Using `pip install -e .` instead installs an editable copy, which is convenient if you plan to read or modify the source while working through the tutorials.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L26-L49)

## Verifying the Installation

Before running anything yourself, confirm that the physics and file handling are intact on your machine:

```bash
python -m pytest
```

The most important check is `test_potentials`, which simulates two free amino acids, re-computes potential energies from the saved trajectory, and compares them against the values OpenMM logged during the run — a direct validation that forces are assembled correctly on your hardware. Two further tests verify bond ordering in the RNA model and the correct application of custom restraints.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L50-L59), [tests/test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py)

## Your First Simulation: Single IDR

The `examples/single_IDR` directory is the canonical minimal project. Its README defines the entire workflow in two commands:

```bash
python prepare.py --name FUSRGG3
python FUSRGG3/run.py --path FUSRGG3
```

`FUSRGG3` is an arginine/glycine-rich IDR whose sequence ships in the example's `input/idr.fasta`. The two commands separate *declaration* (what to simulate) from *execution* (how it runs), and everything they produce lands in a per-system folder named after the system. The complete journey looks like this:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1["1. python prepare.py --name FUSRGG3"] --> S2["Generates config.yaml,<br/>components.yaml, run.py"]
    S2 --> S3["2. python FUSRGG3/run.py --path FUSRGG3"]
    S3 --> S4["sim.run() loads YAML inputs"]
    S4 --> S5["build_system(): components,<br/>topology, forces"]
    S5 --> S6["simulate(): Langevin dynamics,<br/>DCD trajectory + log + checkpoint"]
    S6 --> S7["save_conf_prop(): Rg, Ree,<br/>nu, contact map"]
    S7 --> S8["data/conf_prop.csv and .npy outputs"]
```

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/README.md](examples/single_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [examples/single_IDR/input/idr.fasta](examples/single_IDR/input/idr.fasta#L1-L5)

## Step 1 — Declare the System in prepare.py

Open `prepare.py`; it is a single script that builds two declarative objects and writes them to disk. All simulation-level settings live in a `Config` object:

```python
config = Config(
  sysname = sysname,  # name of simulation system
  box = [L, L, L],    # nm
  temp = 293.15,      # K
  ionic = 0.19,       # M
  pH = 7.5,
  topol = 'center',
  wfreq = N_save,     # dcd writing interval, 1 = 10 fs
  steps = N_frames*N_save,
  platform = 'CPU',   # or CUDA
  restart = 'checkpoint',
  frestart = 'restart.chk',
)
```

The parameters that matter for a first run are summarized below:

| Parameter | Example value | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `box` | `[50, 50, 50]` (nm) | Side length of the periodic cubic box |
| `temp` / `ionic` / `pH` | 293.15 K / 0.19 M / 7.5 | Physical conditions; ionic strength feeds the Debye-Hückel electrostatics |
| `topol` | `'center'` | Single-molecule topology, molecule centered in the box |
| `wfreq` | 7000 | Save a trajectory frame every 7000 steps (1 step = 10 fs) |
| `steps` | 1010 × 7000 | Total integration steps, expressed as frames × save interval |
| `platform` | `'CPU'` or `'CUDA'` | OpenMM execution target |
| `restart` / `frestart` | `'checkpoint'` / `'restart.chk'` | Resume interrupted runs from this checkpoint file |

Molecule definitions live in a separate `Components` object. The example declares defaults (`molecule_type='protein'`, `nmol=1`, `restraint=False`, `charge_termini='both'`), points at the residue parameter table and the FASTA file, then adds the named chain that `--name` selected:

```python
components = Components(
  molecule_type = 'protein',
  nmol = 1,
  restraint = False,
  charge_termini = 'both',
  fresidues = residues_file,
  ffasta = f'{cwd}/input/idr.fasta',
)
components.add(name=args.name)
components.write(path, name='components.yaml')
```

Calling `config.write(path, ...)` then does something essential: it serializes both validated objects into the run directory as `config.yaml` and `components.yaml`, **and generates the `run.py` launcher script** next to them.

<CgxTip>`Config` validates every keyword through the Pydantic model `SimulationInput` before writing YAML, so a typo like `temp=293.15` vs `temprature=293` fails immediately at prepare time — with a clear error — rather than five minutes into a trajectory. Validation happens again inside the simulation itself (`validate_inputs` in `sim.run`), giving you a second safety net.

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L23-L40), [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L52-L72), [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L37-L61), [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L88-L118)

## Step 2 — Build and Run with run.py

The generated `run.py` is deliberately tiny: it parses `--path`, `--config`, and `--components` arguments and calls one function:

```python
sim.run(path=path, fconfig=fconfig, fcomponents=fcomponents)
```

`sim.run()` loads the two YAML files, constructs a `Sim` driver, and executes its two phases in order. `build_system()` assembles the OpenMM `System` and MDTraj topology, instantiates each component (sequence → beads with charge and hydrophobicity from the residue table), initializes the Ashbaugh-Hatch and Debye-Hückel interaction parameters, and places molecules according to the `topol` setting. `simulate()` then attaches a DCD reporter and a state-data reporter to the OpenMM `Simulation` and integrates the trajectory, saving checkpoints along the way and writing final `checkpoint.pdb`/`checkpoint.cif` structures.

By the end of this step your run directory contains:

| File | Producer | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `config.yaml`, `components.yaml`, `run.py` | `prepare.py` | Declarative inputs + generated launcher |
| `top.pdb` | `build_system()` | Reference structure of the built system |
| `<sysname>.dcd` | `DCDReporter` | Trajectory frames, one per `wfreq` steps |
| `<sysname>.log` | `StateDataReporter` | Step, speed, elapsed time, potential energy |
| `restart.chk` | Checkpointing | Resume point for interrupted or extended runs |
| `checkpoint.pdb` / `checkpoint.cif` | Final state | Final frame in standard structure formats |

<CgxTip>Checkpointing is built into the batch loop: if a run is cut off (cluster walltime, laptop sleep), simply rerun the same `run.py` command. With `restart='checkpoint'`, the simulator detects the existing `restart.chk`, skips equilibration adjustments, and appends to the existing DCD rather than starting over.

Sources: [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L886), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L157-L164), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L824-L869), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L851-L857)

## Step 3 — Automatic Trajectory Analysis

Notice that `prepare.py` defined a `analyses` string containing Python code. `Config.write_runfile()` appends this string verbatim to the generated `run.py`, so after the trajectory finishes, the same process immediately runs `save_conf_prop(...)`:

```python
from calvados.analysis import save_conf_prop
save_conf_prop(path="{path}", name="{sysname}", residues_file=..., 
               output_path="data", start=10, is_idr=True, select='all')
```

This function loads `top.pdb` plus the DCD into MDAnalysis and computes single-chain conformational observables, skipping the first 10 frames (`start=10`) to exclude residual equilibration. Results land in the `data/` folder:

| Output | Description |
|---|---|
| `data/conf_prop.csv` | Summary table: mean Rg, mean end-to-end distance, and the scaling exponent ν, each with blocking-error estimates |
| `data/rgs.npy`, `data/rees.npy` | Per-frame radius of gyration and end-to-end distance arrays |
| `data/cmap.npy` | Averaged inter-residue contact map |
| `data/internal_distances.npy` | Internal distance distributions used for the ν fit (IDR mode only) |

A first successful run typically shows a compact, growing chain whose Rg is stable across the sampled frames — the blocking error estimates in `conf_prop.csv` tell you whether the trajectory is long enough for the values to be statistically meaningful.

Sources: [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L63-L84), [calvados/analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L494-L539), [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L44-L50)

## How the Pieces Fit Together

The quick-start experience is the user-facing surface of a four-stage pipeline. Every CALVADOS example — slab phase separation, multi-chain condensates, RNA, crowders — reuses exactly this shape, changing only the declarations:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Declarative inputs<br/>(Config + Components)"] -->|cfg.py<br/>Pydantic validation| B["YAML + generated run.py"]
    B -->|sim.run()| C["Build<br/>(build.py, components.py,<br/>interactions.py)"]
    C --> D["Simulate<br/>(sim.py + OpenMM)"]
    D --> E["Analyze<br/>(analysis.py + BLOCKING)"]
```

The separation has a practical payoff: `config.yaml` and `components.yaml` are plain, version-controllable text that fully describe a simulation, while `run.py` is disposable and regenerable. Changing a condition means editing one line in `prepare.py` and rerunning it — never hand-editing generated files.

Sources: [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L33), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L1-L39)

## Common First-Run Issues

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Topol 'single/center' incompatible with multiple molecules.` | `topol='center'` declared while `nmol > 1` | Use `nmol=1`, or switch to a grid/slab topology for many molecules |
| Slow simulation on GPU machine | `platform='CPU'` left as default | Set `platform='CUDA'` in `Config` after installing with cudatoolkit |
| Simulation restarts from scratch | `frestart` path missing or `restart` set to `'pdb'`/`'cif'` without the file present | Keep `restart='checkpoint'` and let `restart.chk` accumulate in the run directory |
| `FileNotFoundError` for a restart structure | `restart='pdb'`/'cif' points to a nonexistent file | Generate the structure first (any completed run writes `checkpoint.pdb`), or use checkpoint mode |

Sources: [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L126-L130), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L61-L72), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L805-L819)

## Where to Go Next

You now possess the core skill — declaring a system in `prepare.py` and executing it via the generated `run.py`. Recommended progression:

1. **[Simulation Workflow Primer](3-simulation-workflow-primer)** — a guided walkthrough of the same prepare → build → simulate → analyze lifecycle with deeper narration of each stage.
2. **[Example Gallery](4-example-gallery)** — the full set of ready-made projects in `examples/`, from `slab_IDR` phase-separation setups to RNA and crowder systems; each follows the pattern you just ran.
3. **[Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview)** — how `cfg`, `components`, `build`, `interactions`, `sim`, and `analysis` modules relate inside the package.
4. When you are ready to tune physics rather than workflow, **[Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database)** explains the `residues_CALVADOS2.csv` file your `Components` object consumed.


# Simulation Workflow Primer



This primer walks you through the complete lifecycle of a CALVADOS simulation: from writing a small Python *preparation script*, to the generated YAML inputs, to the OpenMM engine that builds and integrates the system, and finally to the trajectory files you analyze. CALVADOS is a coarse-grained platform for biomolecular simulations (intrinsically disordered regions, condensates, membranes, RNA), and every example in the repository follows the same three-act structure — **declare, execute, analyze**. By the end of this page you will understand what each file in a simulation directory is, who creates it, and when it is used.

## The Workflow at a Glance

Every simulation directory in CALVADOS is produced by the same pipeline. You write one script (typically named `prepare.py`), which instantiates two validated configuration objects, `Config` and `Components`. Calling their `.write()` methods produces `config.yaml`, `components.yaml`, and a ready-to-run `run.py`. Launching `run.py` invokes `sim.run()`, which validates the YAML, constructs the OpenMM system, and executes the trajectory while writing checkpoints and a DCD trajectory. Analysis code is optionally appended to `run.py` itself, so post-processing happens automatically after production ends.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["prepare.py<br/>(you write this)"] --> B["Config(**params)"]
    A --> C["Components(**defaults)"]
    B -->|".write()"| D["config.yaml + run.py"]
    C -->|".write()"| E["components.yaml"]
    D --> F["run.py --path ./system"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["sim.run()<br/>1. validate YAML<br/>2. build_system()<br/>3. simulate()"]
    G --> H["top.pdb / top.cif<br/>system.xml"]
    G --> I["&lt;sysname&gt;.dcd<br/>&lt;sysname&gt;.log<br/>restart.chk"]
    G --> J["appended analysis code<br/>(e.g. save_conf_prop)"]
    C -.->|"optional"| K["Job → job.sh<br/>(PBS / SLURM template)"]
```

Sources: [prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L73), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L37-L84), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L886)

This design separates **what** you simulate (declarative YAML) from **how** it runs (the engine). The preparation script never touches OpenMM directly; it only produces validated input files. This means the same `run.py` can be rerun, resumed, or submitted to a cluster without touching a single line of engine code.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L63-L84), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L122-L131)

## Project Structure: Who Does What

The `calvados` package maps cleanly onto workflow stages. As a beginner, you only need to understand three of these modules directly — `cfg`, `sim`, and `analysis` — but knowing the full layout helps you navigate the Deep Dive pages later.

```
calvados/
├── cfg.py           ← Stage 1: Config / Components / Job (declarative inputs)
├── inputmodels.py   ← Pydantic schemas: validation + defaults
├── components.py    ← Molecule classes + COMPONENT_REGISTRY
├── sequence.py      ← FASTA parsing, charge assignment
├── build.py         ← Box grids, random placement, geometry helpers
├── interactions.py  ← Ashbaugh-Hatch, Debye-Hückel, restraints forces
├── sim.py           ← Stage 2: Sim class (build_system + simulate) + run()
├── analysis.py      ← Stage 3: trajectory measurements
├── utilities.py     ← misc helpers
└── BLOCKING/        ← blocking (statistical) error estimation
```

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L15-L20), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L10)

## Stage 1 — Declare the Simulation with `Config`

`Config` is a thin wrapper around the `SimulationInput` Pydantic model. You pass keyword arguments (box size, temperature, ionic strength, runtime settings); they are validated immediately — unknown or misspelled keys fail at *preparation time*, not hours into a run — and serialized into a YAML-compatible dictionary. In the canonical `single_IDR` example, the configuration specifies a 50 nm cubic box, 293.15 K, 0.19 M salt, and runtime settings such as `wfreq` (trajectory write interval) and `platform` (`CPU` or `CUDA`).

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L37-L48), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L122-L153), [prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L42)

The most important keys for a first simulation are summarized below. Note that a duration must be given as *either* `steps` or `runtime` (hours) — supplying both raises a validation error. One step corresponds to the 10 fs integrator timestep, so the example's `N_frames * N_save = 7,070,000` steps equals roughly 70.7 ns of simulated time.

| Key | Type / Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `box` | 3 floats (required) | Box side lengths in nm |
| `temp`, `ionic`, `pH` | floats (required) | Thermodynamic + salt conditions |
| `topol` | `center` (default) | Molecule placement scheme: `single`, `slab`, `grid`, `center`, `shift_ref_bead`, `random` |
| `steps` / `runtime` | exactly one | Simulation length in steps or wall-clock hours |
| `wfreq` | 100000 | Steps between DCD trajectory frames |
| `platform` | `CPU` | `CPU` (with `threads`) or `CUDA` (with `gpu_id`) |
| `restart` / `frestart` | `checkpoint` / `restart.chk` | Resume mode and checkpoint file |
| `eps_lj`, `cutoff_lj`, `cutoff_yu` | 0.2 / 2.0 / 4.0 nm | Nonbonded interaction settings |
| `slab_eq`, `box_eq`, `bilayer_eq` | `False` | Equilibration protocol switches |

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L133-L180), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L181-L190), [prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L18-L19), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L659-L663)

## Stage 2 — Declare the Molecules with `Components`

`Components` collects the molecular inventory. Shared defaults are set in the constructor, then each species is registered with `.add(name, **overrides)`, where every entry is validated against `ComponentInput`. At minimum a component needs a residue-parameter file (`fresidues`, e.g. `residues_CALVADOS2.csv`) and a sequence source (`ffasta`) — unless it uses structure-based restraints, in which case a `pdb_folder` is required instead.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L95-L124), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L39-L76), [prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L58-L72)

The `molecule_type` field selects the component class from `COMPONENT_REGISTRY` during system construction, which in turn determines the bead model, bonded terms, and interactions applied. The validator also enforces physics-driven constraints — for example, RNA may only use harmonic restraints, and lipids/crowders can never be restrained.

| `molecule_type` | Used for |
|---|---|
| `protein` | Standard single-bead-per-residue IDRs/proteins |
| `rna` | Two-bead-per-nucleotide RNA (P + N beads) |
| `lipid` / `cooke_lipid` | Membrane bilayers (mutually exclusive) |
| `crowder` | Inert volume excluders |
| `cyclic`, `seastar`, `ptm_protein` | Specialized topologies / modified proteins |

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L17-L26), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L84-L108), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L110-L117)

## Stage 3 — Write the Artifacts

Calling `config.write(path)` does two things: dumps the validated dictionary to `config.yaml` (preserving your key order), and generates the `run.py` launcher — a small argparse script that forwards `--path`, `--config`, and `--components` to `sim.run()`. This is also where the *analysis hook* lives: any code string you pass as `analyses` is appended verbatim to `run.py`, so functions like `save_conf_prop` execute automatically after the trajectory finishes. `components.write(path)` analogously produces `components.yaml` with a `defaults` block plus a per-component `system` block containing only explicit overrides. For cluster users, the optional `Job` class renders packaged Jinja2 templates (PBS or SLURM) into a `job.sh` that embeds your config values and can be submitted with `.submit()`.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L50-L84), [prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L49-L56), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L126-L134), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L138-L183)

## Stage 4 — Execute: Inside `sim.run()`

The generated `run.py` calls a single function. `sim.run()` loads both YAML files, constructs a `Sim` object, and drives two phases in sequence: `build_system()` and `simulate()`. The `Sim.__init__` constructor already does meaningful work — it re-validates the inputs via `validate_inputs`, converts `eps_lj` from kcal to kJ/mol, and checks restart-file existence, disabling equilibration phases automatically when a checkpoint resume is detected.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L886), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L41-L72)

`build_system()` is the deterministic assembly phase. It creates an MDTraj topology and an OpenMM `System` with periodic box vectors, computes Debye-Hückel parameters from temperature and ionic strength, instantiates components from the registry (calculating charges, sigmas, and lambdas per residue), and initializes the two global nonbonded forces — Ashbaugh-Hatch (`ah`) and Debye-Hückel (`yu`). Then, molecule by molecule, it places coordinates according to the `topol` scheme (e.g. `'center'` puts the molecule at the box midpoint), registers particles into each force object, adds bonds/angles/restraints with nonbonded exclusions, and finally attaches all forces to the system — including optional barostats — and serializes the result to `<sysname>.xml`. The initial structure is saved as `top.pdb` and `top.cif`.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L157-L208), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L265-L303), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L412-L414), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L306-L353), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L368-L393)

`simulate()` is the dynamics phase. It selects the restart source (checkpoint by default, or a PDB/mmCIF you provide), creates a `LangevinMiddleIntegrator` at your temperature with friction coefficient `friction_coeff` and a 0.01 ps (10 fs) timestep, and assembles the OpenMM `Simulation` on the chosen platform. If `restart.chk` exists, the state is loaded and the existing trajectory/log are appended; otherwise positions are set and energy is minimized. Optional staged equilibrations then run: slab equilibration pulls molecules toward the box plane with a harmonic external force that is *removed afterward* (requiring a fresh context), and pressure equilibration scales the box with a barostat. Production then starts with a `DCDReporter` (every `wfreq` steps) and a `StateDataReporter` log.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L646-L687), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L689-L715), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L717-L763), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L765-L842)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S0["sim.run() loads YAML"] --> S1["Sim.__init__<br/>validate + restart setup"]
    S1 --> S2["build_system()<br/>topology, forces, placement"]
    S2 --> S3{"restart.chk<br/>exists?"}
    S3 -->|Yes| S4["loadCheckpoint<br/>append dcd/log"]
    S3 -->|No| S5["setPositions +<br/>minimizeEnergy"]
    S4 --> S6{"slab_eq /<br/>box_eq?"}
    S5 --> S6
    S6 -->|Yes| S7["equilibration steps_eq<br/>then rebuild context"]
    S6 -->|No| S8["production run"]
    S7 --> S8
    S8 --> S9{"runtime<br/>given?"}
    S9 -->|Yes| S10["runForClockTime<br/>chk every 30 min"]
    S9 -->|No| S11["≤10 batches of steps<br/>checkpoint per batch"]
    S10 --> S12["final checkpoint +<br/>checkpoint.pdb/.cif"]
    S11 --> S12
```

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L646-L857)

## Stage 5 — Outputs, Checkpointing, and Resume

A completed run leaves a self-describing directory. Understanding these files is essential because *resume behavior is file-driven*: with the default `restart='checkpoint'`, re-executing `run.py` after an interruption loads `restart.chk` and appends to the existing trajectory; with `restart='pdb'` or `'cif'`, you point `frestart` at a structure to start fresh coordinates from. When starting non-checkpoint runs, any pre-existing DCD is timestamped and backed up rather than overwritten.

| File | Producer | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `config.yaml` / `components.yaml` | `Config`/`Components.write()` | Validated declarative inputs |
| `run.py` | `Config.write()` | Launcher + appended analysis code |
| `top.pdb` / `top.cif` | `build_system()` | Initial coarse-grained structure |
| `<sysname>.xml` | `print_system_summary()` | Full serialized OpenMM system |
| `<sysname>.dcd` | `DCDReporter` | Trajectory, one frame per `wfreq` steps |
| `<sysname>.log` | `StateDataReporter` | Step/speed/energy records |
| `restart.chk` | `simulate()` | OpenMM checkpoint for seamless resume |
| `checkpoint.pdb/.cif` | end of run | Final coordinates snapshot |

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L295-L304), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L368-L373), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L823-L842), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L689-L698), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L707-L712), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L859-L869)

> [!TIP]
> Checkpointing granularity differs by duration mode: with `steps`, progress is checkpointed after each of at most 10 batches (`_split_steps`), but with `runtime`, OpenMM writes the checkpoint every 30 wall-clock minutes via `runForClockTime` — the latter is the right choice for queue systems with wall-clock limits.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L24-L28), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L845-L857)

## The Analysis Hook

Because analysis code is appended to `run.py`, the typical pattern is: import an analysis function at the top of the appended block, then call it with the simulation `path`, system `name`, and the residues file. In the `single_IDR` example, `save_conf_prop` is invoked with `start=10` (skip early frames) and `is_idr=True`. The analysis stack — including slab phase-separation diagnostics and blocking error estimation (`calvados/BLOCKING`) — is covered in depth on its own pages.

Sources: [prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L49-L56), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L21-L23)

## Where to Go Next

You now understand the full declare → execute → analyze loop. Recommended progression from here:

- Run one yourself end-to-end: [Quick Start](2-quick-start), then browse ready-made scenarios in [Example Gallery](4-example-gallery)
- Understand what the engine builds under the hood: [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview)
- Go deeper into the physics you just saw registered as `ah`/`yu` forces: [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions) and [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics)
- Master the declarative layer: [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation) and [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing)

# Example Gallery



The `examples/` directory is CALVADOS' living documentation: 16 self-contained scenarios that demonstrate every supported simulation style, from a single intrinsically disordered region (IDR) in a cubic box to 200-chain protein–RNA coexistence slabs. Each example follows the same skeleton — a `prepare.py` script that emits declarative YAML, plus the model input files it references — so once you can read one example, you can read them all. This page catalogs the gallery, decodes the recurring patterns, and charts a learning path from the simplest scenario to the most advanced.

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L1-L73), [examples/slab_mixed/prepare.py](examples/slab_mixed/prepare.py#L1-L92)

## Gallery at a Glance

Every example directory contains a `prepare.py` that you run first, followed by a generated `run.py` inside the newly created system directory (more on this two-step pattern below). The gallery divides cleanly along two axes: **simulation geometry** (how chains are arranged in the periodic box) and **molecular composition** (what is being simulated). The table below maps all 16 examples to those axes so you can jump straight to the scenario closest to your science.

| Example | Geometry (`topol`) | Molecules | Key Technique Demonstrated |
|---|---|---|---|
| `single_IDR` | `center` | 1 protein | Canonical minimal setup |
| `single_IDR_box_eq` | `center` | 1 protein | MC barostat box equilibration |
| `single_pIDR` | `center` | 1 phospho-protein | pH-dependent phosphorylated-residue charges |
| `single_AF_CALVADOS` | `center` | 1 protein | AlphaFold structure-based GO restraints |
| `single_MDP` | `center` | 1 folded + MDP | MEGABASE folded-domain force field (CALVADOS3) |
| `custom_restraints` | `center` | 1 multi-domain protein | Custom harmonic restraints file + AF restraints |
| `single_RNA` | `center` | 1 RNA | RNA bond/angle/nonbonded parameters |
| `single_dsRNA` | `single` | 1 RNA duplex | Restrained double-stranded RNA |
| `two_IDR` | `random` | 2 proteins | Multi-component contact analysis |
| `two_IDR_MDP` | `random` | 2 folded proteins | CALVADOS3 with domain restraints |
| `ten_IDR_cyl` | `grid` | 10 proteins | Custom external force (cylinder confinement) |
| `slab_IDR` | `slab` | 100 copies, 1 protein | Direct-coexistence phase separation |
| `slab_IDR_MDP` | `slab` | 100 + 100 chains | Per-component restraint overrides |
| `slab_IDR_PEG` | `slab` | 100 proteins + PEG crowders | Crowder count from w/v fraction |
| `slab_MDP` | `slab` | 100 folded chains | Slab of structured domains (CALVADOS3) |
| `slab_mixed` | `slab` | 200 proteins + 60 RNAs | Mixed protein–RNA condensate |

Sources: [examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L31), [examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py](examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py#L28-L30), [examples/single_RNA/prepare.py](examples/single_RNA/prepare.py#L46-L66), [examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py#L95-L96)

## Anatomy of an Example

All `prepare.py` scripts share one five-beat rhythm. The canonical example is `single_IDR`, and studying it first pays off across the entire gallery: (1) parse a system name from the command line, (2) choose box size and sampling constants, (3) build a `Config` object holding general physics and runtime settings, (4) build a `Components` object listing every molecular species and its copy number, and (5) write both to YAML inside the new system directory. An `analyses` block — a raw Python snippet stored inside `config.yaml` — is optionally attached so post-processing runs automatically after simulation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["prepare.py\n(e.g. examples/single_IDR/prepare.py)"] --> B["Config(...)\nbox · temp · ionic · pH · topol\nwfreq · steps · platform · restart"]
    A --> C["Components(...)\nmolecule_type · nmol · fresidues · ffasta"]
    B --> D["config.write(path, 'config.yaml',\nanalyses=analyses_block)"]
    C --> E["components.add(name, **overrides)\ncomponents.write(path, 'components.yaml')"]
    D --> F["System directory\nsysname/{config.yaml, components.yaml, run.py}"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["python sysname/run.py --path sysname\n(generated simulation + post-processing entry point)"]
    G --> H["Outputs: top.pdb · traj.dcd · analysis results"]
```

The two-step execution contract is documented in each example's `README.md`. For a single-chain system:

```bash
python prepare.py --name <protein name>
python <protein name>/run.py --path <protein name>
```

Slab examples extend this with replica and GPU arguments — `prepare.py --name <protein> --replica <replica> --gpu_id <gpu_id>` — and the system directory name then incorporates the replica number (`f'{args.name}_{args.replica}'`), enabling statistically independent replicas for sampling-error estimation. Note that `prepare.py` itself never runs dynamics; it is purely a *configuration generator*, which keeps the gallery's scripts short, diffable, and safe to edit.

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L11-L73), [examples/single_IDR/README.md](examples/single_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [examples/slab_IDR/README.md](examples/slab_IDR/README.md#L1-L9)

> [!TIP]
> The `analyses` block is written as a literal Python string into `config.yaml` and executed after the trajectory completes. This means you can freely edit post-processing (e.g., change `start=10` to skip equilibration frames) *without re-preparing or re-running the simulation* — a deliberate separation of physics from analysis.

## Geometry Configurations

The `topol` parameter in `Config` selects the chain-placement strategy and, with it, the box shape. The gallery exercises five topologies, each suited to a different physical question:

| `topol` Value | Box Shape (example) | Chains | Purpose | Reference Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `center` | Cubic, e.g. 50×50×50 nm | 1 | Single-chain ensemble properties (Rg, internal contacts) | `single_IDR` |
| `random` | Cubic, e.g. 20×20×20 nm | 2+ | Inter-chain contact maps between distinct species | `two_IDR` |
| `slab` | Elongated, e.g. 15×15×150 nm | 100+ | Direct-coexistence phase separation; dense slab forms against dilute phase | `slab_IDR` |
| `grid` | Cubic, 20×20×20 nm | 10 | Regular initial lattice with optional external confinement | `ten_IDR_cyl` |
| `single` | Cubic, 100×100×100 nm | 1 (duplex) | Restrained folded assemblies (dsRNA) | `single_dsRNA` |

Two slab-specific refinements appear in the gallery. `slab_eq = True` with `steps_eq` triggers an initial equilibration phase that compresses chains into the dense slab before production sampling, as configured in `slab_IDR` with `steps_eq = 100*N_save`. For studies where the condensate itself should stay at fixed composition, `slab_IDR_PEG` adds `fixed_lambda` and `slab_outer` parameters to control the interaction scaling and slab boundary treatment around crowder molecules.

Sources: [examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L49), [examples/two_IDR/prepare.py](examples/two_IDR/prepare.py#L29-L34), [examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py](examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py#L25-L31), [examples/single_dsRNA/prepare.py](examples/single_dsRNA/prepare.py#L28-L32), [examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py#L36-L39)

## Molecular Species and Force Field Files

Every `Components` object declares a `molecule_type` (default `'protein'`) and points to a **residues file** — a CSV defining each coarse-grained bead's mass, charge, and interaction parameters. The gallery ships five residue files, and choosing the right one is inseparable from choosing the model:

| Residues File | Species / Model | Used By |
|---|---|---|
| `residues_CALVADOS2.csv` | IDRs, CALVADOS 2 model | `single_IDR`, `two_IDR`, `slab_IDR`, `ten_IDR_cyl`, `single_IDR_box_eq` |
| `residues_CALVADOS3.csv` | Folded domains (MEGABASE-style), CALVADOS 3 | `single_MDP`, `slab_MDP`, `slab_IDR_MDP`, `two_IDR_MDP`, `custom_restraints` |
| `residues_pCALVADOS2.csv` | Phosphorylated residues (SEP, TPO) | `single_pIDR` |
| `residues_C2RNA.csv` | RNA nucleotides | `single_RNA`, `single_dsRNA`, `slab_mixed` |
| `residues_C2PEG.csv` | PEG crowder beads | `slab_IDR_PEG` |

RNA systems activate an additional parameter family directly on `Components` — bond constants (`rna_kb1`, `rna_kb2`), an angle constant (`rna_ka`), a dihedral parameter (`rna_pa`), and nonbonded scaling (`rna_nb_sigma`, `rna_nb_scale`, `rna_nb_cutoff`) — as shown in `single_RNA`. PEG crowders are declared as `molecule_type='crowder'` with `charge_termini='none'` and `ext_restraint=False`, and `slab_IDR_PEG` goes further: a helper function converts a weight/volume PEG concentration into an exact chain count using Avogadro's number and the box volume, so the experimental concentration is reproduced analytically rather than guessed.

The phosphorylation example demonstrates the most sophisticated preparation pattern in the gallery: `single_pIDR` accepts `--pH` on the command line, then *rewrites the residues file in place*, adjusting SEP and TPO charges via Henderson–Hasselbalch-type fractions using `pKa_dict = dict(SEP=6.01, TPO=6.3)`. The input pH flows into both the modified charges and the `Config`'s `pH` field, keeping protonation state and electrostatics consistent.

Sources: [examples/single_RNA/prepare.py](examples/single_RNA/prepare.py#L44-L66), [examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py#L11-L17), [examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR_PEG/prepare.py#L95-L96), [examples/single_pIDR/prepare.py](examples/single_pIDR/prepare.py#L10-L27)

## Restraint, Equilibration, and External-Force Techniques

Beyond plain diffusion, the gallery demonstrates four techniques for keeping folded or structured elements intact — and crucially, restraints are controlled at two levels: global defaults on `Components` and per-molecule overrides in `components.add()`. This two-level scheme is what lets `slab_IDR_MDP` simulate an IDR (no elastic network) alongside a folded MDP domain (elastic network) in one slab.

| Technique | Where Configured | Key Parameters | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| AlphaFold GO restraints | `Components` | `restraint=True`, `pdb_folder`, `restraint_type='go'`, `k_go=15.`, `colabfold` (0 = EBI AFDB, 1–2 = ColabFold PAE format) | `single_AF_CALVADOS` |
| Harmonic AF restraints | `Components` (+ `fdomains`) | `restraint_type='harmonic'`, `k_harmonic=700.`, `use_com=True`, `fdomains=input/domains.yaml` | `custom_restraints`, `slab_MDP` |
| Custom restraint file | `Config` | `custom_restraints=True`, `custom_restraint_type='harmonic'`, `fcustom_restraints=input/cres.txt` | `custom_restraints` |
| External confinement force | `Config` + per-component flag | `ext_force=True`, `ext_force_expr` (OpenMM expression string) | `ten_IDR_cyl` |
| Per-component overrides | `components.add(...)` | e.g. `add(name_1, restraint=False)` vs `add(name_2, ext_restraint=False)` | `slab_IDR_MDP`, `single_dsRNA` |

The external-force example is the gallery's gateway to arbitrary user forces: `ten_IDR_cyl` confines ten chains to a cylinder of radius 3 nm with a single expression — `ext_force_expr = 'step(d-3)*0.5*(d-3)^2; d=periodicdistance(x, y, z, L/2, L/2, z)'` — applied only to components added with `ext_restraint=True`. On the equilibration side, two mechanisms coexist: slab systems use `slab_eq` (chains collapse into the dense phase before production), while `single_IDR_box_eq` demonstrates the MC barostat (`box_eq=True`, `pressure=[0.1, 0, 0]`, `boxscaling_xyz=[False, False, True]`) that scales only the z box dimension toward a target pressure, useful for studying single-chain osmotic properties. Finally, `custom_restraints` shows the optional batch route via a commented-out `Job(envname='calvados-public')` block — the third configuration object in the framework, used for submitting prepared jobs rather than running them locally.

Sources: [examples/single_AF_CALVADOS/prepare.py](examples/single_AF_CALVADOS/prepare.py#L53-L63), [examples/custom_restraints/prepare.py](examples/custom_restraints/prepare.py#L37-L39), [examples/custom_restraints/prepare.py](examples/custom_restraints/prepare.py#L84-L86), [examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py](examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py#L29-L30), [examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py](examples/ten_IDR_cyl/prepare.py#L59-L65), [examples/slab_IDR_MDP/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR_MDP/prepare.py#L95-L96), [examples/single_IDR_box_eq/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR_box_eq/prepare.py#L25-L29)

> [!TIP]
> When reading any example, compare the `Components(...)` constructor (global defaults) against each `components.add(...)` call (per-molecule overrides). This diff tells you instantly which molecules deviate from the default force-field treatment — the entire physical narrative of mixed systems like `slab_IDR_MDP` is encoded in two `add()` lines.

## Built-In Post-Processing and Analysis Notebooks

Because the `analyses` block travels inside `config.yaml`, every example ships with its post-processing recipe attached. Single-chain examples embed lightweight functions — `save_conf_prop` for conformational property distributions in `single_IDR` and `single_pIDR`, and `save_rg` for radius-of-gyration time series in `single_IDR_box_eq`. Multi-chain examples layer on `calc_com_traj` (center-of-mass distances between species, keyed by a `chainid_dict`) and `calc_contact_map` (inter-chain contact matrices).

Slab examples use the full `SlabAnalysis` object pipeline: `center()` recenters the trajectory on the dense phase (either `center_target='all'` or, in mixed systems, only on a chosen reference species like `ref_name='A1'`), then `calc_profiles()` and `calc_concentrations()` compute density profiles and phase concentrations, and `plot_density_profiles()` renders them. Multi-species slabs identify each species by chain ranges — for example `slab_mixed` assigns proteins to `ref_chains=(0, 199)` and the 60 RNA chains to `client_chain_list=[(200, 259)]` — and `slab_IDR` documents why replicas matter: the README explicitly recommends independent replicas to estimate sampling error on phase properties. Two examples (`slab_IDR`, `slab_mixed`) additionally include an `example_slab_analysis.ipynb` notebook for interactive exploration of the outputs, making them the natural bridge from batch examples to hands-on analysis.

Sources: [examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L53-L66), [examples/slab_IDR_MDP/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR_MDP/prepare.py#L45-L69), [examples/slab_mixed/prepare.py](examples/slab_mixed/prepare.py#L40-L53), [examples/slab_IDR/README.md](examples/slab_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb)

## Suggested Learning Path Through the Gallery

The gallery is intentionally ordered for cumulative learning, and it pairs naturally with the documentation catalog. A beginner-friendly progression:

1. **Read `single_IDR` first** — it is the minimal template every other example extends, and pair it with the conceptual grounding in [Simulation Workflow Primer](3-simulation-workflow-primer) and the hands-on steps in [Quick Start](2-quick-start).
2. **Add chemistry variation with `single_pIDR` and `single_RNA`** — these show how residue files and molecule types parameterize the force field; the underlying parameter database is detailed in [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database).
3. **Add structure with `single_AF_CALVADOS` and `custom_restraints`** — restraint mechanics and AlphaFold guidance are explained in [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidance), and the `ext_force_expr` technique connects to [Extension & Custom Forces](18-extension-and-custom-forces).
4. **Scale up with `two_IDR` → `ten_IDR_cyl` → `slab_IDR`** — this sequence teaches multi-component bookkeeping (chain indices, per-species overrides) before committing to 100+ chain slab simulations.
5. **Analyze with the notebooks** — run the `example_slab_analysis.ipynb` in `slab_IDR` or `slab_mixed`, then continue to [Slab Phase-Separation Analysis](16-slab-phase-separation-analysis) for the physics behind density profiles and phase concentrations, and [Blocking Error Estimation](17-blocking-error-estimation) for quantifying sampling uncertainty.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Foundation
        S1["single_IDR\ncenter · 1 protein"]
        S2["single_RNA\nrna parameters"]
        S3["single_pIDR\npH-dependent charges"]
    end
    subgraph Structure
        T1["single_AF_CALVADOS\nGO restraints"]
        T2["custom_restraints\ndomains + cres.txt"]
        T3["ten_IDR_cyl\next_force expression"]
    end
    subgraph Condensates
        U1["two_IDR\n2 species contact map"]
        U2["slab_IDR\n100 chains + replicas"]
        U3["slab_mixed\nprotein + RNA"]
        U4["slab_IDR_PEG\ncrowders"]
    end
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> U1 --> U2 --> U3 --> U4
```

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/README.md](examples/single_IDR/README.md#L1-L9), [examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb), [examples/slab_mixed/example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_mixed/example_slab_analysis.ipynb)

## Where to Go Next

The gallery gives you working configurations; the Deep Dive section explains why they work. After running `single_IDR` end-to-end, trace where `Config` and `Components` values are validated and consumed in [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation) and [Component Registry & Molecule Types](9-component-registry-and-molecule-types); then understand the physics those parameters drive in [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions) and [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics). When you are ready to write your own example, start by copying `single_IDR`, change one dimension at a time (box → species → topol → restraints), and let the gallery's per-example diffing discipline keep your configuration honest.


# Architecture Overview



CALVADOS is a Python package for coarse-grained simulations of biomolecular phase separation — proteins, RNA, lipids, and crowders modeled as one-bead-per-residue (or per-monomer) chains driven by the OpenMM engine. This page maps the package's layered architecture: how declarative YAML inputs are validated, how molecular components are constructed from a registry, how the simulation engine assembles OpenMM forces, and how trajectories flow into the analysis stack. All claims below are verified directly against the source tree; deeper physics and component details are deferred to the dedicated Deep Dive pages.

Sources: [calvados/__init__.py](calvados/__init__.py#L1-L19), [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L42)

## Project Structure at a Glance

The package lives entirely under `calvados/` as a flat set of single-responsibility modules, with one nested subpackage (`BLOCKING/`) for statistical error estimation and one data directory (`calvados/data/`) holding residue parameters and batch-job templates. The `__init__.py` deliberately re-exports all eight modules so users can address any subsystem through a single import root, mirroring the flat module layout rather than hiding a deep internal hierarchy.

```
calvados/
├── BLOCKING/          # Block-averaging error estimation (subpackage)
├── analysis.py        # Trajectory analysis toolkit
├── build.py           # Geometry: boxes, grids, PDB/CIF coordinates
├── cfg.py             # Config / Components / Job writers
├── components.py      # Component classes + COMPONENT_REGISTRY
├── data/              # residues.csv, job templates
├── inputmodels.py     # Pydantic validation models
├── interactions.py    # Force-field force constructors
├── sequence.py        # FASTA/PDB sequence I/O, charge assignment
├── sim.py             # Sim engine class + run() entry point
└── utilities.py       # Shared helpers
```

Sources: [calvados/__init__.py](calvados/__init__.py#L1-L19), [calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L11-L25)

## Design Principles: Declarative Inputs, Validated Everywhere

The architecture's first principle is that **everything the user writes is declarative data, not code**. Simulation settings and molecule definitions are expressed as keyword arguments, validated by Pydantic models in `inputmodels.py`, and serialized to YAML. The `ComponentInput` model is configured with `extra="forbid"`, so a misspelled key fails immediately at preparation time rather than silently at runtime; cross-field validators enforce invariants such as "a FASTA must be supplied unless restraints are used" and "Go restraints are invalid for RNA."

Sources: [calvados/inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L39-L48), [calvados/inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L91-L119)

The three configuration writers in `cfg.py` — `Config`, `Components`, and `Job` — form the user-facing preparation API. `Config` validates against `SimulationInput` and writes both `config.yaml` and a generated `run.py` script; `Components` merges shared defaults with per-component overrides before writing `components.yaml`; `Job` renders packaged Jinja templates (`calvados/data/templates`) into PBS or SLURM submission scripts. This trio cleanly separates *what to simulate* from *how to execute it*.

| Class | Validates against | Emits | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Config` | `SimulationInput` | `config.yaml` + `run.py` | Simulation settings and runner script |
| `Components` | `ComponentInput` | `components.yaml` | Defaults + per-molecule overrides |
| `Job` | `JobInput` | `job.sh` (Jinja-rendered) | PBS/SLURM batch submission |

Sources: [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L37-L84), [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L88-L134), [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L138-L183)

> [!TIP]
> The generated `run.py` is not a static template — `Config.write()` accepts an `analyses` string that is appended verbatim to the runner, so each example bakes its post-processing calls (e.g., `save_conf_prop`) directly into the executable pipeline.

Sources: [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L63-L84), [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L49-L56)

## The Layered Architecture

The modules form a strict dependency hierarchy: a validation foundation, a preparation layer above it, and a simulation core that consumes both. Higher layers depend only on modules below them — for instance, `components.py` imports from `build`, `interactions`, `sequence`, and `inputmodels`, while `sim.py` orchestrates all of them through the registry. The analysis stack is a peer of the simulation core: it reads trajectories produced by `sim` and delegates error statistics to `BLOCKING`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph PREP["Preparation Layer"]
        CFG["cfg.py<br/>Config / Components / Job"]
        IM["inputmodels.py<br/>Pydantic validation"]
    end
    subgraph CORE["Simulation Core"]
        SIM["sim.py<br/>Sim + run()"]
        COMP["components.py<br/>Component classes + registry"]
        SEQ["sequence.py<br/>FASTA / PDB, charges"]
        BLD["build.py<br/>boxes, grids, geometry"]
        INT["interactions.py<br/>force constructors"]
    end
    subgraph POST["Analysis Stack"]
        ANA["analysis.py"]
        BLK["BLOCKING/<br/>error estimation"]
    end
    CFG --> IM
    SIM --> IM
    SIM --> COMP
    SIM --> BLD
    SIM --> INT
    COMP --> SEQ
    COMP --> BLD
    COMP --> INT
    ANA --> BLK
    ANA --> BLD
    SIM -. writes .-> TRJ[".dcd / .log / checkpoint"]
    TRJ -. read .-> ANA
```

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L16-L25), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L15-L20), [calvados/analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L21-L23)

## Module Map

Each module has a sharply bounded responsibility, which makes the codebase navigable by name alone:

| Module | Responsibility | Key symbols |
|---|---|---|
| `cfg.py` | Write validated YAML configs, runner scripts, batch jobs | `Config`, `Components`, `Job` |
| `inputmodels.py` | Pydantic schemas + cross-field validation | `SimulationInput`, `ComponentInput`, `JobInput` |
| `components.py` | Coarse-grained molecule classes and registry | `Component`, `Protein`, `RNA`, `COMPONENT_REGISTRY` |
| `sequence.py` | Sequence I/O, charge assignment, MW calc | `read_fasta`, `seq_from_pdb`, `get_qs` |
| `build.py` | Geometry: box vectors, grids, PDB coordinate extraction | `build_box`, `geometry_from_pdb`, `get_ssdomains` |
| `interactions.py` | OpenMM force constructors for all potentials | `init_ah_interactions`, `init_yu_interactions`, `genParamsDH` |
| `sim.py` | Orchestration: build system, integrate, report, restart | `Sim`, `run()` |
| `analysis.py` | Trajectory processing and observables | `center_traj`, `calc_energy`, `save_conf_prop` |
| `BLOCKING/` | Block-averaging statistical error estimation | `BlockAnalysis`, `blocking`, `blocker` |

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L1005-L1014), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L31-L39), [calvados/interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L117-L137), [calvados/analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L32-L66)

## The Component Registry: One Base Class, Eight Molecule Types

`components.py` implements a template-method pattern. The base `Component` class owns the shared workflow — reading residue parameters from a CSV, extracting sequences from FASTA or PDB/CIF, computing per-bead properties (σ, λ, charge, bond length, MW), and generating harmonic bonds via a `bond_check` hook that subclasses override. `Protein` adds structure-derived harmonic or Go-like restraints; `PTMProtein` extends the sequence with PTM branches and redefines bonding for the branched topology; `Seastar` implements a star (multi-branch) bond topology.

| `molecule_type` key | Class | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `protein` | `Protein` | 1 bead/residue; optional harmonic/Go restraints |
| `rna` | `RNA` | Harmonic restraints only; dedicated bond/angle parameters |
| `lipid` / `cooke_lipid` | `Lipid` | Two lipid models; mutually exclusive in one system |
| `crowder` | `Crowder` | Inert crowding particles |
| `cyclic` | `Cyclic` | Ring topology |
| `seastar` | `Seastar` | Star topology with center-to-branch bonds |
| `ptm_protein` | `PTMProtein` | Protein + post-translational modification branches |

Sources: [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L28-L100), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L948-L1014)

At runtime, `sim.Sim.make_components()` looks each component up in `COMPONENT_REGISTRY` by its `molecule_type` string and instantiates the matching class — the registry, not inheritance, is the dispatch point. This is the package's principal extension seam: adding a new molecule type means writing a `Component` subclass and registering it.

> [!TIP]
> The registry keys are frozen by the `MoleculeType` Literal type alias in `inputmodels.py`, so validation and dispatch stay in lockstep — extending the registry requires updating both `components.py` and `inputmodels.py` in the same change.

Sources: [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L84-L108), [calvados/inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L16-L26)

## The Simulation Engine Pipeline

`sim.py` centers on a single `Sim` class with a two-phase lifecycle, exposed to users through the one-call `run()` function that loads both YAML files, builds, and simulates. Phase one (`build_system`) constructs the MDTraj topology and OpenMM System, generates Debye-Hückel parameters from temperature and ionic strength *before* instantiating components, initializes the Ashbaugh-Hatch and Yukawa nonbonded forces, and places molecules according to the requested topology (`slab`, `grid`, bilayer, etc.) using geometry helpers from `build.py`. Phase two (`simulate`) attaches a Langevin integrator (0.01 ps timestep), DCD and StateData reporters, and either runs to a fixed step count in checkpointed batches or for wall-clock time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["run()<br/>load YAML"] --> B["validate_inputs<br/>Pydantic check"]
    B --> C["build_system()"]
    C --> C1["genParamsDH<br/>eps_yu, k_yu"]
    C1 --> C2["make_components<br/>registry dispatch"]
    C2 --> C3["init nonbonded<br/>AH + Yukawa forces"]
    C3 --> C4["place molecules<br/>slab / grid / bilayer"]
    C4 --> D["simulate()"]
    D --> D1["LangevinIntegrator<br/>0.01 ps"]
    D1 --> D2["DCD + log reporters"]
    D2 --> D3["checkpoint loop<br/>or runForClockTime"]
```

Sources: [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L157-L208), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L798-L857), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L887)

Restart handling is a first-class architectural concern: the engine supports `pdb`/`cif` structure restarts (verified to exist at init) and OpenMM checkpoint restarts, with equilibration flags (`slab_eq`, `box_eq`, `bilayer_eq`) automatically suppressed when resuming from a checkpoint. Checkpoints are saved every 30 minutes under clock-time runs and after every batch under step-count runs, so long phase-separation trajectories are always resumable.

Sources: [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L59-L83), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L845-L857)

## File Artifacts: The Preparation-to-Execution Contract

The architecture communicates between preparation and execution purely through files in the job directory. This is what allows `prepare.py` to run on a laptop while `run.py` executes on an HPC node via the `Job`-rendered submission script.

| Artifact | Producer | Consumer | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `config.yaml` | `Config.write()` | `sim.run()` | Validated simulation settings |
| `components.yaml` | `Components.write()` | `sim.run()` | Defaults + per-molecule definitions |
| `run.py` | `Config.write()` | Batch system | `sim.run()` call + appended analyses |
| `job.sh` | `Job.write()` | `sbatch`/`qsub` | Rendered PBS/SLURM script |
| `bonds_<name>.txt` | `Component.write_bonds()` | Inspection | 1-based bond records |
| `<sysname>.dcd` / `.log` | `simulate()` | `analysis.py` | Trajectory frames, thermodynamic log |
| `restart.chk` / `checkpoint.pdb|.cif` | `simulate()` | Restart / analysis | OpenMM checkpoint, final structures |

Sources: [calvados/cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L50-L61), [calvados/components.py](calvados/components.py#L172-L177), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L824-L869)

## Analysis Stack and Force-Field Separation

The analysis module is deliberately decoupled from simulation: it operates on trajectory files (DCD) through MDAnalysis and mdtraj rather than OpenMM objects, and includes a numba-JIT reimplementation of the Ashbaugh-Hatch and Yukawa pairwise energies (`calc_energy`) for per-frame energy decomposition. Statistical rigor is delegated to the `BLOCKING` subpackage — `analysis.py` imports `BlockAnalysis` from it, and the underlying `blocking()` function performs block averaging to estimate standard errors with their own uncertainty.

Sources: [calvados/analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L21-L23), [calvados/analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L68-L80), [calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L52-L79)

Within the simulation core, force-field code is isolated in `interactions.py` as pure constructors: each function returns an OpenMM force object (e.g., `init_ah_interactions` returns a `CustomNonbondedForce` in force group 0, `init_yu_interactions` a shifted Yukawa force in group 1) without touching positions or the system. Physical constants and the Debye-Hückel parameter derivation (`genParamsDH` — Bjerrum length, Yukawa prefactor, and inverse Debye length from temperature and ionic strength) live in the same module, keeping all potential mathematics in one auditable file while `sim.py` handles only assembly.

Sources: [calvados/interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L15-L52), [calvados/interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L63-L115), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L181-L188)

## Where to Go Next

With the architectural map in place, the Deep Dive sections follow the layering order of the package itself. For the physics inside `interactions.py`, start with [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions) and [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics), then [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database) for the CSV-driven bead parameters consumed by `calc_properties`. For the component layer, [Component Registry & Molecule Types](9-component-registry-and-molecule-types), [Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment](10-sequence-handling-and-charge-assignment), and [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidagement) cover `components.py` and `sequence.py` in depth; for the engine layer, [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation), [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry), and [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing) expand on `inputmodels.py`, `build.py`, and `sim.py`. The analysis side is detailed in [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](15-trajectory-analysis-toolkit), [Slab Phase-Separation Analysis](16-slab-phase-separation-analysis), and [Blocking Error Estimation](17-blocking-error-estimation), while [Extension & Custom Forces](18-extension-and-custom-forces) shows how to grow the registry and force set following the patterns described above.


# Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions



This page documents the Ashbaugh-Hatch (AH) pair potential — the short-range nonbonded interaction that governs both steric repulsion and hydrophobic attraction between coarse-grained beads in CALVADOS. We trace the potential from its OpenMM energy expression, through the residue-level parameterization pipeline (σ and λ values), into the configuration surface that controls its energy scale and cutoff, and finally through the energy-validation harness that guarantees numerical fidelity.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L63-L93), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L13-L17)

## Position in the Force Field Architecture

CALVADOS decomposes nonbonded protein physics into exactly two `CustomNonbondedForce` instances with distinct force groups: **AH** on group 0 and the Yukawa (**YU**) electrostatic force on group 1. The factory `init_nonbonded_interactions` receives `eps_lj`, `cutoff_lj`, `eps_yu`, `k_yu`, `cutoff_yu`, and `fixed_lambda`, then delegates AH construction to `init_ah_interactions` and YU construction to `init_yu_interactions`, naming the forces `'AH'` and `'YU'` for downstream identification. The simulation orchestrator `Sim.build_system` computes Debye-Hückel parameters first (`genParamsDH`), instantiates both forces, and holds them as `self.ah` and `self.yu` before any particles exist. One subtle but critical unit conversion happens upstream: `sim.py` multiplies the configured `eps_lj` by 4.184, converting the kcal/mol input convention into OpenMM's native kJ/mol.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L117-L137), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L173-L188), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L55)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Sources["Parameter Sources"]
        CSV["residues.csv<br/>sigmas, lambdas"]
        CFG["SimulationInput<br/>eps_lj / cutoff_lj / fixed_lambda"]
    end
    subgraph Comp["Component Layer"]
        CP["Component.calc_properties<br/>(calvados/components.py)"]
    end
    subgraph Force["Force Construction"]
        INIT["interactions.init_ah_interactions<br/>(calvados/interactions.py)"]
        CNF["openmm.CustomNonbondedForce<br/>per-particle: s, l, id"]
    end
    SIM["Sim.build_system<br/>(calvados/sim.py)"]
    VAL["Reference HASP<br/>(tests/test_potentials.py)"]
    CSV --> CP
    CP --> CNF
    CFG --> INIT
    SIM --> INIT
    INIT --> CNF
    CNF -. energy validated against .-> VAL
```

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L63-L137), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L70-L100), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L157-L188)

## Mathematical Formulation

The AH potential is a piecewise modification of the Lennard-Jones 12-6 form, expressed as a single OpenMM energy string in `init_ah_interactions`:

```python
energy_expression = (
    f'{eps}*select(step(r-2^(1/6)*s),'
    '4*l*((s/r)^12-(s/r)^6-shift),'
    '4*((s/r)^12-(s/r)^6-l*shift)+(1-l))'
)
```

The `select(step(...), y, z)` construct routes evaluation between two branches. For separations beyond the Lennard-Jones minimum, `r ≥ 2^(1/6)·σ`, the energy is `ε·4λ[(σ/r)^12 − (σ/r)^6 − shift]` — the attractive LJ tail **scaled by λ** and shifted by `shift = (σ/rc)^12 − (σ/rc)^6` so the potential vanishes at the cutoff. Inside the minimum, `r < 2^(1/6)·σ`, the branch becomes `ε·{4[(σ/r)^12 − (σ/r)^6 − λ·shift] + (1−λ)}` — a WCA-type repulsive wall whose `(1−λ)ε` constant term is precisely what makes the two branches continuous at the crossover point (both evaluate to `−λ(1+shift)ε` there). The physical consequence: **λ modulates well depth without altering the contact radius** — monomer excluded volume is preserved regardless of hydrophobicity.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L69-L81), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L14-L17)

| λ_ij regime | Effective form | Physical interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| λ = 0 | Pure WCA wall `4[(σ/r)^12 − (σ/r)^6] + ε` | Good solvent; no attraction, steric wall intact |
| 0 < λ < 1 | Reduced-depth LJ well + raised wall | Partial hydrophobicity; collapse tendency scales with λ |
