| λ = 1 | Fully shifted Lennard-Jones | Unmodified LJ attraction with U(rc) = 0 |

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L69-L78)

The two λ limits also explain the reference implementation in the test suite: `HALR` (attractive branch, no shift), `HASR` (repulsive branch with the `+ε(1−l)` constant), `HA` (the `np.where` crossover at `2^(1/6)·s`), and `HASP` (shift subtracted at rc, zero beyond) compose the identical function in NumPy form.

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L13-L17)

## Pair Mixing Rules and Residue-Level Data

The parameter expression appended to the energy function defines how per-particle values combine into pair values:

```python
parameter_expression = (
    f'; l=select(id1+id2,(id1*id2)*0.5*(l1+l2),{fixed_lambda})'
    f'; shift=(s/{rc})^12-(s/{rc})^6'
    '; s=0.5*(s1+s2)'
)
```

**σ follows the Lorentz–Berthelot arithmetic mean** `s = ½(s₁+s₂)`, and for pairs whose `id` type flags are both nonzero, **λ likewise mixes as the arithmetic mean** `½(λ₁+λ₂)` — exactly the rule the integration test assumes when reconstructing energies (`lambda_ij = 0.5*(l1+l2)` from the residue table). The `select(id1+id2, ...)` routing adds a per-particle type flag `id` as a third per-particle parameter: pairs where `id₁+id₂ = 0` fall back to the configured `fixed_lambda`, and the `id₁·id₂` factor inside the mixing branch drives mixed flagged/unflagged pairs toward λ = 0 attraction. This flag mechanism lets one force object serve chemically distinct particle classes (e.g., solutes versus generic crowd particles) without separate force instances.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L74-L85), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L104-L107)

Per-residue σ and λ originate from a CSV database indexed by one-letter code, loaded at `Component` initialization and mapped onto the sequence in `calc_properties` as NumPy arrays (`self.sigmas`, `self.lambdas`). The same λ values feed a separate derived quantity, `self.alphas = self.lambdas * self.params.alpha`, used outside the AH force. Representative values from the bundled default database illustrate the hydrophobicity ordering that drives IDP collapse behavior:

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L48-L51), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L83-L99), [residues.csv](residues.csv#L1-L21)

| Residue | λ (hydrophobicity) | σ (nm) | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| W (Trp) | 0.9894 | 0.678 | Most hydrophobic; near-full LJ |
| Y (Tyr) | 0.9775 | 0.646 | Aromatic |
| F (Phe) | 0.8672 | 0.636 | Aromatic |
| R (Arg) | 0.7308 | 0.656 | Large σ, moderate λ |
| D (Asp) | 0.0416 | 0.558 | Charged, weakly attractive |
| E (Glu) | 0.0007 | 0.592 | Least attractive (near-WCA) |

Sources: [residues.csv](residues.csv#L1-L21)

## Energy Scale, Cutoff, and Runtime Configuration

Three `SimulationInput` fields control the AH force: `eps_lj` (default 0.2), `cutoff_lj` (default 2.0 nm), and `fixed_lambda` (default 0.0). The constructor validates cutoffs are strictly positive before force creation (`init_nonbonded_interactions` raises `ValueError` otherwise), attaches `CutoffPeriodic` nonbonded method with the cutoff in nanometers, and assigns **force group 0** so AH energies are independently reportable from YU (group 1) energies. Notably, the factory also emits a runtime diagnostic printing the well depth between reference beads of σ = 0.68 nm at the configured cutoff — a convenient cross-check that ε and rc propagated correctly.

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L141-L144), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L79-L93), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L127-L130)

| Configuration parameter | Default | Unit | Effect on AH force |
|---|---|---|---|
| `eps_lj` | 0.2 | kcal/mol | Well depth ε; converted ×4.184 to kJ/mol (→ 0.8368) |
| `cutoff_lj` | 2.0 | nm | Truncation radius; sets the LJ shift reference |
| `fixed_lambda` | 0.0 | dimensionless | λ fallback for pairs with `id₁+id₂ = 0` |

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L141-L144), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L55)

> [!TIP]
> The 4.184 kcal→kJ multiplication in `Sim.__init__` means your YAML `eps_lj` is always specified in kcal/mol, but the diagnostic print in `init_ah_interactions` reports kJ/mol. Grep simulation logs for the "Ashbaugh-Hatch potential between particles" line to confirm the effective well depth (≈0.8368 kJ/mol at defaults) before committing to long production runs.

## Variant: Scaled Bonded AH for Structure-Based Restraints

A second implementation of the same functional form exists as a **bonded** force: `init_scaled_LJ` builds a `CustomBondForce` replicating the piecewise AH expression, but with global parameters `eps` and `rc` instead of baked-in constants, and per-bond parameters `s`, `l`, and `n`. The extra `n` factor multiplies the entire expression, allowing per-pair attenuation by `bondscale` — a sigmoid of AlphaFold-derived PAE distances and B-factors computed during Go-restraint setup (`bondscale = expit(−bscale_width·(scale − bscale_shift))`). Pair assembly in `add_scaled_lj` applies the identical ½(s₁+s₂)/½(λ₁+λ₂) mixing rules, keeping bonded and nonbonded variants numerically consistent. Expression-level equivalence between the two variants is pinned by unit tests comparing the exact OpenMM energy strings.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L178-L194), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L260-L275), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L216-L234), [test_interactions.py](tests/test_interactions.py#L106-L120)

| Property | `init_ah_interactions` (nonbonded) | `init_scaled_LJ` (bonded) |
|---|---|---|
| OpenMM force type | `CustomNonbondedForce` | `CustomBondForce` |
| Energy scale ε | Per-force constant | Global parameter `eps` |
| Cutoff / shift | Per-force cutoff; pair-level shift | Global parameter `rc` |
| σ source | Per-particle `s`, mixed ½(s₁+s₂) | Per-bond `s` |
| λ source | Per-particle `l` + `id`-flag mixing | Per-bond `l`, mixed ½(λ₁+λ₂) |
| Per-pair scaling | — (all non-excluded pairs) | Per-bond `n` (AlphaFold-derived) |
| Scope | All intermolecular/intramolecular pairs | Selected Go-restrained pairs only |

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L63-L93), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L178-L194)

## Exclusions and Boundary Conditions

Both AH and YU forces use `CutoffPeriodic` so pair distances respect the periodic box vectors established in `build_system`. Bonded neighbors are removed from the nonbonded calculation through the exclusion mechanism: `Component.add_bonds` returns an `exclusion_map` explicitly annotated "for ah, yu etc.", and the generic `add_exclusion` helper registers these particle pairs on any `CustomNonbondedForce`, preventing double counting where the `HarmonicBondForce` already acts.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L87-L89), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L292-L297), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L150-L166), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L166-L169)

## The Energy Validation Harness

Numerical correctness of the AH force is enforced by `tests/test_potentials.py`, which runs genuine two-bead OpenMM simulations parametrized over residue pairs (`Y`/`W`, `R`/`W`, `E`/`D`, `E`/`W`, `E`/`R`) in an 8 nm cubic box, then asserts that the logged potential energy matches the NumPy reference `HASP + DHSP` with `rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-8`. The harness independently reconstructs every ingredient: σ and λ as arithmetic means from `residues_CALVADOS2.csv`, the 0.8368 kJ/mol energy scale, the 2 nm AH cutoff, and the Debye-Hückel parameters at 298 K / 0.15 M ionic strength — making this test a true end-to-end contract on the mixing rules, shift convention, and unit conversion simultaneously.

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L23-L33), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L95-L123)

> [!TIP]
> The parametrized pair matrix in `test_ah_dh_potentials` deliberately spans extreme λ contrasts (W↔Y near λ=1, E↔D near λ=0). Any modification to the energy expression, shift convention, or mixing rules should be validated against this full matrix — a single pair would not catch a sign error in the `(1−λ)` continuity constant, which only manifests in mixed-λ regimes.

## Summary and Related Pages

The Ashbaugh-Hatch interaction in CALVADOS is a λ-interpolated, cutoff-shifted LJ 12-6 potential whose per-residue σ and λ values flow from a CSV database through `Component.calc_properties` into per-particle parameters on a single `CustomNonbondedForce`, with arithmetic-mean pair mixing governed by an `id` type flag and a configurable `fixed_lambda` fallback. Its bonded twin (`init_scaled_LJ`) reuses the identical functional form for AlphaFold-scaled Go restraints, and the entire construction is locked to reference physics by an integration-level energy validation suite. For the companion long-range electrostatic force sharing this architecture, continue to [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics); for the provenance and customization of λ/σ residue values, see [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database); for the restraint context of the scaled variant, see [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidance); for the validation methodology in depth, see [Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation); and for adding new nonbonded forms alongside AH, see [Extension & Custom Forces](18-extension-and-custom-forces).


# Debye-Hückel Electrostatics



This page documents the electrostatic interaction model in CALVADOS: the shifted-truncated **Debye-Hückel (Yukawa) potential** that mediates charge effects between coarse-grained beads. It covers the physical parameterization (dielectric model, Bjerrum length, Debye length), the OpenMM force construction, the pH-dependent charge assignment pipeline that feeds the force, and the numerical validation strategy. Material scope is limited to electrostatics; the companion hydrophobic term is covered in [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions).

## Physical Model: The Shifted Yukawa Potential

CALVADOS replaces explicit solvent ions with a **mean-field electrostatic term**: each charged bead interacts pairwise through a screened Coulomb (Yukawa) potential derived from linearizing the Poisson–Boltzmann equation. The implemented form is energy-shifted at the cutoff so the potential decays smoothly to zero:

```
U_YU(r) = ε_yu · q₁q₂ · [ e^(−κr)/r − e^(−κr_c)/r_c ]   for r < r_c
U_YU(r) = 0                                             for r ≥ r_c
```

where `ε_yu = l_B · k_B T` is the Yukawa prefactor, `κ` is the inverse Debye length, and `q₁q₂` is the product of the two bead charges in units of the elementary charge. The shift constant `e^(−κr_c)/r_c` is identical for all pairs, so the potential is **continuous but not force-continuous** at `r_c` — a standard coarse-grained compromise that avoids long-range truncation artifacts in energy reporting.

The functional form and its shifted reference are encoded directly in the test suite's analytical reference, confirming this convention is the contract the implementation must satisfy:

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L95-L115), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L19-L21)

## Electrostatic Parameter Generation: `genParamsDH`

The two global parameters `ε_yu` and `κ` are derived from exactly two user inputs — temperature and ionic strength — through a deterministic physical chain:

1. **Water permittivity** `_calc_relative_permittivity(temp)` evaluates a temperature polynomial for the relative dielectric constant of water: `ε_r(T) = 5321/T + 233.76 − 0.9297·T + 0.1417·10⁻²·T² − 0.8292·10⁻⁶·T³` (T in K).
2. **Bjerrum length** `l_B = e²/(4π·ε₀·ε_r) · N_A·1000 / k_B·T` — the distance at which two unit charges interact at thermal energy, expressed in nm via the ×1000 scaling.
3. **Yukawa prefactor** `ε_yu = l_B · k_B·T`, converted to kJ/mol scale.
4. **Inverse Debye length** `κ = √(8π·l_B·I·N_A/10)` with ionic strength `I` in mol/L; the `N_A/10` factor converts molar concentration to number density in nm⁻³.

Guard clauses enforce physical validity upfront: temperature must be positive and ionic strength non-negative.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L15-L18), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L20-L28), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L31-L52)

**Physical constants embedded in the module:**

| Constant | Value (module-level) | Role in electrostatics |
|---|---|---|
| `GAS_CONSTANT` | 8.3145 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ | Thermal energy `k_B T` |
| `ELEMENTARY_CHARGE` | 1.6021766 × 10⁻¹⁹ C | Charge quantum in `l_B` |
| `VACUUM_PERMITTIVITY` | 8.854188 × 10⁻¹² F·m⁻¹ | Coulomb prefactor denominator |
| `AVOGADRO_CONSTANT` | 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ | Molar → number-density conversion |

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L15-L18)

> [!TIP]
> All electrostatic lengths are computed in **nanometers** and energies in **kJ/mol** by pre-scaling the SI constants (`×1000` in the Bjerrum length, `N_A/10` in the Debye length). The values are then baked into the OpenMM energy expression string as literal numbers — meaning changing temperature or ionic strength requires a **full system rebuild**, not a context parameter update, because `ε_yu` and `κ` are compile-time constants of the custom force, not global parameters.

## OpenMM Force Construction

`init_yu_interactions(eps, k, rc)` materializes the potential as an `openmm.CustomNonbondedForce` with these architectural properties:

- **Energy expression**: `q*{eps}*(exp(-{k}*r)/r-{shift})` with `q=q1*q2` — the pair charge product is a per-particle-parameter combination; `eps`, `k`, and `shift` are formatted literals.
- **Per-particle parameter**: a single dimensionless `q` per bead, set during system assembly.
- **Boundary handling**: `CutoffPeriodic` nonbonded method with cutoff `rc` — electrostatics respect the periodic box without lattice sums, consistent with mean-field screening (beyond `κ⁻¹` the interaction is negligible).
- **Force group 1**: isolates electrostatic energy reporting from the Ashbaugh-Hatch term (group 0), enabling per-component energy diagnostics in logs.

The diagnostic print statement reports `ε_yu · e^(−κr_c)/r_c` — the residual energy between unit charges at the cutoff — as a sanity check of the shift magnitude.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L95-L115), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L117-L137)

**Related electrostatic force variants:**

| Force | OpenMM type | Energy form | Purpose | Force group |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `YU` | `CustomNonbondedForce` | `ε_yu·q₁q₂·(e^(−κr)/r − shift)` | Inter-molecule electrostatics | 1 |
| Scaled `YU` | `CustomBondForce` | `n·q·ε_yu·(e^(−κr)/r − shift)` | Intra-molecule electrostatics for Go-restrained proteins (bond-scale factor `n`) | — |
| Charge-nonpolar | `CustomNonboundForce` variant | `−step(id₁+id₂)·ε·αq²R³/2·(1/r − 1/r_c)` | Lipid–protein attraction mixing charge with hydrophobic exposure | 1 |

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L196-L210), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L277-L290), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L341-L358)

## Charge Assignment Pipeline

The per-particle `q` values originate from sequence analysis, not from the force module. The pipeline runs during `calc_properties`, which is invoked per component with the configuration-level pH:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[residues.csv<br/>column 'q'] --> C[get_qs]
    B[FASTA / PDB sequence] --> C
    D[config pH] --> C
    C -->|flexhis: q_H = 1/&#40;1+10^&#40;pH-6&#41;&#41;| E["qs array<br/>(signed charges)"]
    E --> F["Sim.add_interactions<br/>yu.addParticle&#40;&#91;q&#93;&#41;"]
```

`get_qs` consults the residue parameter table (`residues.csv`, indexed by one-letter code) for static charges, while **flexible histidine** receives a Henderson–Hasselbalch fractional charge with pKa = 6: `q = 1/(1 + 10^(pH − 6))`, making protonation state a continuous function of simulation pH. A numba-jitted fallback `get_qs_fast` hardcodes R/K = +1, E/D/p = −1 for table-free contexts.

Terminal charges are governed by the component-level `charge_termini` option (`none` / `N` / `C` / `both`, default `both`), patched onto the sequence via terminal-charge utilities before the force assembly. This coupling between pH, sequence, and electrostatics is elaborated in [Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment](10-sequence-handling-and-charge-assignment).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L70-L100), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L95-L113), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L116-L130), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L50-L56)

## System Integration: Build Order and Exclusions

Within `Sim.build_system`, electrostatic parameters are generated **before** any component is instantiated, then consumed in a strict ordering:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Config
    participant S as Sim.build_system
    participant I as interactions
    participant K as Component
    C->>S: temp, ionic, cutoff_yu
    S->>I: genParamsDH(temp, ionic)
    I-->>S: eps_yu, k_yu
    S->>I: init_nonbonded_interactions(..., cutoff_yu)
    I-->>S: ah (group 0), yu (group 1)
    S->>K: calc_properties(pH)
    K-->>S: comp.qs
    S->>I: yu.addParticle([q]) per bead
    S->>I: add_exclusion(i, j) for bonded/restrained pairs
```

Two exclusion classes keep electrostatics physically consistent:

- **Bonded neighbors** (consecutive beads along a chain) are excluded from `YU` alongside `AH`, since their separation is governed by harmonic bonds.
- **Restrained pairs** (harmonic or Go restraints, including custom restraints) are excluded from both nonbonded forces, so restraint energy is not double-counted with electrostatics.

For Go-restrained components, an additional scaled Yukawa `CustomBondForce` captures *intra*-molecular electrostatics between restraint-partner beads, modulated by a per-bond scale factor — the intermolecular force alone would otherwise leave these pairs unshielded after exclusion.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L157-L188), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L98-L107), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L493-L501), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L503-L533)

## Configuration Surface

Electrostatics is fully controlled through the declarative configuration layer (validated by `SimulationInput`, see [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation)):

| Parameter | Unit | Effect | Propagates to |
|---|---|---|---|
| `temp` | K | Sets water `ε_r(T)`, `l_B`, `k_B T` | `eps_yu`, `k_yu` |
| `ionic` | mol/L | Sets screening strength | `k_yu` (inverse Debye length) |
| `pH` | — | Sets histidine (and optionally termini) charge states | per-particle `q` |
| `cutoff_yu` | nm | Shift location and interaction range | shift constant, force cutoff |

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L172-L188), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L55-L73), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L50-L56)

## Numerical Validation Strategy

`tests/test_potentials.py` validates the full electrostatic stack end-to-end: it builds two-bead dimers (e.g., `E–R`, `E–D` for attraction/repulsion, `E–W` and `R–W` for charge-neutral controls) at T = 298 K, I = 0.15 M, pH = 7, runs short simulations on the CPU platform, and reconstructs the potential energy purely from the bead–bead distance trajectory. The reference implementation independently re-derives `l_B`, `ε_yu = q₁q₂·l_B·k_BT`, and the Debye length from first constants, then asserts:

```python
assert np.allclose(u, u_calc, rtol=1e-3, atol=1e-8)
```

The test's config does not override `cutoff_yu`, and the reference shift uses `r_c = 4` nm — corroborating that 4 nm is the shipped default cutoff, distinct from the 2 nm Ashbaugh-Hatch cutoff used in the same test. Because the check compares the *logged total potential energy* against an analytical sum of AH + DH terms, it jointly validates the energy expression, the charge assignment, the parameter generation, and the shift convention. The AH reference halves of the same test are detailed in [Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation).

Sources: [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L34-L79), [test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L104-L123)

> [!TIP]
> When debugging electrostatic anomalies, exploit the **force-group separation**: `yu` is group 1, `ah` group 0 — you can query `context.getState(getEnergy=True, groups={1<<1})` on a live context to isolate electrostatic energy without rerunning. The build log's `yu: N particles, M exclusions` line (sim.py) is the fastest integrity check that charge attachment and exclusion counting match your expected molecule topology.

## Suggested Reading Progression

Electrostatics is one leg of the force-field triad. Recommended continuation paths:

- **[Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions)** — the short-range reference term built by the same `init_nonbonded_interactions` call.
- **[Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database)** — where the static per-residue `q` values in `residues.csv` are defined and curated.
- **[Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment](10-sequence-handling-and-charge-assignment)** — deeper treatment of flexible histidine, termini patching, and PTM charges.
- **[Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation)** — the full energy-decomposition test methodology that this page's validation section summarized.

# Residue Parameter Database



The residue parameter database is the bridge between the *alphabet* of a sequence and the *physics* of a simulation. CALVADOS models biomolecules as chains of coarse-grained beads — one bead per amino acid (or two per RNA nucleotide) — so every physical property a bead can possess must be resolvable from a single letter. This page explains the database schema, the shipped parameter variants, the runtime loading path, and exactly how each column feeds the Ashbaugh-Hatch and Debye-Hückel force fields. By the end, you will be able to read, modify, or extend a residue table with full knowledge of the consequences downstream.

## Role in the Architecture: Sequence Alphabet → Bead Physics

From first principles, a one-bead-per-residue force field needs exactly five things per bead type: a size (for excluded volume), a hydrophobicity (for attractive dispersion), a charge (for electrostatics), a mass (for dynamics), and a bond length (for chain connectivity). The residue database packages all five into a flat CSV keyed by the one-letter amino acid code, making the mapping explicit, inspectable, and — critically — *user-replaceable*. Rather than hard-coding parameters in Python, CALVADOS treats the CSV as configuration: swap the file, and you have swapped the effective force field.

The data flow is strictly one-directional: the CSV is read once at component construction time, exploded into per-bead NumPy arrays, and those arrays are then consumed by the OpenMM force objects. Nothing writes back to the database, and no force reads the CSV directly.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph DB["Residue Parameter Database (CSV)"]
        CSV["one | three | MW | lambdas | sigmas | q | bondlength"]
    end
    subgraph CFG["Declarative Input Layer"]
        CY["components.yaml<br/>(fresidues path)"]
        CI["ComponentInput.fresidues<br/>required field"]
    end
    subgraph COMP["Component Construction"]
        RES["self.residues<br/>DataFrame indexed by 'one'"]
        ARR["Per-bead arrays:<br/>sigmas, lambdas, bondlengths, mws"]
        Q["qs: charge state<br/>+ terminal patching"]
    end
    subgraph FF["OpenMM Force Field"]
        AH["AH force: per-particle s, l, id"]
        YU["YU force: per-particle q"]
        HB["HarmonicBondForce: d0"]
    end
    CY --> CI --> RES
    CSV --> RES
    RES --> ARR
    RES --> Q
    ARR --> AH
    ARR --> HB
    Q --> YU
```

The database sits upstream of everything: component classes only translate rows into arrays, and force objects only consume arrays. This clean separation is what makes custom parameter sets a first-class workflow rather than a code fork.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L36-L51), [residues.csv](/residues.csv#L1-L21), [interactions.py](/calvados/interactions.py#L63-L115)

## Database Schema and Parameter Semantics

The canonical protein table ships at the repository root with 20 rows — one per canonical amino acid — and a seven-column header: `one, three, MW, lambdas, sigmas, q, bondlength`. Each column has a precise physical role in the simulation, summarized below.

| Column | Unit | Physical role | Range in shipped table |
|---|---|---|---|
| `one` | — | Join key; one-letter sequence code | `A`–`Y` (20 codes) |
| `three` | — | Three-letter label (documentation only, never joined on) | `ARG`…`PHE` |
| `MW` | g/mol | Bead mass | 57.05 (G) – 186.22 (W) |
| `lambdas` | dimensionless | Hydrophobicity λ for the Ashbaugh-Hatch attractive term | 0.00069 (E) – 0.989 (W) |
| `sigmas` | nm | Lennard-Jones diameter σ for excluded volume | 0.450 (G) – 0.678 (W) |
| `q` | e | Nominal charge for Debye-Hückel electrostatics | −1 (D, E), +1 (K, R), 0 (rest) |
| `bondlength` | nm | Equilibrium bond length d₀ between consecutive beads | 0.38 (uniform) |

A representative sample of rows shows how the table encodes chemistry: glycine is the smallest bead (σ = 0.45) but strongly hydrophobic (λ ≈ 0.71) in this parametrization, while glutamate carries the maximum negative charge with near-zero hydrophobicity (λ ≈ 0.0007). Tryptophan is simultaneously the largest, most massive, and most hydrophobic bead.

| `one` | `three` | `MW` | `lambdas` | `sigmas` | `q` | `bondlength` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `W` | TRP | 186.22 | 0.9894 | 0.678 | 0 | 0.38 |
| `G` | GLY | 57.05 | 0.7059 | 0.450 | 0 | 0.38 |
| `K` | LYS | 128.17 | 0.1790 | 0.636 | 1 | 0.38 |
| `E` | GLU | 129.11 | 0.0007 | 0.592 | −1 | 0.38 |

Note the deliberate asymmetry in the design: `three` is decorative metadata, while `one` is the sole lookup key. The charged residues (K, R, D, E) carry integer ±1 charges in the table, but the effective charge of a bead is not always its table value — pH-dependent histidine and charged termini are patched at construction time, as described below.

Sources: [residues.csv](/residues.csv#L1-L21), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L70-L100)

## Shipped Variants: Protein, Packaged Default, and the C2 RNA Extension

Three parameter files exist in the repository, and their differences are instructive. The root `residues.csv` and the packaged `calvados/data/residues.csv` contain the same 20 protein rows but differ in column order (`one,three,…` vs `three,one,…`) and in numeric precision (root values are rounded to ~12 digits; packaged values carry full precision). Crucially, both load identically because the loader re-indexes on the `one` column by *name*, not position. The RNA variant `residues_C2RNA.csv` keeps all 20 protein rows and appends six additional bead types for the two-beads-per-nucleotide RNA model.

| File | Bead alphabet | Column order | Precision | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `residues.csv` (root) | 20 amino acids | `one` first | rounded | example workflows |
| `calvados/data/residues.csv` | 20 amino acids | `three` first | full | packaged default reference |
| `residues_C2RNA.csv` (tests + example) | 20 amino acids + 6 RNA beads | `three` first | full | C2 two-bead RNA model |

The RNA additions encode a two-bead nucleotide architecture: each nucleotide contributes a negatively charged backbone bead `p` (`RBC`, q = −1, σ = 0.6954 nm, bondlength 0.59 nm) and a hydrophobic base bead (`ADE/a` or `URI/u`, λ = 1.18, bondlength 0.54 nm). The table also defines two phantom-like beads `LPH/B` (MW 100, σ 0.855) and `LPT/Z` (MW 200, σ 0.9) inherited from the published C2 parametrization; they are simply unused unless their letter codes appear in an input sequence.

| Code | `three` | `MW` | `lambdas` | `sigmas` | `q` | `bondlength` | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `r` | RNA | 126.3 | 1.18 | 0.6238 | 0 | 0.54 | generic base bead |
| `a` | ADE | 134.1 | 1.18 | 0.6430 | 0 | 0.54 | adenine base |
| `u` | URI | 111.1 | 1.18 | 0.5958 | 0 | 0.54 | uracil base |
| `p` | RBC | 194.1 | 0.00 | 0.6954 | −1 | 0.59 | charged phosphate/backbone |
| `B` | LPH | 100.0 | 0.4625 | 0.855 | 0 | 0.38 | large phantom bead (defined, not FASTA-driven) |
| `Z` | LPT | 200.0 | 0.9775 | 0.900 | 0 | 0.38 | large phantom bead (defined, not FASTA-driven) |

The example RNA workflow makes the mechanism concrete: its FASTA file contains nothing but the letter `r` repeated 30 times, and the `Components` defaults point `fresidues` at the local `residues_C2RNA.csv`. The table, not the code, decides what a `p` or an `r` *means*.

Sources: [residues.csv](/residues.csv#L1-L21), [calvados/data/residues.csv](/calvados/data/residues.csv#L1-L21), [tests/data/residues_C2RNA.csv](/tests/data/residues_C2RNA.csv#L22-L27), [examples/single_RNA/rna.fasta](/examples/single_RNA/rna.fasta#L1-L3), [examples/single_RNA/prepare.py](/examples/single_RNA/prepare.py#L44-L65)

> [!TIP]
> The loader calls `.set_index("one")`, so the *column order* in your CSV is irrelevant — but the *column names* are contract. Renaming `sigmas` to `sigma` will not fail at load time; it will fail later, as an `AttributeError` when `calc_properties` reads `.sigmas` off the DataFrame rows.

## Runtime Loading Path: From components.yaml to a DataFrame

The database path travels through the declarative configuration layer before any file is read. `fresidues` is a **required** field on the `ComponentInput` Pydantic model — it has no default — which forces every workflow to make its parameter choice explicit. The `Components` builder merges `model_defaults(ComponentInput)` with user-supplied defaults, validates each added component, and serializes the merged dictionary into `components.yaml`. At simulation time, the `Sim` class re-validates that YAML and instantiates components, whose base-class constructor performs the only CSV read in the entire pipeline.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as prepare.py
    participant C as Components (cfg.py)
    participant Y as components.yaml
    participant S as Sim (sim.py)
    participant CT as Component.__init__
    participant DF as pandas DataFrame
    U->>C: Components(fresidues="residues_C2RNA.csv", ...)
    C->>C: merge model_defaults + user defaults
    U->>C: components.add(name="polyR30")
    C->>C: ComponentInput.model_validate(raw)
    C->>Y: write components.yaml
    S->>Y: safe_load + validate_inputs
    S->>CT: Component(name, params)
    CT->>DF: read_csv(params.fresidues).set_index("one")
```

This design has three practical consequences. First, because validation happens in `ComponentInput` before serialization, a missing `fresidues` key fails at *prepare* time with a clear Pydantic error rather than deep inside simulation setup. Second, `fresidues` can be set as a shared default (as the RNA example does) or overridden per component — a mixed protein/RNA system simply uses two different tables in one simulation. Third, the path is resolved relative to the process working directory at *build* time, not YAML-write time, so generated `components.yaml` files embed whatever path string you provided.

Sources: [inputmodels.py](/calvados/inputmodels.py#L39-L58), [cfg.py](/calvados/cfg.py#L88-L134), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L48-L51), [examples/single_RNA/prepare.py](/examples/single_RNA/prepare.py#L49), [sim.py](/calvados/sim.py#L41-L51)

## From Table to Beads: `calc_properties`

The base `Component.calc_properties` method is the translation layer that converts sequence letters into per-bead NumPy arrays. It iterates the sequence once per property, performing a `DataFrame.loc` lookup on the one-letter code for each position: `sigmas`, `lambdas`, `bondlengths`, and `mws` are extracted positionally, and `alphas` is derived — not stored — as `lambdas * alpha` where `alpha` is the component-level scaling parameter (default 0.0, meaning fully water-like beads unless you opt in to hydrophobic attraction). Charges are handled by `get_qs` with the component's residue table passed in.

The charge path deserves special attention because it is the one place where the table is *conditionally* consulted. `get_qs` honors `flexhis=True` by overriding the table for histidine with a pH-dependent protonation fraction q = 1/(1 + 10^(pH−6)), taken from the simulation-level `pH` setting. For every other residue, the table's `q` column is used verbatim.

| Residue context | Charge source | Applied value |
|---|---|---|
| Any residue except H | table `q` column | −1 / 0 / +1 |
| `H` with `flexhis=True` | Henderson-Hasselbalch form | 1/(1 + 10^(pH−6)) |
| N-/C-termini (`charge_termini`) | `patch_terminal_qs` / `patch_terminal_mws` | ±1 charge and MW deltas added |

The `Protein` subclass then layers terminal chemistry on top: after the base lookup, it calls `patch_terminal_qs` and `patch_terminal_mws` to add end-group charges and masses according to the component's `charge_termini` setting (`none`, `N`, `C`, or `both`). This means the table defines *interior* residue physics while terminal corrections live in code — a separation you must remember when authoring custom tables with nonstandard termini.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L70-L100), [sequence.py](/calvados/sequence.py#L95-L113), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L236-L267)

> [!TIP]
> When `flexhis=True` (the standard path for proteins built through `calc_properties`), the `q` value in the HIS row of the table is never used — the pH formula always wins. The HIS table charge only takes effect through the table-driven `get_qs` branch when flexibility is disabled, or via the table-free `get_qs_fast` shortcut used in other modules.

## Force Field Integration: Which Column Feeds Which Force

Each database column maps to exactly one OpenMM force construct. The Ashbaugh-Hatch force is a `CustomNonbondedForce` declaring three per-particle parameters — `s` (σ), `l` (λ), and `id` (a regularity flag) — with arithmetic mixing rules baked into its expression: pairwise σ is the arithmetic mean `s = 0.5·(s₁+s₂)`, and pairwise λ averages as `0.5·(l₁+l₂)` for regular particles, while particles flagged `id = 0` (crowders) fall back to a fixed λ passed at force initialization. The Yukawa (Debye-Hückel) force declares a single per-particle `q` and evaluates products `q₁·q₂` scaled by the salt- and temperature-dependent prefactors computed by `genParamsDH`.

| Database column | Becomes | Consumed by | Mixing rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sigmas` → bead array | AH per-particle `s` | `init_ah_interactions` | arithmetic mean of pair |
| `lambdas` × `alpha` → `alphas` | AH per-particle `l` | `init_ah_interactions` | arithmetic mean (id = 1); `fixed_lambda` otherwise |
| `q` (+ HIS pH formula, termini) | YU per-particle `q` | `init_yu_interactions` | product q₁·q₂ |
| `bondlength` | equilibrium d₀ | `HarmonicBondForce` via `calc_bondlength` | d₀ = 0.5·(blᵢ + blⱼ) |
| `MW` | bead masses | system particle masses | per particle |

The RNA component demonstrates how the same table serves a *different topology* without any schema change. Its `calc_comp_seq` expands the FASTA sequence `rrr…` into a two-bead string `prprpr…`, so `nbeads = 2 × nres`, and every property lookup runs over that expanded sequence. Backbone and phosphate–base bonds take their equilibrium length directly from the per-bead `bondlength` entries, and the neighboring-base pair restraint averages the two bases' λ values — `(λᵢ + λⱼ)/2` — into the bonded Lennard-Jones-like interaction, reusing the table's hydrophobicity column for a *bonded* rather than nonbonded purpose.

Sources: [interactions.py](/calvados/interactions.py#L63-L115), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L83-L99), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L511-L539), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L541-L552), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L660-L676)

## Extending the Database: Custom Residues and PTMs

Because the table is the single source of truth, adding new chemistry is a data problem, not a code problem. The contract is minimal: every one-letter code that can appear in a component's sequence — or in the expanded RNA two-bead string — must exist as a row keyed on `one`, otherwise the `DataFrame.loc` lookup fails at build time. The post-translational modification workflow shows the intended pattern: `PTMProtein.calc_comp_seq` appends the PTM's FASTA record letters onto the protein sequence at each configured `ptm_location`, so the PTM beads are just ordinary rows in your residue table.

A minimal extension recipe:

1. Copy an existing table (start from `calvados/data/residues.csv` for full precision).
2. Append one row per new bead: a fresh one-letter code, a mass, a λ, a σ, a charge, and a bond length.
3. In your FASTA file, place the new codes where the modification belongs (for `PTMProtein`, list the PTM sequence as a separate record named by `ptm_name`).
4. Point `fresidues` at your table via `Components` defaults.

Reasonable invariants to preserve, based on how the columns are consumed: keep `q` within {−1, 0, +1} unless you specifically intend fractional charges (the only fractional charge in the shipped system is the pH-dependent histidine); keep `bondlength` uniform (0.38 nm) for one-bead proteins, since the mixed d₀ = 0.5·(blᵢ + blⱼ) rule assumes homogeneous chains; and be aware that a new residue's *terminal* behavior is governed by the code patches, not the table — `patch_terminal_qs`/`patch_terminal_mws` apply fixed terminal deltas regardless of what the table says.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L959-L1003), [inputmodels.py](/calvados/inputmodels.py#L88-L89), [sequence.py](/calvados/sequence.py#L137-L140), [cfg.py](/calvados/cfg.py#L107-L124)

## Key Takeaways and Reading Progression

The residue parameter database embodies CALVADOS's central design decision: *parameters are data*. One flat CSV, keyed by sequence letter, determines bead sizes, hydrophobicities, charges, masses, and bond lengths for proteins, RNA, lipids, crowders, and PTM-tagged chains alike. The `fresidues` field makes that choice explicit and validated at the configuration layer, and the `set_index("one")` loader makes table authoring forgiving of column order but strict about names and codes. Understanding this table is understanding the effective force field: to predict how a mutation changes your simulation, you look up its row.

To continue exploring:

- How λ and σ enter the dispersion term: [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions)
- How `q` and the DH prefactors produce electrostatics: [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics)
- How components map to molecule types and the registry: [Component Registry & Molecule Types](9-component-registry-and-molecule-types)
- How sequences are read and charges finalized: [Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment](10-sequence-handling-and-charge-assignment)
- How `fresidues` fits the YAML validation pipeline: [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation)
- How parameter changes are caught in tests: [Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation)


# Component Registry & Molecule Types



CALVADOS simulates heterogeneous coarse-grained systems — IDRs, folded proteins, RNA, lipids, crowders — inside a single OpenMM `System`. The mechanism that makes this possible is a deliberately small piece of architecture: a **type-keyed registry** (`COMPONENT_REGISTRY`) that maps declarative `molecule_type` strings from `components.yaml` to concrete Python classes in `calvados/components.py`. Each class encapsulates one molecular model: its bead granularity, its bonded topology, its restraint semantics, and its initial-coordinate strategy. This page documents that registry, the class hierarchy behind it, and the lifecycle that turns a YAML stanza into particles and forces. For the broader context of where these objects sit in the runtime, see [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview); for the physics they parameterize, see [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database).

## The Registry: One Dict, Two Sources of Truth

The registry is a module-level dictionary at the very end of `components.py`, typed as `dict[str, type[Component]]`:

```python
COMPONENT_REGISTRY: dict[str, type[Component]] = {
    "protein": Protein,
    "lipid": Lipid,
    "cooke_lipid": Lipid,
    "crowder": Crowder,
    "rna": RNA,
    "cyclic": Cyclic,
    "seastar": Seastar,
    "ptm_protein": PTMProtein,
}
```

Eight molecule types resolve to seven classes, because `"lipid"` and `"cooke_lipid"` deliberately share a single `Lipid` implementation that branches internally on `params.molecule_type` to select its force model. The registry's keys are mirrored by a Pydantic `Literal` type alias, `MoleculeType`, declared in `inputmodels.py` — this is the validation gate that rejects unknown molecule types *before* any class lookup happens:

```python
MoleculeType: TypeAlias = Literal[
    "protein", "rna", "lipid", "cooke_lipid",
    "crowder", "cyclic", "seastar", "ptm_protein",
]
```

The design has a notable property: **the class registry and the validation schema are decoupled but must stay synchronized**. A new entry in `COMPONENT_REGISTRY` without a matching `MoleculeType` literal will pass class lookup conceptually but fail Pydantic validation; the reverse fails at `COMPONENT_REGISTRY[...]` with a `KeyError`. There is no third source of truth — this coupling is intentional to keep the mapping auditable in two readable locations.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L1005-L1014), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L17-L26)

## Class Hierarchy: Template Method Over Subclass Polymorphism

The hierarchy follows a classic **template method** pattern. The `Component` base class fixes the processing pipeline (sequence → per-bead properties → coordinates → bonds → forces), while subclasses override narrow predicates — most importantly `bond_check(i, j)` — to express topology differences. This is why a cyclic peptide and a linear protein differ by eight lines of code rather than a parallel implementation.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Component {
        +comp_setup = "compact"
        +__init__(name, params)
        +calc_comp_seq()
        +calc_properties(pH, eps_lj)
        +calc_x_setup(d, n_per_res)
        +bond_check(i, j)*
        +calc_bondlength(i, j)
        +add_bonds(offset)
        +get_forces()
    }
    class Protein {
        +calc_x_from_pdb()
        +calc_go_scale()
        +add_restraints(offset)
        +init_scaled_nonbonded(...)
    }
    class RNA {
        +comp_setup = "spiral"
        +calc_comp_seq() two-bead seq2
        +add_angles(offset)
        +basebase_check(i, j)
    }
    class Lipid {
        +comp_setup = "linear"
        lipid | cooke_lipid variants
    }
    class Crowder {
        generic linear chain
    }
    class Cyclic {
        closure bond last-to-first
    }
    class Seastar {
        +branch_starts set
        n_ends branches
    }
    class PTMProtein {
        +ptm_locations
        PTM branch bonds
    }
    Component <|-- Protein
    Component <|-- RNA
    Component <|-- Lipid
    Component <|-- Crowder
    Protein <|-- Cyclic
    Protein <|-- Seastar
    Protein <|-- PTMProtein
```

Every subclass also inherits the residue-parameter lookup from the base constructor, which loads a residues CSV (`read_csv(self.params.fresidues).set_index("one")`) keyed by one-letter code. `RNA` reuses this table for its `p`-prefixed two-bead sequence (`pA`, `pG`, …), which is why the RNA residue CSV must contain those composite keys — a direct consequence of the inheritance design.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L28-L52), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L898-L910), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L536-L539)

## Anatomy of the Base Class Pipeline

`Component` defines the lifecycle that `Sim.make_components()` drives. The pipeline stages, all verifiable in the base class:

1. **Sequence resolution** — `calc_comp_seq()` branches on `params.restraint`: if restraints are enabled, the sequence (and multi-chain termini indices) is extracted from a PDB/CIF structure; otherwise it comes from a FASTA record keyed by the component name, with single N- and C-termini at positions `0` and `len(seq)-1`.
2. **Per-bead property vectorization** — `calc_properties()` maps every residue through the loaded CSV to build parallel NumPy arrays: `sigmas`, `lambdas`, `bondlengths`, `mws`, charges `qs` (via `get_qs` with `flexhis=True` and the simulation `pH`), and hydrophobicity scales `alphas = lambdas * alpha`.
3. **Coordinate synthesis** — `calc_x_setup()` dispatches on the class attribute `comp_setup`: `"spiral"` → `build.build_spiral`, `"compact"` → `build.build_compact`, anything else → `build.build_linear`. The attribute defaults to `"compact"` in the base class, is `"spiral"` for RNA (two beads per residue need the arc layout), and `"linear"` for lipids.
4. **Bonded topology** — `bond_check(i, j)` is the base extension point returning `False` (no bonds); `add_bonds(offset)` iterates all pairs, calls the predicate, and registers harmonic bonds into an OpenMM `HarmonicBondForce` at `d0 = 0.5*(bondlengths[i] + bondlengths[j])` with stiffness `params.kb`, accumulating 1-based `bond_pairlist` records for later serialization.
5. **Force export** — `get_forces()` returns the component's force objects, which `Sim` adds to the global system.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L53-L68), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L70-L100), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L113-L137), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L149-L170)

> [!TIP]
> The bond/property computation is deliberately offset-transparent: `add_bonds(offset)` receives the global particle index offset from `Sim`, so each component class is written as if it owns particles `0..nbeads-1`. Any custom subclass must preserve this local-indexing contract — all `i + offset` arithmetic lives inside these methods.

## The Eight Molecule Types Compared

| `molecule_type` | Class | Bead model | `comp_setup` | Bonded topology | Restraints supported | Defining feature |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `protein` | `Protein` | 1 bead/residue | `compact` | chain `j = i+1`, skipping charged termini | harmonic & Go | structure-derived restraints, terminal charge patching |
| `rna` | `RNA` | 2 beads/residue (P + base) | `spiral` | P–P (`j = i+2`), P–base (`j = i+1`), angles `i,i+2,i+4` | harmonic only | `seq2 = "p"+res` composite keys, neighboring-base LJ |
| `lipid` | `Lipid` | 3 beads | `linear` | bonds + harmonic angles (k=1700) | forbidden | bilayer placement via `place_bilayer` |
| `cooke_lipid` | `Lipid` | 3 beads | `linear` | WCA-FENE bonds + FENE-kink bends | forbidden | Cooke force field, mutually exclusive with `lipid` |
| `crowder` | `Crowder` | 1 bead/residue | `compact` | consecutive beads only | forbidden | inert excluded-volume filler |
| `cyclic` | `Cyclic` | 1 bead/residue | inherited | chain + closure bond `(0, nbeads-1)` | harmonic & Go (inherited) | ring closure in `bond_check` |
| `seastar` | `Seastar` | 1 bead/residue | inherited | star: center bead 0 to `branch_starts` | harmonic & Go (inherited) | branch partition via `divmod(n-1, n_ends)` |
| `ptm_protein` | `PTMProtein` | 1 bead/residue + PTM branches | inherited | chain + residue↔PTM branch bonds | harmonic & Go (inherited) | PTM sequences appended at `ptm_locations` |

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L298-L303), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L597-L623), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L793-L797), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L904-L910), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L948-L956), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L985-L1003)

### Protein: the restraint-capable archetype

`Protein` overrides `calc_properties()` to call the base implementation, then patches terminal charges and masses according to `charge_termini` (`none`/`N`/`C`/`both`) via `patch_terminal_qs` and `patch_terminal_mws`. The significant addition is the dual-path geometry: with `restraint=True`, coordinates come from `build.geometry_from_pdb` (PDB or CIF, auto-detected), an intracomponent distance map `dmap` is computed (periodic-aware via `self_distances`), and either `calc_ssdomains()` (harmonic, from a domain file) or `calc_go_scale()` (Go-like, from B-factors × PAE sigmoid products via `expit`) is prepared. Its `calc_bondlength(i, j)` override is the most intricate in the codebase: for Go restraints it blends the default bond length with the structural distance using the `bondscale` sigmoid, with special-casing at `min_scale=0.05` and `cutoff_mix_in_LJYU=0.15`. That last constant drives a *mixed* regime where weakly-restrained pairs additionally receive scaled Lennard-Jones and Yukawa terms (`init_scaled_nonbonded`, `add_scaled_lj`, `add_scaled_yu`) so that contacts are neither ignored nor fully locked — the restraint language itself is documented in [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidance).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L236-L267), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L269-L296), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L328-L387), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L216-L234)

### RNA: two beads per residue, done by string manipulation

`RNA` inherits nothing restraint-specific from `Protein` — it reimplements the property pipeline because its bead count differs from its residue count. The mechanism is compact: `self.seq2 = "".join(f"p{s}" for s in self.seq)`, giving `nbeads = 2 × nres`; even indices are phosphates, odd indices are bases. Three topology predicates encode the polymer physics: `bond_check` (P–P backbone and P–base bonds with distinct stiffnesses `rna_kb1`/`rna_kb2`), `angle_check` (backbone angles over beads `i, i+2, i+4`, equilibrium `rna_pa`, stiffness `rna_ka`), and `basebase_check` (stacking-like LJ between neighboring bases, sigma adjustable by restraint-derived distances). Notably, `RNA.add_bonds()` does double duty — it also registers the neighboring-base `scLJ_rna` bonds — and `RNA.add_angles()` returns exclusions, so both nonbonded exclusion bookkeeping and bonded records flow through the same pair loops. When restraints are enabled, structured domains are mapped from residue space to bead space by doubling (`2*s` and `2*s+1`), and RNA *only* accepts harmonic restraints — the Go path raises immediately.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L416-L510), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L536-L539), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L597-L623), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L639-L704), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L442-L453)

### Lipid: one class, two force-field variants

`Lipid` is the registry's only *parameterized* class: the same object behaves differently depending on `params.molecule_type`. In `"lipid"` mode it builds harmonic bonds (k = 1700 kJ/mol/nm²) plus harmonic angles with a special kinked first angle (`2/3·π`, k = 3.5); in `"cooke_lipid"` mode it uses a WCA-FENE bond (`kfene = 30·3·eps/d²`) plus FENE-anchored bends at `4d` equilibrium (`kbend = 30·eps/d²`). The mutual exclusivity of the two variants is enforced twice — once during input validation (see below) and once in `build_system` — because both share the same lipid pair-interaction force slots (`init_lipid_interactions` with different factors: 1.9 vs 3.0).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L777-L875), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L189-L200)

### Cyclic, Seastar, PTMProtein: topology variants by predicate override

The three `Protein` subclasses demonstrate how little code a topology change costs when the template pipeline is well-factored. `Cyclic` adds one clause to `bond_check`: `(j == nbeads-1) and i == 0` closes the ring. `Seastar` overrides `calc_comp_seq` to compute `branch_starts` — a set of bead indices where branches leave the center bead — by distributing `nbeads-1` branch beads across `n_ends` branches with `divmod` (larger branches absorb the remainder first); its `bond_check` then bonds center→branch-start and within-branch, suppressing chain-continuation across branch boundaries. With `n_ends ≤ 2` it degenerates gracefully to linear `Protein` behavior. `PTMProtein` overrides `calc_comp_seq` to concatenate `len(ptm_locations)` copies of the `ptm_name` FASTA record onto the protein sequence, and its `bond_check` implements three bond kinds — protein chain, protein-residue→PTM-branch attachment (index arithmetic via `nbeads_protein + idx * len(ptm_seq)`), and intra-PTM chain. All three inherit the full restraint machinery unchanged.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L898-L910), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L913-L956), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L959-L1003)

## From YAML Stanza to OpenMM Forces

The registry is consumed in exactly one place, `Sim.make_components()`, but the component objects then participate in four distinct system-assembly stages. The full data flow:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Components.add(name, molecule_type=...)<br/>cfg.py — merge defaults + overrides"] --> B["components.yaml<br/>{defaults: ..., system: {name: overrides}}"]
    B --> C["validate_inputs()<br/>inputmodels.py — ComponentInput.model_validate<br/>per component; cross-component checks"]
    C --> D["Sim.__init__<br/>stores comp_dict"]
    D --> E["make_components()<br/>COMPONENT_REGISTRY[molecule_type] → class<br/>comp.calc_properties(pH, eps_lj)"]
    E --> F{restraint?}
    F -- yes --> G["init_restraint_force()<br/>(+ init_scaled_nonbonded for Go)"]
    F -- no --> H["reorder_components()<br/>solutes before lipids/crowders"]
    G --> H
    H --> I["build_system() per-molecule loop<br/>add_mdtraj_topol · add_particles_system<br/>place_molecule | place_bilayer · add_interactions"]
    I --> J["add_forces_to_system()<br/>global ah/yu + lipid forces<br/>+ per-component comp.get_forces()"]
```

Two structural decisions in this flow deserve attention. First, **reordering**: `reorder_components()` partitions components into `solute_types = ["protein", "rna", "cyclic", "seastar", "ptm_protein"]` and everything else, placing solutes first so that slab/bilayer grids can reserve interior coordinates for solutes and assign lipids/crowders to outer regions — the dispatch between `place_molecule` and `place_bilayer` is again keyed on the raw `molecule_type` string, not on the class. Second, **force aggregation**: each component owns its bonded/restraint `Force` objects (created inside its own `init_*_force` methods), and `add_forces_to_system()` simply concatenates `comp.get_forces()` into the shared `openmm.System` — global nonbonded forces (Ashbaugh-Hatch, Yukawa) are created once by `Sim` and never owned by components. Charge assignment details behind the `qs` arrays are covered in [Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment](10-sequence-handling-and-charge-assignment); how placement geometry works is [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry).

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L84-L108), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L137-L155), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L265-L293), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L306-L336), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L88-L134)

## Validation Guards Around the Registry

`ComponentInput` is a strict Pydantic model (`extra="forbid"` — misspelled keys fail immediately) whose `model_validator` encodes the semantic contracts between molecule types and their required inputs:

| Rule | Condition | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| FASTA required | `restraint=False` and `ffasta is None` | validation error — unrestrained sequences must come from FASTA |
| PTM needs FASTA | `molecule_type="ptm_protein"` without `ffasta` | validation error |
| Structure for restraints | `restraint=True` without `pdb_folder` | validation error |
| Domains for harmonic | `restraint=True`, `restraint_type="harmonic"`, no `fdomains` | validation error |
| No restraints for passive species | restraint requested for `lipid`/`cooke_lipid`/`crowder` | validation error |
| RNA harmonic-only | `molecule_type="rna"` with `restraint_type="go"` | validation error |
| Lipid variant exclusivity | `{"lipid", "cooke_lipid"}` ⊆ system molecule types | rejected in `validate_inputs` |
| Slab crowder placement | slab topology + crowders without `slab_outer` | rejected in `validate_inputs` |

The defaults themselves are worth knowing: `kb = 8033.0` kJ/mol/nm², `charge_termini = "both"`, `alpha = 0.0` (so `alphas = lambdas × 0` unless overridden — hydrophobic scaling is opt-in per component), `k_harmonic = 700.0`, `k_go = 15.0`, and a full `rna_*` parameter family (`rna_kb1`, `rna_kb2`, `rna_ka`, `rna_pa`, `rna_nb_sigma`, `rna_nb_scale`, `rna_nb_cutoff`). The user-facing writer API (`Components` in `cfg.py`) merges `model_defaults(ComponentInput)` with user defaults, validates each `add()` call eagerly, and serializes only *overridden* keys per component — so `components.yaml` stays minimal while remaining fully reproducible. The configuration layer overall is [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation).

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L39-L119), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L270-L327), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L95-L134)

> [!TIP]
> The registry lookup in `make_components()` uses `COMPONENT_REGISTRY[comp_params.molecule_type]` — a bare subscript with no error message of its own. If you register a custom class but forget to extend the `MoleculeType` literal, Pydantic intercepts it first with a clear Literal-validation error; if you extend the literal but forget the registry, you get an opaque `KeyError` at system-build time. Extend the literal first, then the registry.

## Extending the Registry: A Four-Point Contract

Adding a new molecule type touches exactly four locations, in order:

1. **Schema** — extend `MoleculeType` in `inputmodels.py` and add any new fields to `ComponentInput` (this is how `n_ends` for `Seastar` and the `ptm_*` family for `PTMProtein` were added), plus any validator rules the type requires.
2. **Class** — subclass the most specific existing class (`Protein` if restraint machinery is needed, `Component` otherwise) and override only the predicates: `bond_check` for topology, `calc_comp_seq`/`calc_properties` if bead granularity differs, `calc_x_setup` if `comp_setup` doesn't fit.
3. **Registry** — add the mapping to `COMPONENT_REGISTRY`.
4. **Sim dispatch lists** — audit the string-keyed lists in `sim.py`: `solute_types` in `reorder_components()` and the `place_molecule` vs `place_bilayer` branch in `build_system()`. A solute-like type must be appended to `solute_types` or it will be grid-placed as a passive species.

The pattern's trade-offs are visible in this contract. The template-method design makes new chain topologies nearly free (a predicate override), at the cost of several string-keyed dispatch points in `sim.py` that the registry itself does not own — a known coupling surface. Conversely, keeping `lipid`/`cooke_lipid` as one parameterized class rather than two subclasses was a pragmatic choice that avoids duplicated coordinate/bond logic but requires the double exclusivity guard. Both choices are consistent with the codebase's philosophy: validation at the boundary, dispatch by string, physics in the class.

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L17-L89), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L137-L143), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L274-L285), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L1005-L1014)

## Where to Go Next

The registry you've just explored is the spine connecting the surrounding chapters. To understand how the residue CSV values consumed in `calc_properties()` were derived, continue to [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database). For the sequence-to-charge machinery (`get_qs`, `seq_from_pdb`, termini patching) that the base pipeline calls, see [Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment](10-sequence-handling-and-charge-assignment). To go deeper into the Go/harmonic restraint semantics that `Protein` and `RNA` orchestrate, read [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidance). Finally, for how `Sim` assembles the OpenMM `System` after the registry resolves — particles, nonbonded forces, integrator, checkpointing — proceed to [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry) and [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing).

# Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment



In a one-bead-per-residue force field, the sequence *is* the molecular model: bead identities, hydrophobicity parameters, and electrostatic charges are all derived from the letter string itself. This page documents how CALVADOS acquires sequences (from FASTA records or PDB/mmCIF structures), how per-residue charges are assigned (including pH-dependent histidine and phosphorylation semantics), how terminal chemistry is patched onto chains, and how the component layer consumes these primitives to build simulation-ready molecules. The logic concentrates in a single module, `calvados/sequence.py`, with a thin consumption layer in `calvados/components.py`.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L1-L34), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L19-L25)

## Module Architecture at a Glance

`sequence.py` is organized into four labeled internal sections — input/output, analysis, manipulation, and fast kappa — plus a feature-aggregation class. The module is deliberately free of OpenMM dependencies for its core charge math (numba-jitted, nopython), which keeps charge computation vectorizable and testable in isolation; OpenMM is imported only for structure parsing in `seq_from_pdb` and for the Ashbaugh-Hatch integral helpers used by descriptor calculation.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L28-L94), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L242-L339), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L502-L587)

The following diagram shows how raw sequence sources flow through the module's four sections into the component layer. Prerequisite reading: `residues` refers to a pandas `DataFrame` indexed by one-letter code (see [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database)); `qs` refers to the per-residue charge array produced by the functions covered in the next section.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph sources[Sequence Sources]
        FASTA[FASTA file]
        PDB[PDB / mmCIF file]
        CSV[residues DataFrame<br/>column: q]
    end
    subgraph seqmod[calvados/sequence.py]
        IO[Input / Output<br/>read_fasta · seq_from_pdb · write_fasta]
        CHARGE[Analysis<br/>get_qs · get_qs_fast<br/>patch_terminal_qs · patch_terminal_mws]
        DESC[Descriptors<br/>calc_SCD · calc_SHD · calc_kappa_manual<br/>SeqFeatures]
        MANIP[Manipulation<br/>split_seq · shuffle_str<br/>construct_deltamax]
    end
    subgraph comp[calvados/components.py]
        CP[Component.calc_properties<br/>per-bead σ, λ, MW, q arrays]
    end
    FASTA --> IO
    PDB --> IO
    CSV --> CHARGE
    IO --> CHARGE
    CHARGE --> CP
    CHARGE --> DESC
    MANIP --> DESC
    CP -->|qs feed Yukawa / particle charges| OUT[OpenMM system]
```

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L28-L34), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L53-L100), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L365-L374)

## Sequence Ingestion: FASTA and Structure-Derived Sources

A component acquires its sequence through exactly two routes, chosen by whether structure-based restraints are enabled. When `params.restraint` is set, `Component.calc_comp_seq` prefers a `.cif` file over `.pdb` in the configured `pdb_folder` and derives the sequence from the structure; otherwise it reads the FASTA record whose ID matches the component name and assigns a single N-/C-terminal pair spanning the whole chain. This design couples sequence extraction to the restraint workflow so the modeled chain always matches the structural template residue-for-residue.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L53-L68), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L29-L34)

| Function | Input | Returns | Key behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| `read_fasta` | FASTA path | `dict[str, SeqRecord]` keyed by record ID | Biopython `SeqIO` passthrough; components look themselves up by `name` |
| `seq_from_pdb` | PDB/CIF path, `fmt` | sequence (`string`/`list`), `n_termini`, `c_termini` | Converts 3-letter codes via MDAnalysis `convert_aa_code`; unknown codes map to `X` |
| `write_fasta` | records, output path | `None` | Creates file, or appends only records whose ID is not already present |
| `record_from_seq` | sequence, name | `SeqRecord` | Minimal annotation for writing new records |

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L29-L34), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L37-L72), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L75-L89)

The multi-chain handling in `seq_from_pdb` is the foundation of correct charge assignment for assemblies. The parser explicitly does *not* assume residues are numbered from 1; instead it computes each segment's chain boundaries positionally — `n_termini` starts at `0`, each subsequent segment's N-terminus is `previous C-terminus + 1`, and C-termini accumulate segment lengths. A three-letter code that `convert_aa_code` cannot translate (returning `""`) is defensively replaced with the generic `X`. The test suite pins this contract with a hand-written two-chain PDB: a four-residue `AKDE` extract yields `n_termini == [0, 2]` and `c_termini == [1, 3]`.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L37-L72), [test_sequence.py](tests/test_sequence.py#L44-L68)

## The Charge Assignment Core

Charge assignment is dual-path. `get_qs` is the dispatcher: if a residue parameter table is supplied, each residue's charge is looked up as `residues.loc[s].q`; if no table is passed (`residues=None`), control transfers to the numba-jitted `get_qs_fast`, which encodes the CALVADOS standard charge alphabet directly. Both paths return a `(qs, qs_abs)` tuple — signed and absolute charge arrays — because downstream descriptors such as the center of charge operate on magnitudes only.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L95-L134)

| Aspect | `get_qs` (table-driven) | `get_qs_fast` (jitted fast path) |
|---|---|---|
| Charge source | `residues.loc[s].q` column | Hardcoded: `R`,`K` → +1; `E`,`D` → −1 |
| Phosphosite `p` | Whatever the table defines | −1 only when `phos_negative=True` (default) |
| Histidine | Table value unless `flexhis` overrides | Fractional only when `flexhis=True` |
| All other residues | Table values (e.g., neutral in `residues.csv`) | 0.0 |
| Dependency | pandas `DataFrame` | None (pure numba, no Python objects) |
| Primary consumers | `Component.calc_properties`, `SeqFeatures` | Kappa machinery, `check_dmax` |

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L95-L113), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L116-L134), [residues.csv](residues.csv#L1-L21)

The pH-dependent histidine ("flexible histidine") mechanism applies a Henderson–Hasselbalch fractional charge with an implicit pKa of 6: `q = 1 / (1 + 10 ** (pH - 6))`. At pH 6 the histidine carries exactly +0.5; at neutral pH 7 it decays to +0.0909. The identical formula appears in both code paths, keeping fast and table-driven modes physically consistent. The tests verify the full default alphabet on the string `"KRHDEpA"` (histidine neutral, phosphosite `p` −1) and confirm the fractional result at pH 6 via the table-driven path.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L107-L108), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L130-L133), [test_sequence.py](tests/test_sequence.py#L16-L41)

> [!TIP]
> Component-level calls hardcode `flexhis=True` — `Component.calc_properties` invokes `get_qs(..., flexhis=True, pH=pH, ...)` — so simulated histidines *always* receive fractional pH-dependent charges, whereas kappa analysis internally uses `get_qs_fast` with integer-only charges. The same sequence string therefore yields two different charge representations depending on which consumer asks.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L98), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L439-L455)

## Terminal Chemistry: Patching Charges and Masses

Free chain termini carry real chemistry that a residue lookup cannot supply: an extra proton on the N-terminus and an extra hydroxyl oxygen on the C-terminus. `patch_terminal_qs` adds +1.0 to every index listed in `n_termini` and −1.0 to every index in `c_termini`, gated by the `loc` switch (`"none"`, `"N"`, `"C"`, `"both"`). Its mass counterpart `patch_terminal_mws` adds +2 Da (two hydrogens) at N-termini and +16 Da (one oxygen) at C-termini, keeping molecular-weight reporting consistent with the charge model. Both functions copy-then-mutate, so the input arrays are never aliased.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L137-L165)

| `loc` value | N-terminal charge/mass patch | C-terminal charge/mass patch |
|---|---|---|
| `"none"` | none | none |
| `"N"` | `qs += 1`, `mws += 2` | none |
| `"C"` | none | `qs -= 1`, `mws += 16` |
| `"both"` (default) | `qs += 1`, `mws += 2` | `qs -= 1`, `mws += 16` |

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L137-L165)

The multi-chain case is where positional termini bookkeeping pays off: `Protein.calc_properties` patches *all* chain ends of an assembly in one call, using the `n_termini`/`c_termini` lists produced by `seq_from_pdb`, and the `loc` value is user-configurable per component (see [Configuration Touchpoints](#configuration-touchpoints)). The regression test demonstrates exactly this: zero-filled charges patched across both chains of the `AKDE` extract produce `[1.0, -1.0, 1.0, -1.0]`.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L246-L257), [test_sequence.py](tests/test_sequence.py#L61-L68)

## Charge-Derived Descriptors and SeqFeatures

`SeqFeatures` is the aggregation layer that converts a charge array into the physicochemical vocabulary of the IDP literature. Charge-based attributes are computed unconditionally; hydropathy, mass, and Ashbaugh-Hatch attributes are added only when a residue table is supplied; and the scaling-exponent prediction runs only when a serialized `nu_file` model path is provided.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L502-L524)

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class SeqFeatures {
        +str seq
        +FloatArray qs
        +FloatArray qs_abs
        +float charge
        +float fcr
        +float ncpr
        +float scd
        +float shd
        +float mw
        +float ah_ij
        +float kappa
        +float nu_svr
        +__init__(seq, residues, charge_termini, nu_file, ...)
    }
    class get_qs {
        <<dispatch>>
    }
    class patch_terminal_qs {
        charge_termini gate
    }
    class frac_charges {
        fpos / fneg
    }
    class calc_SCD {
        Sawle-Ghosh SCD
    }
    class calc_SHD {
        Zheng et al. SHD
    }
    class calc_kappa_manual {
        delta / delta_max
    }
    SeqFeatures --> get_qs : qs, qs_abs
    SeqFeatures --> patch_terminal_qs : if charge_termini
    SeqFeatures --> frac_charges : fpos, fneg
    SeqFeatures --> calc_SCD : scd
    SeqFeatures --> calc_SHD : shd (needs lambda_map)
    SeqFeatures --> calc_kappa_manual : if nu_file
    get_qs ..> make_ah_intgrl_map : ah_ij (pair integral map)
```

*Reading guide*: solid arrows denote direct calls inside `SeqFeatures.__init__`; `shd`, `mw`, and `ah_ij` exist only when `residues` is provided, while `kappa` and `nu_svr` exist only when `nu_file` is provided — the class degrades gracefully by feature tier.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L526-L561), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L294-L336)

The attribute semantics are best understood as three tiers. The test suite exercises all three tiers on the sequence `"KAFD"` and asserts exact reference values, including `scd == -√3/4` and `shd == 13/24`, which makes the descriptor definitions verifiable from first principles.

| Attribute | Tier | Definition in code |
|---|---|---|
| `charge`, `qs`, `qs_abs` | always | Sum of `qs`; optionally termini-patched first |
| `fpos`, `fneg`, `fcr`, `ncpr` | always | `frac_charges` counts only unit charges (≥1 / ≤−1); `ncpr = charge / N` |
| `scd` | always | Sawle–Ghosh sequence charge decoration, `Σ qᵢqⱼ √(j−i) / N` |
| `rY`, `rF`, `rW`, `faro` | always | Aromatic fractions |
| `mean_lambda`, `shd`, `mw`, `ah_ij` | requires `residues` | Mean hydropathy; pair-weighted SHD (`beta=-1`); table MW; integrated AH energy |
| `kappa`, `nu_svr` | requires `nu_file` | Das–Pappu κ via deltamax search; SVR prediction from `[scd_noflex, shd, kappa, fcr, mean_lambda]` |

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L191-L199), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L202-L239), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L477-L499), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L544-L586), [test_sequence.py](tests/test_sequence.py#L71-L103)

The kappa computation is a small optimization landmark of the module. κ is defined as the observed charge asymmetry Δ divided by the maximum achievable asymmetry Δ_max for the same composition. `split_seq` partitions the sequence into positive, negative, and neutral groups; `construct_deltamax` then dispatches to one of four numba-jitted case routines depending on composition (missing charge sign, no neutrals, ≥18 neutrals — an approximation — or <18 neutrals — exhaustive block placement), and `calc_delta` averages asymmetry over 5- and 6-residue sliding windows, following the original definition. When a sequence carries no charges, `calc_kappa_manual` returns a `-1` sentinel, which `SeqFeatures` normalizes to `0.0`.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L339-L455), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L563-L566)

> [!TIP]
> `calc_kappa_manual` deliberately calls `get_qs_fast(seq, phos_negative=False)`, excluding phosphosite `p` residues from κ. This means κ describes the *unmodified* sequence's charge patterning even when the sequence string contains phosphorylation marks — a semantic subtlety when comparing `kappa` against `qs`-based descriptors such as `scd` in the same `SeqFeatures` instance.

Sources: [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L439-L455)

## From Sequence to Component: Integration Paths

Each registered molecule type reinterprets the same sequence primitives through its own coarse-graining scheme. The base `Component` performs the canonical one-bead-per-residue translation — arrays of `sigmas`, `lambdas`, `bondlengths`, `mws` pulled row-wise from the residue table, then `get_qs` for charges — while subclasses override `calc_comp_seq` or `calc_properties` to reshape the sequence before translation.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L70-L100), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L1005-L1014)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph intake[calc_comp_seq]
        P1[Protein: FASTA record<br/>n_termini=0, c_termini=N-1] 
        P2[Protein w/ restraint:<br/>seq_from_pdb, per-chain termini]
        R1[RNA: FASTA record → seq<br/>seq2 = p + s per nucleotide<br/>termini ×2]
        R2[RNA w/ restraint:<br/>per-residue s/r coded seq]
        T1[PTMProtein: protein seq<br/>+ PTM branches appended]
    end
    subgraph translate[calc_properties]
        T[per-bead lookup:<br/>σ, λ, bondlength, MW]
        Q[get_qs seq or seq2<br/>flexhis=True, pH]
        PT[patch_terminal_qs<br/>patch_terminal_mws]
    end
    P1 --> T
    P2 --> T
    R1 --> T
    R2 --> T
    T1 --> T
    T --> Q
    Q --> PT
    PT --> NB[Nonbonded forces:<br/>charges feed Yukawa terms]
```

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L53-L100), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L236-L257), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L511-L539), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L965-L983)

| Molecule type | Sequence domain | Charge assignment domain | Termini handling |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Protein` / `Crowder` / `Lipid` | one bead per residue | per residue, table `q` | patch via `charge_termini` (Protein only) |
| `RNA` | `seq` (one per nucleotide) + `seq2` (`p`+base, two beads) | per bead of `seq2`, table `q` | termini indices doubled; patch skipped (phosphate bead chemistry lives in the table) |
| `PTMProtein` | protein seq + PTM branch seq(s) appended | per appended bead, table `q` | single terminal pair spanning full extended sequence |
| `Cyclic` / `Seastar` | Protein sequence, topology changed | identical to Protein | inherits `charge_termini` patching |

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L236-L257), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L455-L539), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L965-L983), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L898-L956)

Two integration details deserve attention. First, the **RNA two-bead encoding**: `calc_comp_seq` builds `self.seq2 = "".join(f"p{s}" for s in self.seq)`, so every nucleotide expands into a phosphate bead (`p`) followed by a base bead; `nbeads` is `len(seq2)` (twice the nucleotide count), all property lookups index `seq2`, and each chain's termini map to two bead indices (`2i, 2i+1`). Under restraints, the per-residue letters are instead replaced by `s` (structured) or `r` (unstructured) before expansion, coupling bead identity to the domain map. Phosphate–phosphate and phosphate–base bonding is then derived positionally (`i % 2 == 0`) rather than from the string itself.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L511-L539), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L455-L475), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L597-L607)

Second, **PTMProtein branch composition**: the component reads two records from the same FASTA — the protein under its own `name` and the modification under `ptm_name` — and appends one copy of the PTM sequence per entry in `ptm_locations` (1-based). Its `bond_check` then rebuilds the connectivity: intra-protein `i → i+1` bonds stop one bead early, each PTM branch connects from `ptm_loc - 1` to the position `nbeads_protein + idx * len(ptm_seq)`, and intra-PTM bonds run consecutively except across branch roots. Charges follow automatically because the appended beads are translated by the same residue-table lookup.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L965-L1003)

Once assigned, the `qs` array flows directly into the interaction layer — for example, in Go-restraint mode, pairs with a nonzero charge product `qs[i] * qs[j]` receive scaled Yukawa terms via `interactions.add_scaled_yu(self.qs, ...)` — and into the general electrostatics described in [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics). The chain-topology consequences of termini bookkeeping (bonding never crosses a chain boundary) are covered in [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidance).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L365-L374), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L298-L303)

## Configuration Touchpoints

Sequence and charge behavior is steered by two user-facing knobs declared in the pydantic input model. `charge_termini` accepts exactly `"none"`, `"N"`, `"C"`, or `"both"` (default `"both"`) and is forwarded verbatim as the `loc` argument to `patch_terminal_qs`/`patch_terminal_mws`. The simulation-level `pH` field (non-negative float) is threaded into every `get_qs` call, governing fractional histidine charge.
