Input validation enforces sequence availability up front: a component without restraints *must* provide `ffasta`, and `ptm_protein` components must always provide it — a misdeclared component fails at configuration time, not at build time.

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L39-L98), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L246-L257)

For a worked example of these settings in a real `prepare.py` script, see [Quick Start](2-quick-start); how these validated inputs flow into system assembly is detailed in [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation) and [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry). To go deeper on where the `q`, `lambdas`, and `sigmas` columns come from, continue to [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database), and for how the assigned charges enter the nonbonded force field, see [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics).

# Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance



CALVADOS treats intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) as flexible beads, but many biologically relevant systems contain folded domains whose shape must persist during coarse-grained simulation. This page explains how the framework converts a PDB/mmCIF structure — typically an AlphaFold prediction — into covalent topology adjustments and long-range restraints. Two restraint philosophies are supported: **domain-based harmonic restraints** for single-chain IDP+folded-domain hybrids, and **Go-type restraints gated by AlphaFold confidence signals** (pLDDT and PAE). The logic lives in three modules: `inputmodels.py` (validation), `build.py` (structure parsing), and `components.py` (restraint assembly).

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L198-L234), [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L398-L490), [inputmodels.py](/calvados/inputmodels.py#L39-L119)

## Design Rationale: One Structure, Two Restraint Modes

The restraint system is a deliberate split of responsibilities. A single `restraint: bool` switch on `ComponentInput` changes the entire construction path of a `Protein`: instead of growing coordinates from geometric templates (`compact`, `spiral`, `linear`), the builder reads atomic coordinates, derives the amino-acid sequence from the structure itself, computes an intramolecular distance map, and uses that map to set both bond equilibrium lengths and non-bonded pair restraints. This design means a folded component never needs a FASTA file — the structure is the single source of truth.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L63-L76), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L236-L267), [inputmodels.py](/calvados/inputmodels.py#L91-L98)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph INPUT["Structure Inputs (pdb_folder)"]
        PDB["{name}.pdb or {name}.cif"]
        JSON["{name}.json (PAE matrix)"]
        DOM["domains YAML (fdomains)"]
    end
    subgraph PARSING["build.py parsing layer"]
        GEO["geometry_from_pdb<br/>CA or residue COM coords"]
        BFA["bfac_from_pdb<br/>residue-averaged pLDDT"]
        PAE["load_pae<br/>symmetrized PAE"]
        SSD["get_ssdomains<br/>1-based → 0-based indices"]
    end
    subgraph GATING["Protein confidence gates"]
        SIG["scale = σ_pLDDT × σ_PAE<br/>bondscale = σ(scale)"]
    end
    subgraph FORCES["interactions.py force objects"]
        HB["HarmonicBondForce (backbone)"]
        CS["HarmonicBondForce / CustomBondForce (restraints)"]
        SCLJ["scaled AH bonded force"]
        SCYU["scaled DH bonded force"]
    end
    PDB --> GEO
    PDB --> BFA
    JSON --> PAE
    DOM --> SSD
    GEO --> HB
    BFA --> SIG
    PAE --> SIG
    HB --> CS --> SCLJ --> SCYU
    SSD -.->|"harmonic mode"| CS
    SIG -.->|"go mode"| CS
```

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L310-L334), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L216-L234)

## Configuration Surface

Restraint behavior is controlled entirely through `ComponentInput` fields validated by Pydantic. The validators enforce the dependency graph between inputs: `pdb_folder` is mandatory whenever `restraint=True`, and `fdomains` is additionally required for the harmonic mode. Lipids and crowders reject restraints outright, and RNA accepts only harmonic mode. If `restraint=False`, the validator flips the requirement — a FASTA file becomes mandatory.

| Field | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `restraint` | `False` | Master switch: structure-derived build path |
| `restraint_type` | `"harmonic"` | `"harmonic"` or `"go"` |
| `pdb_folder` | `None` | Directory holding `{name}.pdb`/`.cif` (+ PAE JSON for Go) |
| `fdomains` | `None` | Domain definition file (harmonic mode) |
| `cutoff_restr` | `0.9` nm | Max native distance for a restraint pair |
| `k_harmonic` | `700.0` | Harmonic restraint force constant (kJ/mol/nm²) |
| `k_go` | `15.0` | Base Go restraint force constant |
| `use_com` | `True` | Bead = residue center of mass instead of Cα |
| `colabfold` | `0` | PAE JSON dialect selector (0, 1, 2) |
| `bfac_shift` / `bfac_width` | `0.8` / `50.0` | pLDDT sigmoid gate center and steepness |
| `pae_shift` / `pae_width` | `0.3` nm / `15.0` | PAE sigmoid gate center and steepness |

Sources: [inputmodels.py](/calvados/inputmodels.py#L29-L29), [inputmodels.py](/calvados/inputmodels.py#L60-L76), [inputmodels.py](/calvados/inputmodels.py#L100-L117)

> [!TIP]
> Because `ComponentInput` uses `extra="forbid"`, a misspelled key such as `restraints=True` fails validation at parse time rather than silently disabling restraints — always spell restraint parameters exactly as in the table above.

## Structural Input Resolution

The builder locates structure files through `Component.get_input_structure_file`, which prefers **mmCIF over PDB** when both exist in `pdb_folder`, and raises `FileNotFoundError` when neither is present. The same CIF-priority rule is duplicated independently in `Component.calc_comp_seq` and `RNA.calc_x_from_pdb`, so every consumer of the structure resolves files identically. Coordinates are extracted by `geometry_from_pdb`: the whole structure is centered on its center of mass, each bead is either the Cα position or the residue center of mass (per `use_com`), and all positions are converted from Ångström to nanometers. If the file contains periodic cell dimensions, they are returned alongside positions and later feed the periodic distance map via `calc_dmap`.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L191-L208), [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L310-L334), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L141-L147)

Sequence derivation bypasses FASTA entirely in restraint mode. `seq_from_pdb` reads residue names through MDAnalysis, converts three-letter codes to one-letter (unknown codes become `X`), and — critically — does **not** assume residues are numbered from 1. Instead it walks atom segments and records zero-based terminal indices per chain, which `Protein.calc_properties` later uses to patch terminal charges and masses (`patch_terminal_qs`, `patch_terminal_mws`). This is what makes multi-segment AlphaFold constructs (e.g., multimers in one file) charge-correct without extra configuration.

Sources: [sequence.py](/calvados/sequence.py#L37-L72), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L63-L76), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L246-L257)

## Harmonic Domain Restraints

The harmonic mode is driven by a domain file (`fdomains`) parsed by `build.get_ssdomains`. The default format is YAML: a top-level mapping from component name to a list of domains, each domain being a 1-based inclusive `[start, end]` range or a list of such sub-ranges (useful for discontinuous domains). An alternative DPAM tab-separated format (`uniprot`/`range` columns) is available through the `dpam` flag. All ranges are converted to zero-based residue index lists (`ssdomains`), and the conversion prints the resolved domains for auditability.

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L448-L476), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L210-L214)

Harmonic restraints apply at two structural levels with asymmetric membership tests:

1. **Backbone bonds** (`Protein.calc_bondlength`): consecutive pairs where *either* residue lies in any domain (`check_ssdomain(..., req_both=False)`) adopt their native distance `dmap[i,j]` as equilibrium bond length instead of the default residue-geometry value; inter-domain linkers keep the flexible default. This prevents domain-boundary bonds from stretching a rigid fold.
2. **Long-range restraint pairs** (`Protein.add_restraints`): all pairs with separation ≥ 2, native distance ≤ `cutoff_restr`, and *both* residues inside the *same* domain (`req_both=True`) receive an independent harmonic restraint with constant `k_harmonic`. IDR–IDR and IDR–domain contacts receive no long-range restraint at all.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L269-L303), [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L479-L490), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L328-L387)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["pair i, j (i+2 ≤ j)"] --> B{"dmap i,j > cutoff_restr (0.9 nm)?"}
    B -- yes --> Z["skip"]
    B -- no --> C{"restraint_type?"}
    C -- harmonic --> D{"both i and j in same domain?"}
    D -- no --> Z
    D -- yes --> E["harmonic restraint<br/>k = k_harmonic (700)"]
    C -- go --> F{"scale i,j < min_scale (0.05)?"}
    F -- yes --> Z
    F -- no --> G["Go bond, k = k_go × scale"]
    G --> H{"scale < cutoff_mix_in_LJYU (0.15)?"}
    H -- yes --> I["add scaled AH-LJ bond<br/>+ scaled DH bond if q_i·q_j ≠ 0<br/>weighted by bondscale"]
    H -- no --> J["restraint only"]
```

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L328-L387)

## Go-Type Restraints with AlphaFold Confidence Gating

The Go mode replaces the binary domain logic with a **continuous confidence weighting** composed from two AlphaFold quality signals. First, residue-averaged B-factors (which AlphaFold populates with pLDDT values) are extracted per residue; values above a `confidence` threshold survive, others are zeroed, and the array is normalized to [0,1]. Second, the predicted aligned error (PAE) matrix is loaded from the companion JSON and converted to nanometers. Each signal is passed through a logistic sigmoid (`expit`) whose center and steepness are the `*_shift`/`*_width` parameters: `bfac_sigm` rises with local pLDDT, `pae_sigm` falls with pair PAE. Their element-wise product — using `np.minimum.outer(bfac, bfac)` so a pair's pLDDT score is limited by its worst residue — yields the pairwise restraint scale.

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L398-L410), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L216-L234)

A third, sharper sigmoid of the scale itself produces `bondscale`, which weights the *hybrid* bonded interactions for low-confidence pairs. The two regimes connect at the cutoffs visible in the decision flow above: pairs with `scale < min_scale` (0.05) are left fully flexible; pairs with `scale ≥ cutoff_mix_in_LJYU` (0.15) are treated as pure Go contacts; the band between receives a Go restraint **plus** scaled Ashbaugh-Hatch and Debye-Hückel *bonded* copies whose weights decay with `bondscale`. This hybrid smooths the transition from folded to disordered character instead of imposing a hard boundary.

| Signal | Source | Gate | Meaning at 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| pLDDT (B-factor) | `{name}.pdb`/`.cif` tempfactors | rising sigmoid at `bfac_shift=0.8` | locally well-resolved |
| PAE | `{name}.json` | falling sigmoid at `pae_shift=0.3` nm | pair placement reliable |
| `scale` | product of gates | Go spring scaling `k_go × scale` | confident native contact |
| `bondscale` | σ(scale − 0.1, width 80) | weights scaled LJ/YU bonds | compensating native attraction |

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L216-L234), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L349-L374)

> [!TIP]
> In Go mode, `calc_go_scale` calls `bfac_from_pdb` with `confidence=0.0`, deliberately disabling the default 70-point hard filter — all soft thresholding is delegated to the sigmoid gates. If you write custom gating logic, do not assume B-factors below 70 have been zeroed.

The PAE JSON dialect must match its producer, selected via `colabfold`: `0` expects the AlphaFold database/EBI layout (`data[0]["predicted_aligned_error"]`), `1` the ColabFold key without list nesting, and `2` the modern `"pae"` key. The loader symmetrizes the matrix (`0.5 × (P + Pᵀ)`), so asymmetric input is tolerated. A related helper, `load_pae_inv`, returns a thresholded inverse PAE for other analyses but is not part of the restraint path.

Sources: [build.py](/calvados/build.py#L413-L445), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L227-L231)

## Force Internals and Bookkeeping

Both restraint modes terminate in dedicated per-component force objects initialized by `interactions.init_restraints`. Harmonic mode reuses OpenMM's `HarmonicBondForce` with equilibrium distance `dmap[i,j]` and constant `k_harmonic`. Go mode constructs a `CustomBondForce` with the classic 10–12 potential `k*(5(s/r)^12 − 6(s/r)^10)`, storing per-bond parameters `s` (native distance) and `k` (scaled force constant). Every added restraint and bond is recorded in one-based pair lists (`restr_pairlist`, `bond_pairlist`) — one-based because that matches residue numbering in output files and user-facing tools.

Sources: [interactions.py](/calvados/interactions.py#L161-L176), [interactions.py](/calvados/interactions.py#L237-L258), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L305-L313)

`Protein.add_restraints` returns an `exclusion_map` of restrained/bonded pairs. Because these pairs now carry explicit bonded interactions, they must be **excluded** from the global Ashbaugh-Hatch and Yukawa `CustomNonbondedForce` objects (commented in source as "for ah, yu etc.") during system assembly — `interactions.add_exclusion` is the corresponding utility, and the assembly orchestration itself is covered in [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry) and [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing). `Protein.get_forces` finally aggregates the bonded force plus, for Go mode, the two scaled-bond forces into the component's force inventory.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L328-L336), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L407-L413), [interactions.py](/calvados/interactions.py#L292-L297)

Every restraint run leaves auditable artifacts next to the simulation inputs, which makes energy validation and restraint inspection possible without re-running the build:

| Artifact | Contents | Mode |
|---|---|---|
| `bonds_{name}.txt` | pair, bond-force index, d₀ [nm], k | always (structure-derived in restraint mode) |
| `restr_{name}.txt` | pair, d₀ [nm], force constant | harmonic & go |
| `scaled_LJ_{name}.txt` | pair, σ, λ, `bondscale[i,j]` | go only |
| `scaled_YU_{name}.txt` | pair, `bondscale[i,j]` | go only |

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L150-L158), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L389-L405)

## RNA Extension: Two-Bead Domain Mapping

RNA components carry two beads per residue (phosphate `p` + nucleobase), so domain logic needs a translation layer. `RNA.calc_ssdomains` expands each zero-based residue index `s` into bead indices `2s` and `2s+1`. Beyond bonds, three RNA structural properties are swapped to structure-derived values inside domains (`req_both=False`): bond equilibrium lengths come from `dmap`, the neighboring-base σ is derived as `dmap/(2^(1/6))`, and backbone angles are computed geometrically by `calc_angmap` from the input coordinates. When restraint mode is on, `RNA.calc_comp_seq` even derives a synthetic one-bead sequence typing each residue as `s` (structured) or `r` (RNA/disordered) based on domain membership — demonstrating that the restraint subsystem can override the entire input model, not just coordinates.

Sources: [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L416-L453), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L511-L565), [components.py](/calvados/components.py#L567-L595)

## Worked Example: `single_AF_CALVADOS`

The reference Go-mode workflow in `examples/single_AF_CALVADOS` shows the minimal configuration surface. The example simulates AF-P00698 (HEWL) as a single copy in a 50 nm cubic box: the component is declared with `restraint = True`, `restraint_type = 'go'`, `pdb_folder` pointing at `input/`, `colabfold = 0` (EBI AlphaFold PAE dialect), `k_go = 15.0`, and `use_com = True`. The `input/` folder ships the PAE JSON (`AF-P00698.json`); the PDB/mmCIF named after the component must sit in the same folder, since `components.add(name=...)` triggers file resolution and sequence extraction at build time. For the harmonic-mode counterpart — full-length A1 with folded-domain residue ranges — see `examples/custom_restraints`, and note that its *simulation-level* `custom_restraints` feature (user-supplied restraint files on `SimulationInput`) is a separate mechanism documented in [Extension & Custom Forces](18-extension-and-custom-forces).

Sources: [examples/single_AF_CALVADOS/prepare.py](/examples/single_AF_CALVADOS/prepare.py#L30-L68), [examples/single_AF_CALVADOS/README.md](/examples/single_AF_CALVADOS/README.md#L1-L9), [examples/custom_restraints/README.md](/examples/custom_restraints/README.md#L1-L9)

## Relation to the Wider System

Structure-based restraints sit at the intersection of several other subsystems: the `kb` backbone spring and residue `bondlength` values it modifies are defined in the residue database covered by [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database); the scaled AH and DH forces it instantiates are bonded replicas of the potentials described in [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions) and [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics); and `Protein` is one member of the molecule-type hierarchy introduced in [Component Registry & Molecule Types](9-component-registry-and-molecule-types). To observe the resulting restraint geometry in a simulation, proceed to [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry), and to validate that restrained structures keep their native distances during dynamics, see [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](15-trajectory-analysis-toolkit).


# Declarative Configuration & Validation



CALVADOS separates *what* a simulation is from *how* it runs. Instead of hand-editing fragile scripts, you declare simulation settings, molecular components, and cluster job parameters as keyword arguments in a `prepare.py` script; the library validates them against strict Pydantic schemas and serializes them to portable YAML artifacts. This page explains that declarative pipeline end-to-end: the facade classes in `calvados/cfg.py`, the validation models in `calvados/inputmodels.py`, the cross-field consistency rules, and how the same schemas re-validate YAML at execution time inside `calvados/sim.py`. It covers the configuration contract only — how validated settings drive OpenMM system construction is deferred to [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry).

## The Three-Layer Validation Architecture

The configuration system follows a deliberate three-layer design. Layer one is the **authoring facade** (`cfg.py`), which accepts keyword arguments and delegates all validation. Layer two is the **schema layer** (`inputmodels.py`), where three Pydantic models — `SimulationInput`, `ComponentInput`, and `JobInput` — define every permitted field, its type, its default, and the cross-field invariants. Layer three is **runtime re-validation**: the generated `run.py` script calls `sim.run()`, which reloads the YAML files from disk and passes them through `validate_inputs()` before any OpenMM object is constructed. The consequence is that a simulation can never start from unvalidated state, whether the YAML was produced by the facade or edited by hand.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph L1["Layer 1 · Authoring facade (cfg.py)"]
        C["Config&#40;**params&#41;"]
        CO["Components&#40;**defaults&#41;<br/>.add&#40;name, **overrides&#41;"]
        J["Job&#40;**settings&#41;"]
    end
    subgraph L2["Layer 2 · Schemas (inputmodels.py)"]
        SI["SimulationInput"]
        CI["ComponentInput"]
        JI["JobInput"]
    end
    subgraph L3["Layer 3 · Runtime (sim.py)"]
        VI["validate_inputs&#40;&#41;"]
        S["Sim → OpenMM"]
    end
    C --> SI
    CO --> CI
    J --> JI
    SI -->|"config.yaml"| Y[(YAML artifacts)]
    CI -->|"components.yaml"| Y
    JI -->|"Jinja render"| RS["run.py + job.sh"]
    Y --> R["run.py → sim.run&#40;&#41;"]
    RS --> R
    R --> VI
    VI --> S
```

Each facade constructor performs validation *immediately* in `__init__` — there is no deferred or lazy checking. `Config.__init__` calls `SimulationInput.model_validate(params)` and stores the JSON-mode dump (`cfg.py` L45–48); `Job.__init__` does the same with `JobInput` (`cfg.py` L146–151); `Components` validates eagerly per-component inside `add()` (`cfg.py` L107–118). At execution time, `Sim.__init__` invokes the exact same schemas through `validate_inputs` (`sim.py` L51), closing the loop.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L37-L61), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L88-L134), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L138-L182), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L270-L328), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L41-L82)

## The Facade Trio: Config, Components, Job

The public API surface for configuration is intentionally small — three classes, each paired with one schema, each producing one artifact. `Config` writes `config.yaml` plus a generated `run.py` runner; `Components` writes `components.yaml` describing the molecular contents; `Job` renders a cluster submission script from packaged Jinja templates. A typical `prepare.py` (as in every example under `examples/`) instantiates all three, calls `write()` on each, and the resulting directory is self-contained and reproducible.

| Facade class | Backing schema | Primary artifact | Companion output | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Config` | `SimulationInput` | `config.yaml` | `run.py` (runner + optional analysis code) | [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L37-L84) |
| `Components` | `ComponentInput` | `components.yaml` | — | [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L88-L134) |
| `Job` | `JobInput` | `job.sh` (Jinja-rendered) | submission via `sbatch`/`qsub` | [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L138-L182) |

The generated `run.py` deserves attention because it is the *contract* between preparation and execution: a static script that parses `--path`, `--config`, and `--components` arguments and calls `sim.run(path=..., fconfig=..., fcomponents=...)` (`cfg.py` L63–84). Crucially, `Config.write(path, name, analyses=...)` appends arbitrary Python code after the runner body (`cfg.py` L83–84), which is how examples such as `single_IDR` inject trajectory-analysis calls that execute automatically after the simulation finishes. This mechanism connects the configuration page to the analysis stack documented in [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](15-trajectory-analysis-toolkit).

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L63-L84), [single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L73), [slab_IDR/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L50-L65)

## Typed Field Discipline in the Input Models

The schemas enforce correctness through Pydantic's constrained types and module-level type aliases, all defined at the top of `inputmodels.py`. Four aliases act as closed vocabularies: `MoleculeType` enumerates the eight supported component classes, `RestraintChoices` restricts restraints to `harmonic` or `go`, and `TopolType` restricts initial placement to six geometry presets. Because `molecule_type` is later used as a dispatch key into `COMPONENT_REGISTRY` (`sim.py` L90), the `Literal` alias guarantees the registry lookup can never fail on a misspelled type at configuration time.

| Type alias | Accepted values | Downstream consumer |
|---|---|---|
| `MoleculeType` | `protein`, `rna`, `lipid`, `cooke_lipid`, `crowder`, `cyclic`, `seastar`, `ptm_protein` | `COMPONENT_REGISTRY` dispatch | 
| `RestraintChoices` | `harmonic`, `go` | restraint force construction |
| `TopolType` | `single`, `slab`, `grid`, `center`, `shift_ref_bead`, `random` | box placement (`build.py`) |
| `InputPath` | `PathLike[str] \| str` | file-path fields throughout both schemas |

Field-level constraints catch physical impossibilities before any code runs: box lengths and temperatures must be `PositiveFloat`, molecule counts `NonNegativeInt`, ionic strength `NonNegativeFloat` (`inputmodels.py` L133–136). Both `SimulationInput` and `ComponentInput` set `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` (`inputmodels.py` L48, L131) — unknown keys are hard errors, not silently ignored kwargs. `SimulationInput` marks exactly four fields as required (`box`, `temp`, `ionic`, `pH`); every other field carries a default matching CALVADOS 2 physics parameters, so a minimal declaration of four values yields a fully specified simulation.

> [!TIP]
> `extra="forbid"` converts the most common configuration bug — a typo such as `tempp` instead of `temp` — into an immediate `ValidationError` at declaration time, rather than a silently ignored key discovered hours into a cluster job. The test suite pins this behavior explicitly: `test_config_rejects_unknown_fields` asserts that `tempp=300` raises (`test_cfg.py` L22–30).

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L17-L37), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L39-L89), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L122-L179), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L89-L91), [test_cfg.py](tests/test_cfg.py#L22-L30)

## Component Configuration: Defaults and Shadow Overrides

`Components` implements an inheritance-by-override pattern modeled directly on the YAML file shape it produces. The constructor captures shared defaults (`cfg.py` L95–101); `add(name, **overrides)` merges defaults with overrides into a *complete* raw dict, validates it as a full `ComponentInput`, then stores **only the override keys** under the component name (`cfg.py` L112–124). The written `components.yaml` therefore contains a `defaults` section plus per-component diffs — the same structure `validate_inputs` reconstructs at runtime by re-merging `{**defaults, **overrides, "name": name}` before validation (`inputmodels.py` L302–307). Two helper functions support this: `model_defaults` extracts declared defaults from non-required model fields (`cfg.py` L13–19), and `serialize_fields` re-validates the defaults dict field-by-field through `TypeAdapter` so the YAML output is canonical JSON-compatible Python (`cfg.py` L22–33).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    D["self.defaults<br/>&#40;model_defaults + kwargs&#41;"] -->|"&#42;&#42;merge"| RAW["raw = defaults ⊕ overrides ⊕ name"]
    RAW --> V["ComponentInput.model_validate"]
    V --> DUMP["model_dump&#40;mode='json'&#41;"]
    D --> SER["serialize_fields → canonical defaults"]
    DUMP --> PICK["system[name] = {override keys only}"]
    SER --> W["components.yaml:<br/>defaults + per-component diffs"]
    PICK --> W
    W --> R["Runtime: validate_inputs re-merges<br/>defaults ⊕ overrides per component"]
```

The examples show how economical this makes multi-component systems. In `slab_IDR/prepare.py`, shared defaults (protein type, single molecule, no restraints, both termini charged, residues and FASTA paths) are declared once, and the entire 100-molecule condensate is a single line: `components.add(name=args.name, nmol=100)` (`slab_IDR/prepare.py` L67–79). Validation still applies per-component even under defaults: the test suite demonstrates that adding a component with `nmol=-1` raises `ValidationError` while the previously added component remains intact (`test_cfg.py` L33–49).

> [!TIP]
> The diff-based YAML means `defaults` is the single point of truth for every field not explicitly overridden. Because `validate_inputs` re-merges defaults with overrides at load time, hand-editing one line in the `defaults:` section of `components.yaml` reconfigures *all* components that don't shadow it — a powerful lever, and one to handle deliberately when editing prepared inputs.

Sources: [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L13-L33), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L95-L124), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L295-L307), [slab_IDR/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L67-L82), [test_cfg.py](tests/test_cfg.py#L33-L49)

## Cross-Field Validation Rules

Field types catch *malformed* values; `@model_validator(mode="after")` hooks catch *inconsistent* combinations. `ComponentInput` implements one composite validator with six rules governing input-source compatibility (`inputmodels.py` L91–119). `SimulationInput` implements five separate validators, each owning one physical concern (`inputmodels.py` L181–250). All rules fire at declaration time and again at load time, so hand-edited YAML cannot bypass them.

**`ComponentInput` source-compatibility rules** (validated by the parametrized test at `test_cfg.py` L134–199):

| # | Condition | Requirement | Failure message |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `restraint=False` | `ffasta` must be provided | "ffasta must be provided when restraint is False" |
| 2 | `molecule_type == "ptm_protein"` | `ffasta` must be provided | "ffasta must be provided for ptm_protein components" |
| 3 | `restraint=True` | `pdb_folder` must be provided | "pdb_folder must be provided when restraint is True" |
| 4 | `restraint=True` + harmonic | `fdomains` must be provided | "fdomains must be provided for harmonic restraints" |
| 5 | `restraint=True` + lipid/cooke_lipid/crowder | forbidden entirely | "Restraints cannot be used for lipids or crowders" |
| 6 | `molecule_type == "rna"` + `restraint_type == "go"` | forbidden | "RNA restraints can only be harmonic." |

**`SimulationInput` cross-field validators**:

| Validator | Invariant enforced | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| `validate_simulation_duration` | `steps` XOR `runtime` (never both, never neither — defaults to 100,000,000 steps) | [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L181-L190) |
| `validate_pressure_settings` | `box_eq` XOR `bilayer_eq`; `box_eq` needs a scalable axis; `pressure` required whenever pressure coupling or either equilibration is enabled | [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L192-L208) |
| `validate_external_force_settings` | `slab_eq` and `ext_force` are mutually exclusive | [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L210-L216) |
| `validate_slab_geometry` | slab mode requires `slab_width < box_z`; `slab_outer` must satisfy `slab_width/2 ≤ slab_outer < box_z/2` | [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L218-L241) |
| `validate_pressure_coupling` | `pressure_coupling` requires `box_eq` or `bilayer_eq` | [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L243-L250) |

The slab-geometry validator illustrates why schema-level checks matter: it compares configured slab regions against the actual box vector (`self.box[2]`), catching a physically unsound declaration — a slab wider than its box — as a `ValueError` with an actionable message rather than as corrupted trajectory output downstream. The slab example's declaration of `box=[15, 15, 150]` with `slab_width=20` satisfies these invariants (`slab_IDR/prepare.py` L21–42).

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L91-L119), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L181-L250), [test_cfg.py](tests/test_cfg.py#L134-L199), [slab_IDR/prepare.py](examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py#L21-L42)

## System-Level Consistency with validate_inputs

Some invariants span the config and components files and therefore cannot live in either single model. `validate_inputs` is the composite gate (`inputmodels.py` L270–328). It first validates the config, then structurally checks the components mapping itself — rejecting unknown top-level sections other than `defaults`/`system`, non-mapping sections, and non-string component names — before validating each resolved component individually (`inputmodels.py` L277–307). It closes with two cross-file rules: a system may not mix `lipid` and `cooke_lipid` types, and a slab system containing crowders must declare `slab_outer` (`inputmodels.py` L309–325).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["config dict"] --> B["SimulationInput.model_validate"]
    B --> C{"components is Mapping?"}
    C -->|no| ERR1["TypeError"]
    C -->|yes| D{"only 'defaults'<br/>and 'system' sections?"}
    D -->|no| ERR2["ValueError: Unknown sections"]
    D -->|yes| E["merge defaults ⊕ overrides<br/>per component → ComponentInput"]
    E --> F{"lipid + cooke_lipid<br/>both present?"}
    F -->|yes| ERR3["ValueError"]
    F -->|no| G{"slab + crowders<br/>without slab_outer?"}
    G -->|yes| ERR4["ValueError"]
    G -->|no| H["&#40;SimulationInput, dict[str, ComponentInput]&#41;"]
```

This function is also the *runtime* validation entry point. `sim.run()` loads `config.yaml` and `components.yaml` with `yaml.safe_load` and passes the raw mappings straight into `Sim.__init__`, which calls `validate_inputs` as its first act (`sim.py` L871–887, L51). Schema validation and environmental validation are deliberately split: the schema confirms logical consistency, while `Sim.__init__` verifies the filesystem — resolving `frestart` to an absolute path under `path` and raising `FileNotFoundError` if a `pdb`/`cif` restart file is missing (`sim.py` L59–67). It also applies temporal context the schema cannot know, such as disabling slab/box equilibration when a checkpoint already exists (`sim.py` L69–72), and enforcing the topology cardinality rule that `single`/`center` topologies cannot host multiple molecules (`sim.py` L126–130).

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L270-L328), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L41-L82), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L887), [test_cfg.py](tests/test_cfg.py#L85-L131)

## The Job Layer: Rendering Cluster Scripts

The `Job` class completes the declarative contract by handling execution logistics. Its settings are validated by `JobInput` — the smallest schema, with four fields: the Jinja template name, the environment setup file, the Conda environment name, and the batch system (`inputmodels.py` L254–267). Templates are resolved from packaged resources via `importlib.resources` into `calvados/data/templates`, which ships three variants: `robust.jinja` (the default), `computerome.jinja`, and `deic.jinja` (`cfg.py` L146–151). Rendering merges job settings with the *entire validated config dict* plus the config and components filenames, so the submission script inherits every simulation parameter without duplication (`cfg.py` L153–171).

| Setting | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `template` | `"robust.jinja"` | packaged template selected for rendering |
| `fbash` | `~/.bashrc` | shell setup sourced in the job |
| `envname` | `"calvados"` | Conda environment activated |
| `batch_sys` | `SLURM` | `SLURM` or `PBS` submission command |

The test suite verifies the rendered output concretely: after writing config, components, and job into a temp directory, it asserts the resulting `job.sh` contains both `source /tmp/test.bashrc` and `conda activate calvados` (`test_cfg.py` L52–73). `Job.submit()` dispatches `sbatch` or `qsub` in a loop with a 0.5 s pause between submissions, with one asymmetry enforced in code: multi-job submission is supported only for SLURM, and PBS raises `ValueError` when `njobs > 1` (`cfg.py` L173–182).

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L254-L267), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L138-L182), [test_cfg.py](tests/test_cfg.py#L52-L82)

## Validation as a Tested Contract

The schema layer is treated as a contract under test rather than incidental plumbing. `tests/test_cfg.py` covers four behavioral axes: (1) *defaults and serialization* — a four-argument `Config` produces a fully populated dump whose YAML round-trip is byte-equal (`test_cfg.py` L11–19); (2) *fail-fast rejection* — unknown fields raise in both `Config` and `Job` (`test_cfg.py` L22–30, L76–82); (3) *shape preservation* — written `components.yaml` keeps the defaults/diff structure with canonicalized values (`test_cfg.py` L33–49); (4) *composite consistency* — `validate_inputs` resolution, malformed-section errors, and all six `ComponentInput` compatibility rules via parametrized cases (`test_cfg.py` L85–199). Together these tests document the intended failure modes as precisely as the schemas document the accepted inputs — further validation strategy, including energy-conservation checks, is covered in [Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation).

Sources: [test_cfg.py](tests/test_cfg.py#L1-L199)

## Next Steps

With the configuration contract established, the natural progression through the Deep Dive is: how `molecule_type` resolves into concrete component classes in [Component Registry & Molecule Types](9-component-registry-and-molecule-types); how the restraint-related fields validated here (`restraint`, `pdb_folder`, `fdomains`, AlphaFold options) drive structure guidance in [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidance); and how validated settings become an OpenMM system in [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry), then execute with checkpointing in [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing). To see the full declarative workflow in a runnable context, the `examples/single_IDR/prepare.py` and `examples/slab_IDR/prepare.py` files are the canonical starting points.

# System Building & Geometry



Every molecular dynamics trajectory is only as trustworthy as its first frame. In CALVADOS, the *System Building & Geometry* subsystem is responsible for producing that frame: the periodic box vectors, the initial coarse-grained conformations of every chain, their spatial placement relative to walls and to each other, and the bonded bookkeeping that the simulation engine will later consume. This page dissects the geometry toolkit in `calvados/build.py` — a library of stateless NumPy/MDAnalysis functions — and shows how the object-oriented `Component` hierarchy in `calvados/components.py` composes those primitives into a complete system. By the end, you will understand how a slab of IDRs, a membrane bilayer, a two-bead RNA model, or an AlphaFold-guided folded protein each acquire their initial geometry, and how concentration-based stoichiometry closes the loop between experiment and simulation box.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L18-L31), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L28-L52)

## Architectural Role: The Geometry Layer

CALVADOS separates *geometry* (pure functions over NumPy arrays) from *component semantics* (classes that own molecular identity). The `build` module contains no classes and no OpenMM forces — it answers questions like "where should bead *k* of a chain sit?" and "does this molecule clash with its neighbors?" The `components` module then consumes these answers: each `Component` subclass declares a `comp_setup` strategy ("compact", "spiral", or "linear") that `calc_x_setup` dispatches to the corresponding `build` function, then overlays structure-derived coordinates when restraints are requested. This layering means geometry primitives are independently testable and reusable across protein, RNA, and lipid components.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph declarative["Declarative Layer (cfg.py)"]
        CFG["Config / Components YAML"]
    end
    subgraph geometry["Geometry Layer (build.py)"]
        BOX["Box & slab sizing"]
        CHAIN["Chain builders<br/>linear / spiral / compact"]
        PLACE["Placement & clash checks"]
        PDB["PDB / AlphaFold ingestion"]
        STOICH["Concentration stoichiometry"]
    end
    subgraph components_layer["Component Layer (components.py)"]
        COMP["Component base class"]
        PROT["Protein"]
        RNA["RNA (2-bead)"]
        LIP["Lipid (3-bead)"]
    end
    CFG --> COMP
    BOX --> COMP
    CHAIN -->|"calc_x_setup dispatch"| COMP
    PLACE --> COMP
    PDB -->|"restraint path"| PROT
    PDB -->|"restraint path"| RNA
    STOICH -->|"molecule counts"| COMP
    COMP --> PROT
    COMP --> RNA
    COMP --> LIP
```

The diagram above shows the dependency direction: declarative YAML parameters (covered in [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation)) flow into components, which call *into* the geometry layer — never the reverse. This one-way dependency keeps the geometry layer free of component-specific knowledge.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L15-L17), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L16-L26), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L113-L133), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L88-L101)

## Box Vectors and Periodic Geometry

The foundation of every system is the orthogonal simulation box. `build_box` converts three edge lengths in nanometers into OpenMM `unit.Quantity` vectors, deliberately zeroing the off-diagonal elements — CALVADOS constructs only orthorhombic boxes with box vectors aligned to the coordinate axes. For typical slab phase-separation setups, `calc_box` provides conservative defaults chosen by chain length: a 20×20×200 nm box for chains of 350 residues or fewer, expanded to 25×25×300 nm for longer chains. The slab geometry assumes an *area* bead density (`pbeads`, default 90 nm⁻²), so `calc_nprot_slab` computes how many chains of length *N* fill the box cross-section: `int(pbeads · Lx · Ly / N)`.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L21-L44)

Placement correctness is enforced by two validation primitives. `check_walls` rejects any coordinate outside `[0, box]`, while `check_clash` computes the full pairwise distance array via MDAnalysis and rejects molecules whose periodic minimum distance to already-placed content falls below a 0.7 nm cutoff.

> [!TIP]
> Note the box augmentation inside `check_clash`: the three box lengths are padded with `[90, 90, 90]` before calling `distances.distance_array`. MDAnalysis expects the full six-parameter cell (three lengths plus three angles), and hard-coding 90° angles silently documents that all clash detection assumes orthorhombic periodicity — a constraint inherited from `build_box` itself.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L47-L63), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L66-L78)

## Chain Conformation Generators

Before placement, each molecule needs an internal conformation `xinit`. CALVADOS offers three procedural generators, selected per component class via the `comp_setup` class attribute:

| Strategy | Algorithm | Bead spacing | Default user | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `linear` | Cumulative sum of midpoints between consecutive bond lengths along z, centered at origin | Per-residue `bondlength` from residue DB | `Lipid` (`comp_setup = "linear"`) | Extended rod for lipids |
| `compact` | Serpentine traversal of a cubic lattice sized `ceil(∛nbeads)`, with direction flips per row and per layer | Uniform `d` (0.38 nm) | `Component` base | Dense globule; keeps bonded neighbors close to avoid initial clashes |
| `spiral` | Archimedean spiral `r = b·φ` with `b = separation/(2π)`; φ advances by `arc/r` per bead | Arc step 0.38 nm, radial separation 0.7 nm | `RNA` (`comp_setup = "spiral"`) | Space-filling, low-strain start for flexible chains |

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L81-L127), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L130-L160), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L34-L34), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L422-L422), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L783-L783)

The dispatch happens in `Component.calc_x_setup`: `"spiral"` routes to `build_spiral` with the per-residue bond lengths as arc segments, `"compact"` routes to `build_compact`, and any other value falls through to `build_linear`. A defensive check then verifies that the generated coordinate array length equals the bead count. The RNA subclass overrides this method entirely: because its two-bead model interleaves phosphate and base beads (`seq2 = "p" + base` per residue, giving `nbeads = 2 × nres`), it feeds only the phosphate bond lengths (`bondlengths[1::2]`) into the spiral with `arc = 0.59` nm and `n_per_res = 2`, and explicitly forbids the compact arrangement for the two-bead model.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L113-L133), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L511-L539), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L625-L637)

The `compact` generator deserves a closer look, since it is the default for IDRs. Rather than scattering beads randomly — which risks bonded pairs starting at unphysically short distances and exploding under the harmonic bond force — it lays beads on a regular cubic grid in a serpentine (boustrophedon) path, then scales and centers the result by `0.5·N·d`. Bonded neighbors therefore always sit exactly one lattice spacing `d` apart in the first frame.

> [!TIP]
> The spiral builder's Archimedean form `r = b·φ` guarantees constant radial spacing between successive turns (`separation`, default 0.7 nm), not constant arc length. The step size `arc` controls *along-chain* spacing while `separation` controls *between-chain* proximity in the coiled state — so these two parameters tune different physical constraints and should not be confused when adjusting initial conformations.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L108-L127), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L144-L160)

## Molecule Placement Strategies

With conformations in hand, molecules must be positioned in the box. CALVADOS implements four placement strategies, each returning a translated copy of `xinit`:

| Function | Geometry | Clash handling | Typical scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| `random_placement` | Uniform random origin anywhere in the box | Wall check + 0.7 nm clash cutoff, up to 10000 attempts | Bulk/dilute-phase boxes |
| `build_xybilayer` | Centered at `z = box[2]/2 − 1.5` nm; `upward=True` flips the chain and shifts +3 nm | Tighter 0.5 nm cutoff; returns `inserted` flag instead of raising | Lipid bilayers, membrane-interacting slabs |
| `build_xygrid` | 2D lattice at fixed z, `nx = ny = ceil(√N) + padding` cells dividing Lx and Ly | None (deterministic spacing) | Slab interfaces with ordered rows |
| `build_xyzgrid` | Staggered 3D lattice; per-axis cell counts allocated proportionally to box aspect ratio, with half-cell offsets between adjacent planes | None (deterministic spacing) | Dense multi-chain bulk fills |

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L163-L179), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L182-L205), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L208-L234), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L237-L306)

The stochastic path is the one worth tracing, because its failure mode is diagnostic:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["draw_starting_vec:<br/>uniform random origin in box"] --> B["xs = origin + xinit"]
    B --> C{"check_walls:<br/>any coord outside [0, box]?"}
    C -->|Yes| A
    C -->|No| D{"check_clash:<br/>min periodic distance<br/>to others < 0.7 nm?"}
    D -->|Yes| A
    D -->|No| E["Accept placement"]
    A -->|"after 10000 tries<br/>(ntries default)"| F["raise ValueError:<br/>'Tried 10000x to add molecule'"]
```

Three properties of this loop matter operationally. First, `draw_starting_vec` uses `np.random.random(size=3) * box` — placement reproducibility therefore depends on the caller seeding NumPy's global RNG. Second, the clash check is *incremental*: `xs_others` accumulates all previously accepted positions, so later molecules see earlier ones. Third, exhausting 10000 attempts raises rather than silently degrading — which means a `ValueError` from `random_placement` is almost always a signal that the box is too small for the requested number of chains, not a transient numerical issue.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L163-L179), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L66-L78)

The deterministic builders encode domain-specific geometry. `build_xybilayer` is notable for its asymmetric leaflet handling: it re-centers the molecule's z-coordinates on bead index 1 (an anchor bead for the lipid geometry), shifts to the bilayer plane at `box[2]/2 − 1.5` nm, and when `upward=True` reverses the bead order and adds a 3 nm offset to produce the opposing leaflet. `build_xyzgrid` performs a nontrivial allocation: it computes `r = box/sum(box)`, solves `a = ∛(N/∏r)` for a proportional grid, floors it, then repairs the product of cell counts upward on the axis with the largest relative deviation until the lattice can hold all `N` molecules — ensuring the grid respects the box's shape rather than forcing a cube.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L182-L205), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L237-L252)

## Structure-Guided Initial Geometry

When a component carries structural restraints, procedural conformations are replaced by real coordinates parsed from PDB or mmCIF files. `geometry_from_pdb` centers the structure on its center of mass, then extracts either the Cα atom positions or — with `use_com=True` — per-residue center-of-mass positions, converting Ångströms to nanometers (`/10.0`) throughout. It also reads the CRYST1 box dimensions when present, returning them so periodic distance maps can be computed. The RNA variant implements the two-bead mapping geometrically: without `use_com`, each residue contributes a phosphate bead (atom `P`) plus a base bead (`N1` for pyrimidines U/C/T, `N9` for purines A/G — an invalid resname raises immediately); with `use_com`, it averages 19 named backbone atoms and the remaining atoms separately.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L310-L334), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L337-L395), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L424-L440)

The restraint path in `Protein.calc_properties` orchestrates the full geometry extraction: load PDB coordinates via `calc_x_from_pdb`, compute the intramolecular distance map `dmap` (respecting periodic dimensions if the input structure declared a cell), then either load structured domains (`calc_ssdomains`) for harmonic restraints or build the AlphaFold confidence scaling (`calc_go_scale`). The latter combines two per-residue quality signals — residue-averaged pLDDT from B-factors (`bfac_from_pdb`, thresholded and normalized to [0,1]) and the PAE matrix from JSON (supporting three AlphaFold/ColabFold JSON layouts, symmetrized, converted to nm) — through logistic sigmoid filters into a pairwise `scale`, from which `bondscale` is derived. Components without restraints simply fall through to `calc_x_setup`.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L236-L267), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L102-L111), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L216-L234), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L398-L445)

Structure knowledge even reshapes *bonded geometry*. The base `Component.calc_bondlength` returns the mean of the two residues' tabulated bond lengths, but `Protein.calc_bondlength` replaces this with the true PDB distance `dmap[i,j]` when either residue lies inside a structured domain (harmonic mode), or blends the tabulated and true distances weighted by `bondscale[i,j]` in the Go-like regime between `min_scale = 0.05` and `cutoff_mix_in_LJYU = 0.15`. The force definitions consuming these lengths are documented in [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidagement) — here we only note that geometry and force fields are co-designed at build time.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L139-L142), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L269-L296), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L448-L490)

## Coordinate Assembly Pipeline

The final step is turning per-component geometry into one global system. CALVADOS uses an **offset-based bead allocation** scheme: each component carries a `start_bead` index, and every `add_bonds` / `add_angles` / `add_restraints` method receives an `offset` parameter to shift its local 0-based indices into the global system numbering. RNA adds a compositional wrinkle — bonds, angles, and neighboring-base terms each return their own exclusion lists so the nonbonded forces (Ashbaugh-Hatch, Yukawa) can omit interactions already covered by bonded terms. `restraint_check` in the RNA class explicitly excludes bead pairs that are already bonded, angled, or neighbor-base-restrained, preventing double-counting of interactions at build time.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L44-L44), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L149-L166), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L597-L623), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L711-L723)

> [!TIP]
> Watch the index base carefully when reading the output artifacts: OpenMM force indices are 0-based, but `bond_pairlist` and `restr_pairlist` records are written **1-based** (the code comments `# 1-based` at `add_bonds`), because they target human-readable audit files like `bonds_{name}.txt`. Off-by-one confusion between these two representations is the most common mistake when programmatically cross-checking written bonds against a generated topology.

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L162-L165), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L172-L177), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L754-L767)

The complete build-time flow, from declarative input to a fully indexed system, looks like this:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CFG as Config/Components (YAML)
    participant COMP as Component subclass
    participant BLD as build.py geometry
    participant SYS as System assembly
    CFG->>COMP: validate params (ComponentInput)
    COMP->>COMP: calc_properties(): residues.csv lookup,<br/>sigmas/lambdas/qs per bead
    alt restraint=True
        COMP->>BLD: geometry_from_pdb / geometry_from_pdb_rna
        BLD-->>COMP: xinit (nm) + CRYST1 dimensions
        COMP->>COMP: calc_dmap() + ssdomains / go scale
    else procedural
        COMP->>BLD: build_compact / build_spiral / build_linear
        BLD-->>COMP: xinit
    end
    SYS->>COMP: assign start_bead offset
    SYS->>BLD: place molecules (random/grid/bilayer)
    BLD-->>SYS: clash-free coordinates
    SYS->>COMP: add_bonds/add_angles/add_restraints(offset)
    COMP-->>SYS: forces + exclusion maps
```

Note that the sequence ends at *forces and exclusions* — handing the OpenMM system to the simulation driver is the next stage, covered in [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing).

Sources: [components.py](calvados/components.py#L70-L100), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L407-L413), [components.py](calvados/components.py#L505-L509)

## Stoichiometry: From Concentration to Chain Count

Geometry fixes *where* molecules go; stoichiometry fixes *how many* go there. CALVADOS converts experimental mass concentrations into integer molecule counts using Avogadro's number and the nm³-to-liter factor: `n = p · 10⁻²⁴ · c · V · N_A / MW`, where `p` is the species' mass fraction, `c` the total concentration in g/L, `V` the box volume in nm³, and `MW` the sequence-derived molecular weight. The pair variant (`calc_pair_n_in_box`) rounds both counts to integers and then *recomputes* the realized mass fraction and concentration from the rounded counts — so the YAML parameters you requested are not exactly what the box contains, and the corrected values are returned for reporting. The N-species variant (`calc_mixture_n_in_box`) generalizes this, returning per-species counts, rounded mass fractions, and the realized total concentration.

| Function | Inputs | Returns | Rounding behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| `conc_to_n` | fraction `p`, concentration, volume, MW | molecule count (float) | none |
| `n_to_conc` | count, volume, MW | g/L concentration | none |
| `calc_pair_n_in_box` | concentration, `pB`, box, two sequences | `nA`, `nB`, corrected `pB`, corrected `c` | rounds counts, back-computes |
| `calc_mixture_n_in_box` | concentration, fraction list, box, sequence list | count list, fraction array, total `c` | rounds counts, back-computes |

This "round-then-report" convention matters for reproducibility: mixing ratios in a simulation of 50 chains can only be approximated, and CALVADOS makes the *actual* composition explicit rather than letting consumers assume the requested one.

Sources: [build.py](calvados/build.py#L493-L505), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L508-L525), [build.py](calvados/build.py#L528-L553), [sequence.py](calvados/sequence.py#L16-L16)

## Key Takeaways

Three patterns define this subsystem. First, **geometry as pure functions**: `build.py` holds no state, making every sizing, placement, and parsing decision independently verifiable against its ~550 lines. Second, **strategy dispatch over inheritance**: `comp_setup` strings select chain builders, while restraint flags select structure-guided paths — one mechanism, no class explosion. Third, **validated assembly**: wall checks, periodic clash detection, exclusion maps, and back-computed stoichiometry all encode the invariant that the first frame must be physically sane before the integrator ever runs. To extend CALVADOS with a new molecule type or geometry, you now know precisely which layer to touch: a new generator function in `build.py`, a new `comp_setup` branch, or a new `Component` subclass.

For the surrounding context, continue with these pages: the force-field parameters that give these beads their physics start at [Residue Parameter Database](8-residue-parameter-database); the charge and terminus patching invoked during `calc_properties` is detailed in [Sequence Handling & Charge Assignment](10-sequence-handling-and-charge-assignment); how these geometry parameters are declared in YAML is covered in [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation); and the trajectory produced from this first frame is consumed by [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing).


# Simulation Engine & Checkpointing



This page explains how CALVADOS executes a coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulation: the `Sim` driver class in `calvados/sim.py`, the staged pipeline it drives (build → equilibration → production), the OpenMM integration details, and — most importantly for long-running HPC jobs — the checkpoint and resume semantics. It is the execution counterpart to [System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry) (what gets built) and [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation) (what gets configured); here we focus on how the validated inputs become a running trajectory that can survive preemption and wall-clock limits.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L31-L39), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L63-L84)

## Architectural Role of the `Sim` Driver

The engine is organized around a single driver class, `Sim`, whose lifecycle is deliberately split into two public phases: `build_system()` (assemble the OpenMM `System`, MDTraj topology, particle positions, and force fields) and `simulate()` (attach an integrator, run equilibration phases, and run production). A module-level convenience function `run()` closes the loop for batch operation: it loads `config.yaml` and `components.yaml` with `yaml.safe_load`, instantiates `Sim`, and invokes both phases in sequence. This is exactly the script emitted by `Config.write_runfile()`, so every prepared example directory contains a runnable `run.py` that ends in `sim.run(path=..., fconfig=..., fcomponents=...)`.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L41-L57), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L886), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L63-L84)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["sim.run(path, fconfig, fcomponents)"] --> B["Sim.__init__<br/>pydantic validation via validate_inputs()"]
    B --> C["build_system()<br/>topology + particles + forces<br/>writes top.pdb / top.cif / sysname.xml"]
    C --> D{"restart == 'checkpoint'<br/>and restart.chk exists?"}
    D -- "yes" --> E["simulation.loadCheckpoint()<br/>append = True<br/>equilibration flags force-disabled"]
    D -- "no" --> F["fresh start:<br/>backup stale .dcd, setPositions,<br/>minimizeEnergy()"]
    E --> H["production"]
    F --> G{"equilibration flags?"}
    G -- "slab_eq" --> G1["restrained eq → remove<br/>CustomExternalForce, rebuild Simulation"]
    G -- "box_eq / bilayer_eq" --> G2["barostat eq → optionally keep<br/>barostat, rebuild Simulation"]
    G -- "none" --> H
    G1 --> H
    G2 --> H
    H --> I{"duration driver?"}
    I -- "runtime (hours)" --> J["runForClockTime()<br/>checkpoint every 30 min"]
    I -- "steps" --> K["≤10 tqdm batches<br/>saveCheckpoint after each batch"]
    J --> L["final saveCheckpoint()<br/>+ checkpoint.pdb / checkpoint.cif"]
    K --> L
```

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L157-L304), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L646-L869)

## The Validation Gate: Mutability Discipline in `__init__`

`Sim.__init__` runs everything through `validate_inputs()`, which converts the raw YAML mappings into two pydantic models — `SimulationInput` for global settings and one `ComponentInput` per named component — before any OpenMM object exists. This means every invalid duration/pressure/restart combination fails at construction time, not mid-trajectory. Notably, options that can *change during* a simulation (`box`, `eps_lj`, the three equilibration flags, the restart path) are copied out of the immutable model into plain attributes: `eps_lj` is converted from kcal/mol to kJ/mol (× 4.184) at this point, and a relative `frestart` is resolved against the simulation directory.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L41-L62), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L270-L327), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L10)

Two `__init__`-time checks directly shape runtime behavior. A `pdb`/`cif` restart without an existing file is a hard `FileNotFoundError`, whereas a `checkpoint` restart is *lenient*: if the checkpoint file is absent the run silently degrades to a fresh start. Conversely, if a checkpoint file **is** present, all three equilibration flags (`slab_eq`, `bilayer_eq`, `box_eq`) are forced to `False` — a resumed run skips straight to production, appending to the existing trajectory. The model also enforces that `steps` and `runtime` are mutually exclusive, defaulting to 100,000,000 steps (1 µs at the fixed 10 fs timestep) when neither is supplied.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L55-L72), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L146-L190)

| Engine-relevant key | Default | Role at runtime |
|---|---|---|
| `restart` | `"checkpoint"` | Input mode: `checkpoint`, `pdb`, `cif`, or `None` |
| `frestart` | `"restart.chk"` | Checkpoint file path (relative to sim dir) |
| `steps` / `runtime` | `100_000_000` / `None` | Exactly one must be set; steps-based runs batch-checkpoint |
| `wfreq` | `100000` | DCD frame interval (1 step = 10 fs) |
| `logfreq` | `1000000` | Log-file reporting interval |
| `platform` | `"CPU"` | `"CPU"` or `"CUDA"` |
| `threads` / `gpu_id` | `1` / `0` | CPU thread pool / CUDA DeviceIndex fallback |
| `friction_coeff` | `0.01` | Langevin friction in 1/ps |
| `random_number_seed` | `None` | Applied to every integrator instance |
| `pressure_coupling` | `False` | Keep the barostat into production (NPT) |

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L146-L179), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L53-L59)

## Phase 1 — `build_system()`: Assembling a Resumable System

`build_system()` materializes the physical system: an empty OpenMM `System` receives default periodic box vectors from `build.build_box()`, Debye-Hückel parameters are computed from temperature and ionic strength, components are instantiated from the registry, and solutes are reordered ahead of lipids and crowders to stabilize bead indexing. Each molecule is then placed according to `topol` (slab/grid/center/shift_ref_bead/random) and wired into the shared Ashbaugh-Hatch (`ah`) and Yukawa/Debye-Hückel (`yu`) force objects, plus lipid `cos`/`cn` forces when present.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L157-L204), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L265-L293)

The method ends with an artifact handoff that matters for restarts: a single MDTraj `Trajectory` covering all placed particles is written as `top.pdb` and `top.cif` — *unless* the run will restart from a user-supplied `pdb`/`cif`, in which case those files are preserved and the restart file's topology is used instead. `print_system_summary()` then serializes the complete `System` (all forces, exclusions, barostats) to `{sysname}.xml` via `openmm.XmlSerializer`, providing a platform-independent, human-inspectable record of exactly what was built. `add_forces_to_system()` attaches barostats conditionally: a `MonteCarloAnisotropicBarostat` (frequency 1000) for `box_eq` honoring per-axis `boxscaling_xyz`, and a `MonteCarloMembraneBarostat` (frequency 10000, XY-isotropic, Z-fixed) for `bilayer_eq`.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L295-L304), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L306-L366), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L368-L393)

## Phase 2 — `simulate()`: Integrator Setup and Platform Binding

`simulate()` opens by selecting the coordinate source — `app.PDBFile`/`app.PDBxFile` for coordinate restarts, else the freshly written `top.cif` — and constructs a `LangevinMiddleIntegrator` at temperature `temp`, friction `friction_coeff / picosecond`, and a **hard-coded 0.01 ps (10 fs) timestep**. The timestep is intentionally not configurable; only friction and the optional random seed are. The seed is re-applied to every integrator instance created in the method, so slab- and pressure-equilibration rebuilds inherit the same stochastic policy.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L646-L666), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L739-L745), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L798-L804)

Platform binding is explicit: `Platform.getPlatformByName(config.platform)`, with the CPU platform receiving a `{"Threads": str(threads)}` property dictionary. For non-CPU platforms, the engine sets the `DeviceIndex` platform *default* from `gpu_id` — but only if `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is absent from the environment, deferring to cluster-level device masking when present. This is the layer where HPC portability is handled; deeper performance analysis is covered in [Hardware Platforms & Performance](20-hardware-platforms-and-performance).

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L668-L687)

### The Phase-Rebuild Pattern for Equilibration

Equilibration is implemented as a chain of scoped phases, each following the same pattern: run `steps_eq` steps with a special force active, dump the final state to `equilibration_final.pdb/.cif`, surgically remove the special force from the `System`, then **rebuild the `Simulation` object from scratch** with a plain `LangevinIntegrator` and re-minimize. `slab_eq` runs under a `CustomExternalForce` harmonic restraint toward the slab plane and removes the first `CustomExternalForce` it finds afterward; `box_eq`/`bilayer_eq` run under their barostats and keep them into production only when `pressure_coupling` is enabled (NPT) — otherwise the barostat is popped from the force list and production proceeds at constant volume with the equilibrated box vectors restored via `setPeriodicBoxVectors`.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L717-L763), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L765-L821)

> [!TIP]
> The integrator deliberately changes across phases: the initial `Simulation` uses `LangevinMiddleIntegrator`, while every post-equilibration rebuild switches to plain `LangevinIntegrator`. Since these split integrators differ in velocity half-step handling, trajectories resumed across a phase boundary are not bitwise-identical to uninterrupted runs — expected for a stochastic Langevin scheme, but worth knowing when reproducing results.

| Equilibration phase | Force used | Reporter target | Post-phase action |
|---|---|---|---|
| `slab_eq` | `CustomExternalForce` (spring `k_eq`, axis-selectable) | `equilibration_{sysname}.dcd` | Remove restraint force, rebuild Simulation, re-minimize |
| `box_eq` | `MonteCarloAnisotropicBarostat` | `equilibration_{sysname}.dcd` | Drop barostat unless `pressure_coupling`; restore box vectors |
| `bilayer_eq` | `MonteCarloMembraneBarostat` (XYIsotropic, ZFixed) | `equilibration_{sysname}.dcd` | Drop barostat unless `pressure_coupling` |

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L330-L366), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L717-L821), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L193-L250)

## Checkpointing & Resume Semantics

CALVADOS offers three restart input modes with distinct fidelity guarantees, selected by the `restart` key. The **checkpoint** mode is the highest-fidelity path: OpenMM's binary `saveCheckpoint`/`loadCheckpoint` round-trips positions, velocities, box vectors, and integrator/RNG state, so a resumed trajectory is a genuine continuation. The `pdb`/`cif` modes restart from coordinates only — velocities are re-drawn and energy is re-minimized, which is why they are treated as fresh starts that may re-run equilibration phases.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L646-L703), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L151-L152)

| Restart mode | State restored | Equilibration re-run? | Trajectory handling | Failure behavior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `None` | Positions from freshly built system | Yes, if flags set | New file (old one backed up) | — |
| `pdb` / `cif` | Positions only, from external file | Yes, if flags set | New file (old one backed up) | `FileNotFoundError` at `__init__` if file missing |
| `checkpoint` | Full state (positions, velocities, RNG) | **No — flags force-disabled** | Appends to existing `.dcd` and `.log` | Graceful fresh start if `.chk` missing; `FileNotFoundError` if `.dcd` missing |

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L64-L72), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L689-L715)

The resume contract is strict about consistency: when `restart == "checkpoint"` and the file exists, `simulate()` demands that `{sysname}.dcd` already exist (raising `FileNotFoundError` if not), sets `append=True` on all reporters, and calls `simulation.loadCheckpoint()`. This guarantees the appended frames continue the same trajectory rather than opening a parallel one. In the fresh-start branch the engine is correspondingly defensive about overwriting: a stale `{sysname}.dcd` is renamed to `backup_{sysname}_{timestamp}.dcd` before `setPositions` and `minimizeEnergy()` run.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L689-L715)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["restart.chk present?"] -- "no" --> N["fresh start<br/>positions only"]
    C -- "yes" --> D["sysname.dcd present?"]
    D -- "no" --> X["FileNotFoundError:<br/>cannot append trajectory"]
    D -- "yes" --> L["loadCheckpoint()<br/>append=True<br/>skip equilibration"]
    N --> M["minimizeEnergy()<br/>→ eq. phases → production"]
    L --> M
```

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L689-L715)

> [!TIP]
> Because a valid checkpoint disables all equilibration flags in `__init__` (lines 69–72 of `sim.py`), deleting `restart.chk` is the *only* way to re-run equilibration on a system that has already been equilibrated once. When you intentionally want a re-equilibration, also expect the production `.dcd` to be backed up and restarted, since `append` remains `False` in that branch.

## Duration Control: Wall-Clock Time vs. Batched Steps

Production is governed by exactly one of two mutually exclusive drivers. When `runtime` (hours) is set, the engine calls OpenMM's `runForClockTime(runtime*hour, checkpointFile=..., checkpointInterval=30*minute)` — the framework itself writes a checkpoint every 30 minutes regardless of crash timing, which is the natural mode for queue-limited HPC jobs (see [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview) for how `Job` templates wrap this). When `steps` is set, the total is decomposed by `_split_steps()` into at most 10 nonempty batches (`divmod` distribution of the remainder), each executed with a `tqdm` progress bar and followed by an explicit `simulation.saveCheckpoint(restart_path)` — so a killed run loses at most one batch of work, not the whole trajectory.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L24-L28), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L844-L855), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L138-L183)

| Aspect | `runtime` mode | `steps` mode |
|---|---|---|
| Termination | Wall clock (`runForClockTime`) | Exact step count |
| Checkpoint cadence | Every 30 min (OpenMM-managed) | After each of ≤10 batches |
| Progress visibility | None from engine | `tqdm` batch progress bar |
| Deterministic length | No (hardware-dependent) | Yes |
| Post-loop safety | Final `saveCheckpoint` still executed | Final `saveCheckpoint` still executed |

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L845-L857), [tests/test_sim.py](tests/test_sim.py#L9-L15)

`_split_steps()` is a pure function with a dedicated unit test asserting that batch sizes sum exactly to the requested step count, never exceed 10 batches, and contain no empty batches. The barostat-selection logic in `add_forces_to_system()` is likewise parametrized-tested against all four `box_eq`/`bilayer_eq`/`pressure_coupling` combinations, confirming that anisotropic vs. membrane barostats are attached per configuration. These tests are good anchors when extending the engine; the validation suite is described further in [Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation).

Sources: [tests/test_sim.py](tests/test_sim.py#L9-L65)

## Production Reporters and the Output Artifact Inventory

Once in production, two reporters are attached with `append` reflecting the resume state: a `DCDReporter` writing `{sysname}.dcd` every `wfreq` steps, and a `StateDataReporter` writing `{sysname}.log` every `logfreq` steps with tab separators, step number, speed, and elapsed time (potential energy only when `report_potential_energy` is enabled). After the run terminates — by clock, by steps, or by crash-and-resume — the engine performs a final `saveCheckpoint` and writes human-readable `checkpoint.pdb`/`checkpoint.cif` snapshots of the final, wrapped positions, which serve as lightweight inspection points without loading the binary checkpoint into OpenMM.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L823-L842), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L857-L869)

| Artifact | Producer | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `top.pdb` / `top.cif` | `build_system()` | Initial topology/coordinates (skipped for `pdb`/`cif` restarts) |
| `{sysname}.xml` | `print_system_summary()` | Full serialized OpenMM System incl. forces & barostats |
| `equilibration_{sysname}.dcd` | Equilibration phases | Frames from restrained/barostatted phase |
| `equilibration_final.pdb/.cif` | Equilibration phases | Handoff state between phases |
| `{sysname}.dcd` | Production `DCDReporter` | Trajectory (appended on checkpoint resume) |
| `{sysname}.log` | Production `StateDataReporter` | Step/speed/energy time series |
| `restart.chk` (default name) | Per-batch / 30-min / final saves | Binary full-state checkpoint |
| `checkpoint.pdb` / `checkpoint.cif` | Post-run | Final wrapped configuration snapshot |
| `backup_{sysname}_{timestamp}.dcd` | Fresh start on stale `.dcd` | Collision-safe trajectory preservation |

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L295-L304), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L707-L712), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L857-L869)

## Operational Recipe: Configure, Run, Resume

A typical workflow (as in `examples/single_IDR`) ties the knobs together: choose `wfreq` as the frames-per-trajectory-unit (`1 = 10 fs`), express total length as `steps = N_frames * N_save`, select `platform = 'CPU'` or `'CUDA'`, and leave `restart = 'checkpoint'` with `frestart = 'restart.chk'`. Running the generated `run.py` produces the full artifact set above; if the job is preempted, re-running the identical command detects the checkpoint, loads full state, and appends frames — no manual intervention required.

```python
config = Config(
  sysname = sysname,
  box = [L, L, L], temp = 293.15, ionic = 0.19, pH = 7.5,
  topol = 'center',
  wfreq = N_save,              # dcd writing interval, 1 = 10 fs
  steps = N_frames*N_save,     # number of simulation steps
  platform = 'CPU',            # or CUDA
  restart = 'checkpoint',
  frestart = 'restart.chk',
  verbose = True,
)
```

Sources: [examples/single_IDR/prepare.py](examples/single_IDR/prepare.py#L26-L42), [cfg.py](calvados/cfg.py#L45-L61)

For trajectory post-processing of the resulting `.dcd`, continue with [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](15-trajectory-analysis-toolkit); for slab-specific phase behavior pipelines, see [Slab Phase-Separation Analysis](16-slab-phase-separation-analysis); for error estimation on the produced time series, see [Blocking Error Estimation](17-blocking-error-estimation).


# Trajectory Analysis Toolkit



The `calvados.analysis` module is the post-processing workhorse of the CALVADOS pipeline: it converts raw MD trajectory files (PDB topology + DCD coordinate frames) produced by the simulation engine into physically meaningful observables — radii of gyration, end-to-end distances, contact maps, scaling exponents, chain center-of-mass trajectories, and pairwise energies. This page explains the module's architecture, its dual-engine design (MDAnalysis + mdtraj), its unit conventions, and how every observable integrates with the blocking-error machinery for statistically honest error bars.

The module is organized as four layers: **trajectory preprocessing**, **per-frame metric kernels**, **composite drivers** that persist results to disk, and **multi-chain topology tools** that reason about components rather than atoms. A single `SlabAnalysis` class also lives in this module, but its phase-separation workflow is documented separately in [Slab Phase-Separation Analysis](16-slab-phase-separation-analysis) — this page covers only the general trajectory toolkit.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1-L29), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L541-L550)

## Architecture: One Module, Three Engines

The toolkit's defining architectural decision is that it does **not** commit to a single trajectory library. Instead, each layer picks the engine whose topology model fits the task best, and `numba` JIT compilation is applied to the hot numeric kernels that would otherwise be Python-loop-bound.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph inputs["Simulation Outputs"]
        PDB["top.pdb<br/>(topology)"]
        DCD["name.dcd<br/>(coordinates)"]
        CSV["residues.csv<br/>(masses, params)"]
    end

    subgraph pre["Preprocessing Layer"]
        CT["center_traj"]
        SST["subsample_traj"]
        UW["unwrap via<br/>TopoAttr bonds"]
    end

    subgraph engines["Computation Engines"]
        MDA["MDAnalysis<br/>AtomGroup metrics<br/>AlignTraj / RMSD / RMSF"]
        MDT["mdtraj<br/>Topology, select_pairs<br/>compute_distances"]
        NB["numba JIT<br/>calc_energy, potentials<br/>binning kernels"]
    end

    subgraph metrics["Metric Kernels"]
        DM["calc_dmap / self_distances"]
        CM["calc_cmap / cmap_traj"]
        OBS["calc_rg / calc_ete / calc_ocf"]
        SCALE["fit_scaling_exp"]
        RMS["calc_rmsd / calc_fnc"]
    end

    subgraph out["Persistence & Errors"]
        BA["BlockAnalysis.SEM()<br/>(correlated-sample errors)"]
        NPY[".npy arrays"]
        CSVO[".csv summaries"]
        DCD2["COM trajectories"]
    end

    PDB --> CT & SST & MDA & MDT
    DCD --> CT & SST & MDA & MDT
    CSV --> OBS
    CT --> UW --> MDT
    MDA --> DM & OBS & RMS
    MDT --> CM & SCALE
    NB --> DM
    DM --> CM & SCALE
    OBS --> BA --> CSVO
    CM --> NPY
    SCALE --> CSVO
    MDT --> DCD2
```

Three external dependencies shape the module's boundaries. `BlockAnalysis` is imported from `calvados/BLOCKING/main.py` and supplies every error estimate; `get_ssdomains` is pulled from `calvados.build` so contact-number analysis can respect secondary-structure domains; and `InputPath` from `calvados.inputmodels` provides a path type alias that the functions normalize with `os.fspath` at entry.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1-L29), [main.py](/calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L10-L31)

## Unit Convention: Å Inside, nm Outside

The toolkit maintains a strict but implicit unit contract that you must understand before interpreting any returned array. MDAnalysis reads coordinates in **ångströms**, and the internal histogramming machinery (notably inside `SlabAnalysis`) works in Å.
