However, the *public* observables returned by the metric kernels — distance maps, Rg, end-to-end distances, OCF coordinates, scaling fits — are all converted to **nanometers** by an explicit `/10.` at the point of computation.

| Quantity | Internal unit | Public output | Conversion site |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pairwise distance map (`calc_dmap`) | Å | nm | `distance_array(...) / 10.` |
| Rg (`calc_rg`) | Å | nm | `(ag.positions - com) / 10.` |
| End-to-end (`calc_ete`) | Å | nm | `np.linalg.norm(...) / 10.` |
| OCF bond vectors (`calc_ocf`) | Å | nm | `ag.positions / 10.` |
| Contact-map cutoff (`calc_cmap`) | nm | nm | taken as nm directly |
| Z-profile bins (`SlabAnalysis`) | Å bins | nm coordinates | `edges / 10` |

This convention means a cutoff of `1.0` in `calc_cmap` means 1 nm, while `rc_yu=4.0` in `calc_energy` means 4 nm. When writing new kernels, follow the same pattern: divide by 10 exactly once, at the metric boundary, and document the result's unit in the docstring.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L132-L146), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L348-L367)

## Trajectory Preprocessing

Before any metric is computed, trajectories typically need two corrections: recentring in the periodic box and (optionally) frame subsampling. The module provides file-to-file utilities for both, each writing a sibling DCD next to the input so downstream tools can pick the corrected file up without argument changes.

`center_traj` builds an `mda.Universe` from the PDB/DCD pair and, for each frame in the `start:stop:step` slice, translates all atoms so the center of geometry sits at the box center (`0.5 * dimensions[:3]`), then streams frames into `<traj>_c.dcd`. `subsample_traj` is the same slicing pattern without translation, writing `<traj>_sub.dcd` — useful for decimating densely-written trajectories before expensive analyses. Both accept `InputPath` (str or `Path`) and normalize it immediately, so callers can pass either form.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L32-L66)

## The Contact Map Family

Contact analysis is the conceptual core of the toolkit, and it rests on one mathematical primitive reused everywhere: the **smooth switching function** `0.5 − 0.5·tanh((d − cutoff)/0.3)`. Instead of a binary "contact / no contact" step, this tanh kernel produces continuous weights between 0 and 1 that decay over roughly ±0.9 nm around the cutoff, which stabilizes trajectory averages against thermal noise at the cutoff boundary.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["AtomGroup / atom group pair"] -->|"calc_dmap<br/>(periodic, nm)"| B["Distance map dmap"]
    B -->|"calc_cmap<br/>0.5 − 0.5·tanh((d−c)/0.3)"| C["Smooth contact map<br/>(per frame)"]
    C -->|"cmap_traj<br/>frame average"| D["Trajectory-averaged cmap"]
    C -->|"calc_fnc<br/>× native reference map"| E["Fraction of native contacts<br/>(per frame)"]
    B -->|"calc_wcn<br/>(1−(d/r0)^6)/(1−(d/r0)^12)"| F["Weighted contact number<br/>(per bead)"]
```

The four members of the family divide the work as follows:

- **`calc_cmap`** — the per-frame primitive: smooth contact map between two MDAnalysis atom groups with a 1.0 nm default cutoff.
- **`cmap_traj`** — the time integrator: iterates `u.trajectory[start:end:step]`, accumulates per-frame maps, and normalizes by the frame count. Its frame slicing is the subject of a dedicated unit test that monkeypatches `calc_cmap` and asserts exact normalization over `start=1, end=9, step=2`.
- **`calc_fnc`** — fraction of native contacts: computes a reference contact map from a reference universe, strips the `kmax` diagonals closest to the chain backbone (trivial bonded contacts), optionally applies a B-factor sigmoid weighting (`exp(width·(bfac−sig_shift))` logistic), and reports `Σ(c·c_ref) / Σc_ref` per frame.
- **`calc_wcn`** — weighted contact number per bead, using a distinct Lennard-Jones-like weight `(1−(d/r0)⁶)/(1−(d/r0)¹²)`. When `ssonly=True` it consults `get_ssdomains` from the build module and counts only bead pairs sharing a secondary-structure domain.

> [!TIP]
> The smooth `0.5 − 0.5·tanh((d − cutoff)/0.3)` kernel is duplicated verbatim in both `calc_cmap` (MDAnalysis path) and `calc_contact_map` (mdtraj path, operating on Å distances with the same nm cutoff). If you ever retune the switching width `0.3`, both sites must change together or component-level and chain-level contact maps become inconsistent.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L171-L246), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L248-L288), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1437-L1447), [test_analysis.py](/tests/test_analysis.py#L12-L33)

## Energy Re-evaluation from Distance Maps

A distinctive capability of the toolkit is that it can **recompute pairwise potential energies after the simulation**, purely from a distance map. `calc_energy` takes a distance matrix plus per-pair `sig`, `lam`, and `q` arrays and evaluates both the Ashbaugh-Hatch and Yukawa pair potentials with `numba` `nopython` JIT, returning two arrays shaped like the input distance map.

This closes a verification loop with the force field: the potentials implemented here (`ah_potential`, `lj_potential`, `yukawa_potential`) are analytic mirrors of the OpenMM custom forces used during simulation. Comparing trajectory-averaged recomputed energies against the simulation's energy log validates that the custom-force implementation and the analysis-layer reference agree. The kernels implement the shifted, cut-off forms exactly as documented in the force field pages:

- `ah_potential(r, sig, eps, lam, rc)` — below `2^(1/6)·σ` it is the full Lennard-Jones plus the constant `eps·(1−λ)` offset; between there and `rc` it is `λ·(LJ(r) − LJ(rc))`; zero beyond `rc`.
- `yukawa_potential(r, q, kappa_yu, rc_yu)` — the shifted form `q·(exp(−κr)/r − exp(−κ·rc)/rc)`, truncated to zero past the cutoff.
- The `same_domain` flag (with the `abs(i−j) <= 1` exclusion) allows skipping bonded-neighbor pairs when the distance map comes from a single structured domain.

For the physics behind these functional forms, see [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions) and [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics).

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L68-L130)

## Single-Chain Observables and the Polymer Scaling Fit

The single-chain layer answers the classical IDP characterization questions with four trajectory-wise kernels plus a fitting routine. All of them share the same slicing signature (`start`, `stop`, `step`) so they can be pointed at equilibrated subsets of a trajectory without copying files.

| Function | Observable | Returns | Mass weighting |
|---|---|---|---|
| `calc_rg` | Radius of gyration per frame | `(n_frames,)` array, nm | residue masses from `residues.csv` if `seq` given, else uniform |
| `calc_ete` | End-to-end distance per frame | array + mean + SEM, nm | none (first/last bead) |
| `calc_ocf` | Bond orientational correlation vs separation | mean + SEM arrays | none |
| `calc_rmsd` | RMSD to reference & to mean structure + RMSF | three tuple entries, Å | alignment via `AlignTraj` |
| `calc_fnc` | Fraction of native contacts per frame | `(n_frames,)` array | optional B-factor sigmoid |

Two implementation details deserve attention. First, mass handling in `calc_rg` is sequence-aware: `get_masses` looks up `MW` from the residues DataFrame indexed by three-letter codes, then applies terminal corrections of **+2 Da at the N-terminus** and **+16 Da at the C-terminus** to account for the charged termini. Second, `calc_rmsd` performs a **two-pass alignment**: it first aligns to the supplied reference structure, computes an iterated mean structure, then re-aligns to that mean and computes a second RMSD curve plus per-atom RMSF — the standard protocol for separating global drift from intrinsic fluctuation, with an optional mean-structure PDB export.

The scaling layer then turns internal distances into the Flory exponent. `fit_scaling_exp` builds the trajectory-averaged RMS internal-distance matrix, buckets distances by sequence separation `|i−j|`, and fits `⟨d⟩ = r0·n^ν` over separations beyond `ij0=5` using `scipy.curve_fit`. Pass `r0=None` to fit both parameters (getting `ν` with covariance-derived error), or fix `r0` to fit `ν` alone. The returned `ν ≈ 0.588` indicates a self-avoiding chain; `ν ≈ 0.33` indicates collapse — the single most cited diagnostic in IDP phase-separation studies.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L290-L367), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L369-L424), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L428-L492), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L329-L338)

## Composite Drivers: `save_conf_prop` and the Error Discipline

Hand-calling kernels is fine for exploration, but the module also ships a **batch driver** that runs the standard single-chain characterization protocol and persists everything to disk. `save_conf_prop(path, name, residues_file, output_path, ...)` loads `top.pdb` + `<name>.dcd` in-memory and produces a complete characterization bundle:

| Output file | Content |
|---|---|
| `rgs.npy` | per-frame radius of gyration |
| `rees.npy` | per-frame end-to-end distance |
| `conf_prop.csv` | value/error table for `Rg`, `Ree`, and (for IDRs) `nu` |
| `internal_distances.npy` | `[ij, dij]` arrays from the scaling fit |
| `cmap.npy` | trajectory-averaged contact map, `kmax` diagonals stripped |

Notice the error-handling pattern: **every** time series is wrapped in `BlockAnalysis` and its `SEM()` method is invoked before the value is written to `conf_prop.csv`. This is not optional decoration — MD observables are strongly time-correlated, so naive `scipy.stats.sem` would understate errors by orders of magnitude. `BlockAnalysis.SEM()` computes blocking statistics at construction and then selects a converged plateau block size, exposing `.bs` and `.sem`. The full algorithm — plateau detection, replica concatenation, weighted reanalysis — is the subject of [Blocking Error Estimation](17-blocking-error-estimation); here it suffices to know that the toolkit treats `BlockAnalysis` as its single source of statistical truth.

> [!TIP]
> `save_conf_prop` distinguishes IDRs from folded domains via the `is_idr` flag: only with `is_idr=True` does it fit the scaling exponent and emit `internal_distances.npy`. For multi-domain constructs, run it once per chain segment rather than once globally, or the scaling fit will average folded and disordered regimes into a meaningless single `ν`.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L494-L539), [main.py](/calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L59-L78)

## Multi-Chain Toolkit: COM Trajectories and Component Contact Maps

For condensate and mixture simulations, analysis must reason in terms of **components and chains**, not atoms. The toolkit addresses chains through a uniform convention encoded in the `ChainIds` type alias: a component may be named by a single chain index (`int`), an inclusive `(start, end)` range tuple, or an explicit integer array. A `chainid_dict` maps component names to these selectors, and every multi-chain driver accepts it with the same semantics — an empty dict means "all chains belong to `sysname`".

`calc_com_traj(path, sysname, output_path, residues_file, chainid_dict, ...)` is the workhorse for coarse-graining chains to single particles. Its pipeline is instructive:

1. If `traj.dcd` does not yet exist, it constructs a **bond topology attribute** by chaining consecutive atom indices within each MDAnalysis segment, then applies `transformations.unwrap` so molecules broken across periodic boundaries become whole, writing the result to `traj.dcd` — an idempotent caching layer that later drivers silently reuse.
2. It loads that file with **mdtraj** (chosen here for its chain-level topology queries), re-centres coordinates to the box center, and reads `MW` values from the residues CSV — again applying the +2/+16 Da terminal corrections.
3. For every chain it computes the mass-weighted center of mass per frame, accumulates an `(n_frames, n_chains)` Rg array in nm, and assembles a synthetic mdtraj trajectory containing one COM "atom" per chain.

Outputs are written per component: `<sysname>_<component>_rg.npy` arrays, plus `<sysname>_com_top.pdb` / `<sysname>_com_traj.dcd` containing the COM trajectory — which downstream consumers (including `SlabAnalysis` and the slab notebooks) treat as a first-class input.

`calc_contact_map(path, sysname, output_path, chainid_dict, is_slab, ...)` produces residue-resolution contact maps **between component chain sets**. With one component it builds a homotypic map by duplicating the chain set under a `<name>_homotypic` alias; with two it builds heterotypic maps. Per chain, it uses mdtraj's `select_pairs` against all surrounding chains and applies the same smooth tanh kernel seen in `calc_cmap`, accumulating over frames and normalizing at the end. In slab mode (`is_slab=True`) it additionally partitions Rg samples and contact contributions into dense and dilute phase subsets using the interface cutoffs previously stored by the slab workflow — which is why it raises an informative `ValueError` if `SlabAnalysis` outputs are missing. That slab-specific path is detailed in [Slab Phase-Separation Analysis](16-slab-phase-separation-analysis).

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1246-L1340), [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L1342-L1447)

## Boundary with SlabAnalysis and Usage Pattern

The `SlabAnalysis` class occupies roughly half of the module's lines but is deliberately excluded from this page's scope: its constructor, centering, concentration profiling, interface fitting, and transfer-free-energy computation form the slab workflow documented in [Slab Phase-Separation Analysis](16-slab-phase-separation-analysis). From this page's perspective it matters as a **consumer** of the toolkit's conventions — it accepts the same PDB/DCD inputs, uses the same `BlockAnalysis` errors, and depends on `calc_com_traj` output for its dense/dilute partitioning.

The example notebook illustrates the canonical call pattern: instantiate with named paths, then invoke methods with explicit frame slicing.

```python
import calvados as cal

system, repl = 'hnRNPA1LCD', 0
name = f'{system}_{repl:d}'

slab = cal.analysis.SlabAnalysis(
    name=name,
    input_path=name,
    output_path='slab_output',
    ref_name=system,
    verbose=True,
)
slab.center(start=600, step=10, center_target='all')
```

The same constructor-then-slice pattern applies to the free functions: load once, slice deliberately, persist deterministically.

Sources: [analysis.py](/calvados/analysis.py#L541-L599), [example_slab_analysis.ipynb](/examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb#L26-L52)

## Verification Patterns in the Test Suite

The analysis toolkit is tested at two distinct levels, and understanding them helps you extend the module safely. The first level is **logic isolation with monkeypatching**: `test_cmap_traj_normalizes_selected_frames` replaces `calc_cmap` with a constant-returning stub and feeds a `SimpleNamespace` fake universe, asserting that `cmap_traj` performs the correct frame slicing and divides by exactly the number of visited frames. This verifies orchestration logic without any trajectory I/O.

The second level is **synthetic-fixture integration**: `test_calc_com_traj_uses_configured_input_and_step` constructs a real mdtraj topology and a 5-frame trajectory in `tmp_path`, writes PDB/DCD files and a minimal residues CSV, then runs `SlabAnalysis.calc_com_traj` with `step=2` and asserts the COM output DCD contains exactly 3 frames. This proves the idempotent `traj.dcd` caching path, the configured-input plumbing, and the subsampling arithmetic end-to-end. The slab-adjacent `test_calc_zpatch_includes_patch_at_final_bin` checks an edge case of the histogram patch finder — patches that extend to the final bin. Broader energy-level verification of the force-field kernels lives in the test suite covered by [Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation).

Sources: [test_analysis.py](/tests/test_analysis.py#L12-L43), [test_analysis.py](/tests/test_analysis.py#L46-L83)

## Key Takeaways and Reading Progression

Three architectural principles summarize the toolkit. First, **engine pluralism with a shared math layer**: MDAnalysis handles atom-group ergonomics, mdtraj handles chain topology, numba handles hot kernels — but the smooth tanh contact kernel and the nm-at-the-boundary unit rule are universal. Second, **errors are never optional**: every persisted observable passes through `BlockAnalysis.SEM()` because correlated MD samples demand block statistics. Third, **drivers are idempotent and file-driven**: caching intermediates like `traj.dcd` and writing `.npy`/`.csv` artifacts makes the analysis pipeline resumable and notebook-friendly.

To continue through the Analysis Stack, the recommended progression is [Slab Phase-Separation Analysis](16-slab-phase-separation-analysis) next, since it builds directly on `calc_com_traj` and the contact-map machinery described here, followed by [Blocking Error Estimation](17-blocking-error-estimation) for the mathematics behind every `.sem` value in this page. For the potentials that `calc_energy` re-evaluates, return to [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions) and [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics), and for how the trajectories analyzed here are produced, see [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing).


# Slab Phase-Separation Analysis



Slab simulations are CALVADOS's workhorse for computing liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) thermodynamics: a dense condensate slab coexists with a dilute gas inside a single periodic box, and the analysis pipeline extracts coexisting concentrations, partitioning coefficients, and transfer free energies directly from the trajectory. This page dissects the `SlabAnalysis` class in `calvados/analysis.py` — its centering algorithm, density profile construction, interface fitting, concentration/free-energy computation, and the auxiliary structural profilers — and walks through the reference notebooks that demonstrate both single-component and mixed-system workflows.

## Why Slab Geometry? The Direct-Coexistence Concept

The core idea is thermodynamic self-assembly: prepare ~100 copies of an IDP in an elongated periodic box and let the system spontaneously demix into a dense slab (centered along z, the box normal) surrounded by a dilute phase. Because both phases coexist in one simulation, their equilibrium concentrations can be read off a density profile without umbrella sampling or reweighting. The slab example README prescribes exactly this setup — direct coexistence simulations of 100 copies of a single IDR — and recommends independent replicas for sampling-error estimation.

The class-level contract is explicit in the `SlabAnalysis` docstring: the workflow centers a trajectory, builds reference and optional client concentration profiles along z, identifies dense and dilute regions, and writes concentrations, blocking errors, and transfer free energies. A critical units convention runs through the entire class — **histogramming happens internally in Ångströms, while all public profile coordinates are in nm and concentrations in mM**.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L541-L550), [README.md](examples/slab_IDR/README.md#L1-L9)

## Pipeline Architecture

`SlabAnalysis` is an orchestrator with a strict three-stage main pipeline plus a family of optional structural profilers. Each stage consumes the previous stage's on-disk artifacts, which means stages can be re-run independently (e.g., re-fit concentrations after extending a trajectory without re-centering):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph INPUTS["Raw simulation output"]
        PDB["top.pdb topology"]
        RAWDCD["name.dcd raw trajectory"]
    end
    subgraph STAGE1["Stage 1: Frame alignment"]
        CEN["center method"]
        CTRAJ["traj.dcd - centered, chains made whole"]
    end
    subgraph STAGE2["Stage 2: Density profiles"]
        PROF["calc_profiles method"]
        IND["name_component_profile.npy - frames x bins in mM"]
        ALL["name_profiles.npy - z_nm plus mean profiles"]
    end
    subgraph STAGE3["Stage 3: Thermodynamics"]
        CONC["calc_concentrations method"]
        FIT["fit_profile - tanh interface model"]
        BLK["BlockAnalysis SEM"]
        DG["calc_dG - Monte Carlo error"]
        CSV["name_ps_results.csv"]
    end
    PDB --> CEN
    RAWDCD --> CEN
    CEN --> CTRAJ
    CTRAJ --> PROF
    PROF --> IND
    PROF --> ALL
    IND --> CONC
    FIT --> CONC
    CONC --> BLK
    CONC --> DG
    BLK --> DG
    CONC --> CSV
    ALL --> PLOT["plot_density_profiles - PDF with cutoffs"]
```

Beyond the main pipeline, five auxiliary methods compute structural and compositional observables along the slab normal (`calc_orientations`, `calc_rgs`, `calc_aa_bins`, `calc_resid_bins`, `calc_com_traj`), all reusing the same centered-trajectory infrastructure. The blocking-error estimation inside Stage 3 delegates to `BlockAnalysis` from the `BLOCKING` package — the dedicated machinery is covered in [Blocking Error Estimation](17-blocking-error-estimation), while the general trajectory toolkit (`calc_rg`, `calc_ete`, contact maps) that shares this module lives in [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](15-trajectory-analysis-toolkit).

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L541-L550), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L21-L21)

## Constructing SlabAnalysis: Geometry and Component Registry

The constructor resolves file paths, establishes the **component registry** (one reference species plus zero or more client species), and pre-computes the z-binning geometry from the topology's box dimensions. Two binning systems are built at construction time: an absolute (origin at z = 0) 1-Å bin set used during histogramming, and a centered nm-coordinate bin set used for reporting, both derived from `u.dimensions[2]`.

| Parameter | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | — | System label; prefixes every output artifact and defaults the input DCD to `{name}.dcd` |
| `input_path` / `output_path` | `"."` | Location of simulation inputs / analysis artifacts (output dir is created if missing) |
| `input_pdb` | `top.pdb` | Beaded topology; `u.dimensions[2]` fixes the slab normal length `lz` |
| `input_dcd` | `{name}.dcd` | Raw trajectory to analyze |
| `centered_dcd` | `traj.dcd` | Destination for the centered trajectory |
| `ref_chains` | `None` → `(0, n_segments−1)` | **Inclusive, 0-based** segment range defining the condensate-forming species |
| `ref_name` | `None` → `"ref"` | Label for the reference component |
| `client_chain_list` | `()` | Sequence of inclusive `(first, last)` segment ranges for co-solutes / partner species |
| `client_names` | `()` → `client_{idx}` | Labels for client components |
| `verbose` | `False` | Progress logging switch |

The reference/client split is the architectural heart of multi-component analysis: the **reference species defines the phase boundaries**, and every client species is measured against those same boundaries. In the mixed FUSR-GG3/polyU40 example, chains 0–199 form the reference condensate while chains 200–259 (60 polyU40 chains) are registered as a client whose partitioning into the protein-dense phase is quantified.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L552-L594), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1093-L1109), [example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_mixed/example_slab_analysis.ipynb#L26-L42)

## Centering: The Two-Pass Density Alignment Algorithm

Centering is the most algorithmically subtle stage. Over a long simulation the slab drifts along z and chains cross periodic boundaries, so every frame must be re-aligned before histogramming. `center()` performs a **two-pass density alignment per frame**, followed by chain unwrapping:

1. **Pass 1 — max-density anchoring.** Histogram the z positions of the target atoms (reference chains by default, or all atoms with `center_target='all'`) into the precomputed 1-Å bins, find the argmax bin, and translate the system so that bin sits at the box center, then wrap into the primary box.
2. **Pass 2 — patch-weighted refinement.** Locate the *largest contiguous occupied z patch* (`calc_zpatch` scans the histogram for the longest run of non-empty bins), compute the density-weighted mean z of that patch, and translate it to the box center, wrapping again.
3. **Unwrapping.** Covalent bonds are synthesized from segment adjacency (`add_TopologyAttr('bonds', ...)`) so MDAnalysis can reconstruct whole chains (`transformations.unwrap`) before the frame is written to `centered_dcd`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Frame t from raw trajectory"] --> B["Histogram z of target atoms - 1 Angstrom bins"]
    B --> C["Translate argmax bin to box center"]
    C --> D["Wrap into primary box"]
    D --> E["Find largest contiguous occupied z patch"]
    E --> F["Density-weighted mean of patch"]
    F --> G["Translate patch mean to box center"]
    G --> H["Wrap again"]
    H --> I["Unwrap chains via synthesized bonds"]
    I --> J["Write frame to centered traj.dcd"]
```

Frame selection parameters (`start`, `end`, `step`) are applied here, which is how the reference notebooks discard equilibration and thin the trajectory — e.g., `slab.center(start=600, step=10, center_target='all')` for the hnRNPA1LCD system.

> [!TIP]
> Pass 1 uses only the single densest bin, which is sensitive to fluctuations; Pass 2's largest-patch weighting is the drift-correcting step. The patch approach matters because the wrap in Pass 1 can split the slab across the periodic boundary — the longest *contiguous* occupied run identifies the true slab body even when its tail has wrapped past z = 0.

For simple cases outside slab analysis, the module also exposes standalone `center_traj` and `subsample_traj` helpers that recenter frames on the global center of geometry or slice frame ranges, but the slab workflow always uses `SlabAnalysis.center` because of the density-based alignment.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L596-L653), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1111-L1139), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L32-L66), [example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb#L51-L51)

## Density Profiles: From Bead Counts to Millimolar

`calc_profiles()` loads the centered trajectory **in memory** and histograms z positions frame-by-frame for the reference species and each client. Two details deserve attention. First, the bin width is fixed at 1 Å (`binwidth = 1`, i.e., 0.1 nm), and the slice volume is `Lx · Ly · binwidth / 1e3` in nm³. Second, raw bead counts are converted to millimolar via

```
conv = 10 / 6.02214 / nbeads / volume * 1e3
```

which is the factor 10³/6.02214·10²³ ≈ 1660 that converts "beads per nm³" to mM, divided by the beads-per-chain count so the profile reports *chain* concentration regardless of chain length.

The outputs are deliberately redundant for downstream flexibility: per-frame profile arrays of shape `(n_frames, n_bins)` in mM are saved as `<name>_<component>_profile.npy` (these are what the notebook visualizes with `imshow` as a time-vs-z heatmap), while `<name>_profiles.npy` bundles the z-coordinates in its first row followed by the trajectory-averaged profiles of the reference and all clients — the single file that `plot_density_profiles()` consumes.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L655-L716), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L808-L819), [example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb#L101-L107)

## Interface Fitting: The Hyperbolic-Tangent Model

Phase boundaries are never hand-drawn. `fit_profile()` fits the trajectory-averaged reference profile to a **symmetric hyperbolic-tangent interface model** on each half of the box separately:

```
profile(x) = ½(a + b) + ½(b − a) · tanh((|x| − c) / d)
```

where `c` is the interface position, `d` the interface width, `b` the dense plateau, and `a` the dilute plateau. Fitting `z > 0` and `z < 0` independently (via `scipy.optimize.least_squares` with all parameters bounded to `[0, 100]`) lets the two interfaces of a finite slab relax to slightly different positions. From each fitted half, the phase cutoffs follow from the width parameter:

- **Dense cutoffs** = interface position − `pden` · width (defaults `pden = 2.0`): placed *two widths inside* the interface so only plateau bins contribute to the dense concentration.
- **Dilute cutoffs** = interface position + `pdil` · width (defaults `pdil = 8.0`): placed *eight widths outside* so interfacial tails cannot contaminate the dilute concentration.

The `pden`/`pdil` offsets embody a bias–variance tradeoff — deeper cuts reduce interfacial bias but shrink the sampling region. As a safeguard, the method computes the magnitude ratio of the left/right dilute cutoffs and emits a `RuntimeWarning` ("The fitted slab interfaces are strongly asymmetric") when it falls outside `[0.5, 2.0]`, which typically signals insufficient sampling or a broken slab.

> [!TIP]
> Cutoffs are fitted **once, from the reference profile only** (inside `calc_single_conc` when `ref=True`) and then frozen on the instance. Client species never re-fit interfaces — `calc_single_conc` for clients reuses `self.cutoffs_dense`/`self.cutoffs_dilute` directly. This guarantees every component is partitioned against an identical, protein-defined phase boundary, making concentration ratios across components directly comparable.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1187-L1226), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L718-L724), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L767-L781)

## Phase Concentrations, Errors, and Transfer Free Energy

`calc_concentrations()` drives the thermodynamic stage: it re-derives `ref_chains` from the topology if needed, processes the reference, then iterates clients, collecting everything into `df_results` and finally `<name>_ps_results.csv`. The per-component workhorse `calc_single_conc()` builds two boolean masks over the centered nm z-grid — *dense* bins strictly between the two dense cutoffs, *dilute* bins strictly outside the two dilute cutoffs — and averages the mean profile within each mask to yield `c_dense` and `c_dilute` in mM. It also projects the masks onto each individual frame (`apply_along_axis`) to produce per-frame concentration time series.

Error estimation then proceeds in two layers. Per-frame dense/dilute arrays are fed to `BlockAnalysis(...).SEM()`, whose blocked standard error accounts for the correlation time of the concentration signal (methodology in [Blocking Error Estimation](17-blocking-error-estimation)). Those errors propagate into the **transfer free energy** ΔG = ln(c_dil/c_den) in units of kT via a Monte Carlo scheme: 10,000 draws from normal distributions centered on each concentration with its blocked error, with the standard deviation of valid `ln(dil/den)` draws reported as `dG_err`:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H["Per-frame profiles h - frames x bins"] --> HM["Mean profile"]
    HM --> FIT["fit_profile - tanh per half-space"]
    FIT --> CUT["cutoffs_dense and cutoffs_dilute"]
    CUT --> MASK["Boolean phase masks"]
    MASK --> C["c_dense and c_dilute in mM"]
    H --> ARR["Per-frame phase arrays"]
    ARR --> BLK["BlockAnalysis SEM"]
    C --> DG["dG = ln of c_dil over c_den"]
    BLK --> MC["10000-draw Monte Carlo spread"]
    MC --> DG
```

Degenerate phase scenarios are handled explicitly rather than crashing:

| Condition | Reported ΔG | ΔG error | Console diagnostic |
|---|---|---|---|
| NaN in either concentration | NaN | NaN | "Not converged" |
| c_dilute = 0, c_dense > 0 | `dGmin` (−10) | NaN | "No dilute phase" |
| c_dense = 0, c_dilute > 0 | `−dGmin` (+10) | NaN | "No dense phase" |
| Both zero | NaN | NaN | "No dense or dilute phase" |
| Both positive | ln(c_dil/c_den) | MC std | — |
| ΔG below `dGmin` | Clipped to `dGmin` | 0 | "dG extremely small" |

The clipping thresholds are controllable through `calc_concentrations(dGmin=...)`. Scalars (cutoffs, concentrations ± errors, ΔG ± error, chain ranges) land in `df_results`/CSV, while the raw per-frame arrays are written as `<component>_dense_array.npy` / `<component>_dilute_array.npy` when `write_conc_arrays=True`.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L718-L754), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L767-L806), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1141-L1185), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1229-L1244)

## Structural and Compositional Profiles Along the Slab Normal

Beyond thermodynamics, `SlabAnalysis` resolves how chain-level properties vary from the condensate interior to the dilute phase. All of these profilers reuse the centered trajectory and per-chain atom groups cached by `load_traj`/`load_ref`, and all bin into 1-Å-wide periodic bins along z with a shared numba-compiled accumulator (`distribute_monomers`) that wraps bead positions into `[0, lz)` before counting:

| Method | Observable | Aggregation per bin | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `calc_orientations` | Nematic order S = (3cos²θ − 1)/2 of each chain's principal axis vs. z | Mean over all sampled beads | `<name>_sz.npy` (empty bins → 0) |
| `calc_rgs` | Radius of gyration (nm) | Root-mean-square: √(mean Rg²) | `<name>_rg.npy` (empty bins → NaN) |
| `calc_aa_bins` | Counts of each of the 20 amino-acid types, mapped via one-/three-letter residue names | Raw counts | `<name>_aa_bins.npy`, shape `(n_bins, 20)` |
| `calc_resid_bins` | Counts per residue *index* along the sequence | Raw counts | `<name>_resid_bins.npy`, shape `(n_bins, n_residues)` |
| `calc_com_traj` | Mass-weighted center-of-mass trajectory (termini corrections +2/+16 Da applied) | One COM bead per reference chain | `<name>_com_top.pdb` + `<name>_com_traj.dcd` |

The amino-acid and residue-index histograms enable spatially resolved composition analysis — for instance, detecting whether aromatic residues are enriched at the slab interface. The COM trajectory artifact is a standard mdtraj-format output suitable for feeding into downstream clustering or radial-distribution analyses.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L832-L910), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1004-L1078), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L938-L1002)

## Output Artifact Map

Every stage writes versioned, self-describing files under `output_path`, all prefixed with the system `name`:

| Artifact | Producer | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `traj.dcd` (in `input_path`) | `center()` | Centered, unwrapped, frame-subsampled trajectory |
| `<name>_<component>_profile.npy` | `calc_profiles()` | Per-frame profiles, `(n_frames, n_bins)`, mM |
| `<name>_profiles.npy` | `calc_profiles()` | Row 0: z coordinates (nm); rows 1+: mean profiles (ref first, then clients) |
| `<component>_dense_array.npy` / `_dilute_array.npy` | `save_conc_results()` | Per-frame phase concentrations for error analysis |
| `<name>_ps_results.csv` | `calc_concentrations()` | One row per component: cutoffs, c_dense/c_dilute ± errors, ΔG ± error, chain ranges |
| `<name>_profiles.pdf` | `plot_density_profiles()` | Log-scale mean profiles with dashed (dense) and dotted (dilute) cutoff lines |
| `<name>_sz.npy`, `<name>_rg.npy` | Structural profilers | Order-parameter and Rg profiles per 1-Å bin |
| `<name>_aa_bins.npy`, `<name>_resid_bins.npy` | Composition profilers | Spatially resolved composition counts |
| `<name>_com_top.pdb`, `<name>_com_traj.dcd` | `calc_com_traj()` | COM-bead topology and trajectory |

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L684-L716), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L754-L765), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L912-L936)

## Worked Example: Single-Component and Mixed Systems

The repository ships two reference notebooks that exercise the identical five-call pipeline. In the single-component hnRNPA1LCD case, all 200 chains form the reference condensate and the analysis begins at frame 600 with every 10th frame retained. In the mixed FUSR-GG3/polyU40 system, the reference is chains 0–199 and a single client range `(200, 259)` registers 60 RNA chains, with equilibration discarded from frame 250 onward:

| Aspect | `slab_IDR` notebook | `slab_mixed` notebook |
|---|---|---|
| System | hnRNPA1LCD, replica 0 | FUSR-GG3 + polyU40 |
| `ref_chains` | Default (all chains) | Explicit `(0, 199)` |
| `client_chain_list` | Commented out | `[(200, 259)]`, named `polyU40` |
| `center()` call | `start=600, step=10, center_target='all'` | `start=250, step=1, center_target='all'` |
| Extra output | 2D `(n_frames, n_bins)` heatmap via `imshow` | Same heatmap under `data/` |

The complete driver sequence, as executed in both notebooks, is:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S1["Instantiate SlabAnalysis with name, paths, ref and client registry"] --> S2["center: discard equilibration, subsample, align slab"]
    S2 --> S3["calc_profiles: mM density profiles for ref and clients"]
    S3 --> S4["calc_concentrations: fit interfaces, phase concentrations, blocking errors, dG"]
    S4 --> S5["Inspect df_results or name_ps_results.csv"]
    S5 --> S6["plot_density_profiles: log-scale PDF with cutoffs"]
    S6 --> S7["Optional: imshow per-frame profile to inspect slab stability over time"]
```

Note that `calc_concentrations` requires the per-frame `.npy` profiles written by `calc_profiles` (it reloads them from disk), so the call order is mandatory — skipping the profile stage yields a file-not-found rather than silent recomputation.

Sources: [example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_IDR/example_slab_analysis.ipynb#L26-L107), [example_slab_analysis.ipynb](examples/slab_mixed/example_slab_analysis.ipynb#L26-L107)

## Position in the Analysis Stack

The slab module sits at the top of CALVADOS's analysis stack: it consumes trajectories produced by the simulation engine ([Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing)) of slab-geometry systems prepared during system building ([System Building & Geometry](13-system-building-and-geometry)), reuses generic observables from the trajectory toolkit ([Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](15-trajectory-analysis-toolkit)), and delegates all error quantification to the blocking machinery ([Blocking Error Estimation](17-blocking-error-estimation)). To see slab systems in the context of the wider example suite — droplet, cylindrical, and MDP co-solvent variants — continue to the [Example Gallery](4-example-gallery).


# Blocking Error Estimation



Every observable extracted from a CALVADOS trajectory — radius of gyration, end-to-end distance, dense-phase concentration — is a *time-correlated* series, not a set of independent samples. The naive standard error `std/√N` therefore systematically underestimates uncertainty. The `calvados.BLOCKING` package solves this with **block averaging**: it partitions a correlated series into blocks of increasing size, measures how the standard error grows toward its asymptotic (uncorrelated) plateau, and selects the converged value. This page documents the package's two layers — the stateless estimators in `block_tools.py` and the `BlockAnalysis` facade in `main.py` — and their integration points in the analysis stack. It covers unweighted and reweighted (bias-corrected) estimators, the fixed-point error-selection algorithm, and the downstream consumers in `analysis.py`.

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L10-L18), [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L52-L79)

## Why Blocking: The Statistical Problem

MD frames are autocorrelated: consecutive configurations share memory, so treating every frame as an independent sample inflates the effective sample count and shrinks the apparent error. The `autocorrelation` utility exposes this directly — it computes the normalized autocorrelation `r(τ)` at every nonnegative lag via `np.correlate`, normalized by `variance × (n − τ)` so that `r(0) = 1`. The decay of this function defines the correlation time that naive error formulas ignore.

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L122-L129)

Block averaging attacks the problem from the measurement side rather than the model side. The series is split into `N_b` contiguous blocks of size `b`, each block is reduced to its mean `B_k`, and the **standard error of the block means** is computed as:

```
ε(b) = sqrt( Σ_k (B_k − x̄)² / (N_b (N_b − 1)) )
```

with the statistical uncertainty of that error given by `σ_ε = ε / √(2(N_b − 1))`. As `b` grows, correlations *within* blocks stop contributing to between-block variance and `ε(b)` rises to a plateau equal to the true asymptotic error. Both formulas are implemented verbatim in `blocking()`, which returns an `(n, 3)` array of `[block size, standard error, uncertainty of that error]` ordered from largest to smallest block size before flipping (see below).

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L52-L79)

## Module Architecture

The package separates **pure numerical kernels** from **stateful orchestration**. `block_tools.py` holds five dependency-light NumPy functions with full type aliases (`FloatArray`, `IntArray`); `main.py` holds the single `BlockAnalysis` class that sequences those kernels, applies reweighting, and derives final observables. Nothing in the package imports trajectory machinery — it operates on plain float arrays, which makes it independently testable and reusable outside CALVADOS.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph BLOCKING["calvados.BLOCKING"]
        BT["block_tools.py<br/>blocker / check / blocking / fblocking / autocorrelation"]
        BA["BlockAnalysis (main.py)<br/>__init__ → SEM → get_pdf / get_fes / get_av_err"]
        BT --> BA
    end
    SCP["analysis.save_conf_prop<br/>(Rg, Re time series)"] --> BA
    SAB["SlabAnalysis.calc_block_errors<br/>(dense / dilute conc. arrays)"] --> BA
    BA --> CSV1["conf_prop.csv<br/>value + error rows"]
    BA --> CG["SlabAnalysis.calc_dG<br/>Monte Carlo propagation"]
    SAB --> CG
```

The two consumers shown on the left live in `calvados/analysis.py`, which imports the facade at module scope. Each arrow is a verified call site: `save_conf_prop` blocks Rg and end-to-end series; `SlabAnalysis.calc_block_errors` blocks per-frame dense and dilute concentrations before Monte Carlo propagation of the transfer free energy.

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L1-L9), [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L7), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L21), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L518-L528), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1229-L1244)

### Kernel Function Reference

| Function | Signature core | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `blocker` | `(array, multi) → (N, n_blocks, block_sizes)` | Enumerate block counts `n` for which the split is exactly divisible both globally (`N % n == 0`) and per replica (`(N/multi) % bs == 0`) |
| `check` | `(array, multi) → trimmed array` | Iteratively strip `c` trailing frames from *each* replica until ≥ 20 valid blocking transforms exist |
| `blocking` | `(array, multi) → (n, 3) stats` | Unweighted block-error scan over all valid block sizes |
| `fblocking` | `(cv, w, kbt, multi, interval) → (n, 3) stats` | Weighted free-energy-profile error scan over 50 histogram bins |
| `autocorrelation` | `(x) → r(τ)` | Normalized autocorrelation at all lags for correlation diagnostics |

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L11-L25), [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L28-L48), [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L82-L119), [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L122-L129)

## Block Schedule and Replica Hygiene

The scan does not test arbitrary block sizes. `blocker` builds candidate block counts `n ∈ [2, N]` (starting at `multi` when replicas are present) and keeps only those satisfying two divisibility constraints: the total length must divide evenly into `n` blocks, and the block size `bs = N/n` must evenly tile each replica of length `N/multi`. This second constraint is what makes **multi-replica blocking safe** — a block never straddles a replica boundary unevenly, so block means are never contaminated by mixing independent replicas mid-block.

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L11-L25)

> [!TIP]
> The `check` function enforces a hidden floor: a blocking scan needs **at least 20 valid transforms** to resolve a plateau. If the raw array supports fewer, it removes 1, 2, 3, … trailing frames from *every* replica (up to 101 iterations) until the constraint is satisfied, then returns the trimmed concatenation. Practically, this means `BlockAnalysis` may silently shorten the tail of your series — do not assume the output length equals the input length.

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L28-L48)

## The `BlockAnalysis` Facade

The class constructor is the single entry point for both weighted and unweighted analysis. It accepts the observable series `x`, a replica count `multi`, optional `weights` **or** a `bias` array at temperature `T` for reweighting, optional histogram `interval_low`/`interval_up` bounds, and a time step `dt` for the block-size axis.

| Parameter | Default | Semantics |
|---|---|---|
| `x` | required | Time series (possibly concatenated replicas) of the observable |
| `multi` | `1` | Number of concatenated independent replicas; activates replica-aware divisibility and trimming |
| `weights` | `None` | Per-frame statistical weights; normalized to sum 1 when supplied |
| `bias` | `None` | Bias potential per frame; converted to weights `w = exp((bias − max bias)/k_BT)` when no weights given |
| `T` | `None` | Temperature (K); `k_BT = 0.008314463 × T` (R in kJ·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹), required for bias reweighting and any free-energy output |
| `interval_low` / `interval_up` | `None` | Clip bounds for the histogram/PDF range: each replaces the data bound only when the data overshoot it |
| `dt` | `1` | Divisor applied to the block-size column, converting frame counts to physical time units |

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L20-L57)

Initialization runs a fixed decision sequence, summarized below. The output is always `self.stat`, an `(n, 3)` matrix whose columns are `[block size, error, uncertainty of error]`, with the block-size column subsequently scaled by `1/dt`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["x: raw series"] --> E["check(x, multi): trim replica tails<br/>until ≥ 20 transforms"]
    E --> F["blocker(x, multi): valid (n_blocks, bs) pairs"]
    A --> B{"weights None<br/>and bias given?"}
    B -- "yes" --> C["w = exp((bias − max)/k_BT)<br/>k_BT = 0.008314463 × T"]
    B -- "no" --> D["w = None"]
    C --> W2{"w is None?"}
    D --> W2
    W2 -- "yes" --> H["blocking(x): per-block means → ε(b)"]
    W2 -- "no" --> I["fblocking(x, w, k_BT):<br/>per-block histograms → FE error"]
    H --> J["stat[..., 0] /= dt"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["ready for SEM()"]
```

Note the flip performed by the kernels: candidate counts run from many blocks (small `b`) to few (large `b`), and both `blocking` and `fblocking` reverse the row order, so `self.stat[0]` corresponds to block size ≈ 1 and `self.stat[-1]` to the largest testable block. This ordering matters for interpreting the `SEM` warning condition discussed next.

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L31-L57), [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L79), [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L119)

## Fixed-Point Error Selection: `SEM()`

The blocking scan produces an error *curve*; `SEM()` extracts the single converged number. Its criterion is an **interval-intersection count**: for each row `b` of `self.stat`, it searches within that row's error interval `[b[1]−b[2], b[1]+b[2]]` for the value `x` that lies inside the error intervals of the maximum number of *other* rows with strictly larger block size. The inner scorer `find_n_intersect` counts containment and returns its negation so that `scipy.optimize.minimize` performs a maximization; the block size and error of the row whose interval wins are stored as `self.bs` and `self.sem`. Intuitively, the plateau is the region where many consecutive error estimates mutually agree within their own uncertainties.

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L59-L78)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    S0["stat: ascending block sizes,<br/>rows = [b, ε, σ_ε]"] --> L1["for each row b:<br/>bounds = [ε − σ_ε, ε + σ_ε]"]
    L1 --> L2["minimize find_n_intersect over bounds<br/>vs rows with b' > b<br/>(count of containing intervals)"]
    L2 --> L3["c[i] = − best count"]
    L3 --> L4["argmax(c) → self.bs, self.sem"]
    L4 --> W{"self.bs > stat[-1,0] / 3 ?"}
    W -- "yes" --> W1["WARNING: fixed point of the error<br/>may have not been reached"]
    W -- "no" --> OK["converged: use .sem"]
```

> [!TIP]
> The guard at the end of `SEM()` is the honest failure signal of the whole method: because `stat` rows ascend by block size, `stat[-1, 0]` is the *largest* testable block. If the selected block size exceeds one third of that maximum, the error plateau could only be reached by blocking beyond what the data support — typically meaning the simulation is too short relative to its correlation time. Treat this warning as a prompt to extend sampling rather than a rounding detail.

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L59-L81)

## Weighted Observables and Free-Energy Estimators

When weights are present — either supplied directly or derived from a bias via the Maxwell-reweighting transform `w = exp((bias − max bias)/k_BT)` — the constructor routes through `fblocking` instead of `blocking`. The weighted scan histograms the collective variable `cv` into 50 bins over the clipped interval, deletes zero-count bins and their edges, normalizes by the total frame count, and then, for each block size, accumulates squared deviations of *per-block* histograms from the full-sample histogram. The per-bin relative error is `k_BT · e_bin / u` (fluctuation-to-free-energy propagation), averaged over surviving bins; the error-of-error column again uses `ε/√(2(N_b − 1))`.

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L42-L55), [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L82-L119)

The same machinery then powers three derived estimators, all built on a Silverman-bandwidth Gaussian KDE of the (weighted) series:

| Method | Returns | Error construction |
|---|---|---|
| `get_pdf(cv=None)` | `(x_grid, density, σ_density)` | Per-block KDEs at the chosen `self.bs`; error `√(Σ_k w_k (P_k − P)² / (N_b (W − S/W)))` with `W = Σw`, `S = Σw²` — the Kish effective-sample-size correction |
| `get_fes(maxkj=25, cv=None)` | `(x, F, σ_F)` | `F = −k_BT ln P`, propagated as `σ_F = k_BT σ_P / P`; output cropped to `F < maxkj` and shifted so `min(F) = 0` |
| `get_av_err(cv=None)` | `(average, σ_average)` | Density-weighted mean over the KDE grid; error accumulated as `√(Σ x² σ_P²)` after normalization |

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L83-L130), [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L132-L146), [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L148-L158)

The `cv` argument on each method is notable: it allows computing the density, free energy, or average of a *different* collective variable (itself passed through `check` for replica hygiene) while inheriting the blocking error scale selected on the primary series. This couples the error estimate and the observable deliberately, which is why the class docstring describes `SEM()` as the pivot between "selecting a converged error" and "constructing densities, surfaces, or weighted averages."

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L13-L17), [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L91-L96)

## Integration with the Analysis Stack

Two verified call sites consume the facade, and they illustrate the two canonical usage patterns.

### Single-chain conformational properties

`save_conf_prop` computes per-frame Rg and end-to-end arrays from a trajectory, then wraps each in the minimal pattern `BlockAnalysis(series)` + `.SEM()`. The resulting `block_rg.sem` and `block_ree.sem` populate the `error` column of `conf_prop.csv` alongside the plain means — so every published Rg/Re pair from this pipeline already carries a blocking-corrected uncertainty.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L494-L539)

### Slab phase-equilibrium concentrations

`SlabAnalysis.calc_single_conc` reduces the `(n_frames × n_bins)` density profile to per-frame dense and dilute concentration arrays (using the hyperbolic-tangent interface fit cutoffs), then delegates uncertainty to the static helper `calc_block_errors`, which runs the same instantiate-then-`SEM()` pattern on both arrays.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as calc_concentrations
    participant C as calc_single_conc
    participant E as calc_block_errors
    participant B as BlockAnalysis
    participant G as calc_dG
    U->>C: profile h (n_frames × n_bins, mM)
    C->>C: interface fit → dense/dilute masks,<br/>cden, cdil, per-frame arrays
    C->>E: denarray, dilarray
    E->>B: BlockAnalysis(arr); SEM()
    B-->>E: .sem for each phase
    E-->>C: eden, edil (mM)
    C->>G: cdil, edil, cden, eden
    G->>G: 10 000 normal draws per phase,<br/>std of log(dil/den) over valid draws
    G-->>C: dG, dG_err (kT) → ps_results.csv
```

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L767-L806), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1229-L1244)

The final hop is worth noting architecturally: `calc_dG` does not do analytic propagation of `dG = log(c_dil/c_den)`. Instead it draws 10 000 normal samples per phase around `(c, σ)` from the blocking analysis, takes the standard deviation of the log-ratios over draws where both concentrations remain positive, and handles degenerate regimes (NaN or zero concentrations) with explicit clipping to `dGmin`. The blocking error is thus the *seed* of a Monte Carlo propagation, not the final word.

Sources: [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1141-L1185)

## Standard Usage Pattern

For direct use outside the built-in pipelines, the pattern is deliberately two-step: construct (which computes the full blocking scan) and select (which fixes the plateau). The minimal unweighted case needs only the series; reweighting adds `bias`, `T`, and optionally explicit histogram bounds:

```python
from calvados.BLOCKING.main import BlockAnalysis

# Unweighted: Rg series from N frames (optionally nrep concatenated replicas)
block = BlockAnalysis(rgs, multi=nrep, dt=output_frequency)
block.SEM()
print(block.bs, block.sem)   # converged block size (time units) and standard error

# Reweighted: bias in kJ/mol at temperature T, density over [0, 1]
block = BlockAnalysis(cv, bias=bias_array, T=300, interval_low=0.0, interval_up=1.0)
block.SEM()
x, pdf, pdf_err = block.get_pdf()      # density with blocking errors
x, F, F_err  = block.get_fes(maxkj=25) # free energy surface in kJ/mol
```

Every keyword in this snippet maps one-to-one to the constructor semantics table above; the `dt` argument is what converts the reported block size from frame counts into physical time, because `stat[..., 0]` is divided by `dt` at the end of initialization.

Sources: [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L20-L57)

## Summary and Position in the Catalog

The blocking stack follows a clean layering: **kernels** (`blocker`, `check`, `blocking`, `fblocking`) do divisibility-constrained scheduling and error scanning; the **facade** (`BlockAnalysis`) adds replica hygiene, bias reweighting, fixed-point selection, and derived density/free-energy estimators; and the **analysis stack** treats it as a black box that turns a correlated series into `(value, error)` pairs — both in `save_conf_prop` and in the slab concentration workflow whose errors seed the `dG` Monte Carlo. The two failure modes to watch in practice are the silent tail-trimming in `check` and the plateau warning in `SEM` — both are documented behaviors, not bugs, and both signal something about your sampling rather than the estimator.

Sources: [block_tools.py](calvados/BLOCKING/block_tools.py#L11-L129), [main.py](calvados/BLOCKING/main.py#L10-L159), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L494-L539), [analysis.py](calvados/analysis.py#L1229-L1244)

For where blocking errors are consumed downstream, continue with [Slab Phase-Separation Analysis](16-slab-phase-separation-analysis); for the observables that feed it (Rg, Re, contact maps), see [Trajectory Analysis Toolkit](15-trajectory-analysis-toolkit); to understand how the trajectories themselves and their sampling length are produced, see [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing).

# Extension & Custom Forces



Every CALVADOS system is ultimately an OpenMM `openmm.System`, and everything beyond the built-in Ashbaugh-Hatch and Debye-Hückel pair physics is injected through a deliberate extension layer: a set of **force factory functions** in `calvados/interactions.py`, an orchestration pipeline in `calvados/sim.py`, and a **declarative configuration surface** in `calvados/inputmodels.py`. This page covers the three supported extension pathways — declarative external forces (`ext_force`), file-driven custom restraints (`custom_restraints`), and programmatic composition of the factory layer — showing exactly where forces are created, validated, populated, excluded from nonbonded interactions, and registered in the final system.

## The Extension Architecture at a Glance

The extension surface follows a strict **factory → orchestrator → system** data flow. Factory functions never mutate global state: each one constructs a fresh OpenMM force object (e.g., `openmm.CustomNonbondedForce`, `openmm.CustomBondForce`, `openmm.CustomExternalForce`) configured with energy expressions, per-particle/per-bond parameters, force groups, and periodic boundary settings. The `Sim` class then owns those objects, populates them particle-by-particle as molecules are placed, and finally hands everything to `openmm.System` in `add_forces_to_system` before serializing to `sysname.xml`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["Declarative inputs"]
        CFG["config.yaml<br/>ext_force / ext_force_expr<br/>custom_restraints / _type / _file"]
        CRESC["cres.txt<br/>name copy bead&#124;name copy bead&#124;r k"]
    end
    subgraph Validation["inputmodels.py"]
        V["SimulationInput + validators<br/>(slab_eq xor ext_force)"]
    end
    subgraph Factories["interactions.py force factories"]
        F1["init_nonbonded_interactions → AH, YU"]
        F2["init_restraints → HarmonicBond / CustomBond"]
        F3["init_slab_restraints → CustomExternalForce"]
        F4["init_scaled_LJ / init_scaled_YU / init_wcafene"]
    end
    subgraph Orch["Sim.build_system (sim.py)"]
        MC["make_components: component-owned forces"]
        AE["add_ext_restraints (per particle)"]
        MCR["map_custom_restraints → add_custom_restraints"]
        AF["add_forces_to_system"]
    end
    SYS["openmm.System → sysname.xml"]
    CFG --> V --> Orch
    CRESC --> MCR
    F1 --> AF
    F2 --> MCR
    F3 --> AE
    F4 --> MC
    MC --> AF
    AE --> AF
    MCR --> AF
    AF --> SYS
```

Three distinct extension pathways exist, differing in trigger mechanism and effort level. The table below anchors the rest of this page.

| Pathway | User-facing trigger | OpenMM force produced | Code entry point |
|---|---|---|---|
| Declarative external potential | `ext_force=True` + `ext_force_expr` string | `CustomExternalForce` | `Sim.__init__` / `add_ext_restraints` |
| File-driven custom restraints | `custom_restraints=True` + restraint file | `HarmonicBondForce` or `CustomBondForce` (go) | `parse/map/add_custom_restraints` |
| Programmatic force composition | Python imports of `interactions.*` factories | Any factory return type | `Sim.build_system` pattern |

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L54-L176), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L157-L204), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L306-L319)

## Force Factory Layer: `interactions.py`

`interactions.py` is the module to study before writing any custom force, because it codifies CALVADOS's conventions for OpenMM force construction. Each factory builds an energy expression as an f-string (physical constants interpolated numerically), registers per-particle or per-bond parameters, enables periodic boundary conditions where relevant, and assigns a **force group** — `AH` sits in group 0 and `YU` in group 1 ([interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L89), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L111-L115)) — which is what makes per-force energy decomposition possible at runtime.

The restrained-force factories are especially relevant for extension work. `init_restraints(restraint_type)` returns a plain `openmm.HarmonicBondForce` for `'harmonic'` or a `CustomBondForce` implementing the 10–12 Go potential `k*(5*(s/r)^12-6*(s/r)^10)` with per-bond parameters `s` and `k` for `'go'` ([interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L161-L176)). `RestType = Literal['harmonic', 'go']` is the single type alias governing both component restraints and custom restraints, so any extension that accepts a restraint type should reuse it ([interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L13)).

| Factory | Returns | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `init_nonbonded_interactions` | `(CustomNonbondedForce, CustomNonbondedForce)` | AH + YU pair physics |
| `init_lipid_interactions` | cosine + charge-nonpolar forces | Membrane components |
| `init_restraints` | `HarmonicBondForce` \| `CustomBondForce` | Harmonic or Go restraints (custom & component) |
| `init_scaled_LJ` / `init_scaled_YU` | `CustomBondForce` | Intra-molecular scaled AH/YU for Go-type components |
| `init_slab_restraints` | `CustomExternalForce` | Box-center equilibration restraints |
| `init_wcafene` | `CustomBondForce` | WCA-FENE bonds at energy scale `3*eps_lj` |
| `init_bonded_interactions` / `init_angles` | `HarmonicBondForce` / `HarmonicAngleForce` | Chain connectivity & RNA angles |

Pairwise population helpers complete the pattern: `add_single_restraint` adds one bond and returns a **one-based record** for output files, converting units per type (`dij*nanometer, k*kJ/mol/nm²` for harmonic; `[dij*nanometer, k*kJ/mol]` for go), and `add_exclusion` registers a pair exclusion on a nonbonded force ([interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L237-L297)). Note the unit discipline: distances in nm, force constants in kJ·mol⁻¹·nm⁻², energy scales in kJ/mol — always wrapped in OpenMM units.

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L54-L115), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L156-L176), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L237-L297)

## Declarative External Forces: `ext_force`

The lightest-weight extension requires no code at all. Setting `ext_force=True` in the configuration causes `Sim.__init__` to construct `openmm.CustomExternalForce(self.config.ext_force_expr)` directly from your energy expression string ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L81-L82)). During `build_system`, every component whose `ext_restraint` flag is `True` (the default) contributes all of its beads to this force via `add_ext_restraints`, which loops `rcent.addParticle(i+offset)` over the component's beads with the system-level offset ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L550-L555)). The application is gated at the per-molecule level by `(self.slab_eq or self.config.ext_force) and comp.params.ext_restraint` ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L287-L289)), so individual molecules can opt out via the component's `ext_restraint` field ([inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L70)).

The default expression, `"step(d2-18)*d2; d2=periodicdistance(x, y, z, 0, 0, z)^2"`, applies a confining cost to beads far from the z-axis and is the shipped example of what an external potential looks like ([inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L164-L165)). Validation enforces that `slab_eq` and `ext_force` are **mutually exclusive**, since both bind the same `rcent` slot ([inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L210-L216)). The lifecycle is also fully managed: after slab equilibration completes, `simulate` scans `system.getForces()` for the first `CustomExternalForce` instance and removes it from the system before rebuilding the simulation ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L734-L738)).

> [!TIP]
> Unlike `init_slab_restraints`, the `ext_force` path registers **no** global parameter — not even `k` — so your `ext_force_expr` must be fully self-contained: hardcode constants inline (as the default expression does with `18`) or reference only OpenMM built-in variables like `x`, `y`, `z` and `periodicdistance`. An expression referencing `k` will fail at context creation, not at config validation.

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L41-L82), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L287-L289), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L550-L555), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L734-L738), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L164-L177), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L210-L216)

## File-Driven Custom Restraints

Custom restraints solve a different problem: **bespoke pair restraints between arbitrary beads, potentially in different molecules, without touching library code**. Three config fields control the feature: `custom_restraints` (enable), `custom_restraint_type` (`'harmonic'` or `'go'`), and `fcustom_restraints` (path to the restraint file, default `custom_restraints.txt`) ([inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L175-L177)). A full working configuration is shown in the shipped example, where A1 with folded domains is restrained via `fcustom_restraints = f'{cwd}/input/cres.txt'` ([examples/custom_restraints/prepare.py](examples/custom_restraints/prepare.py#L44-L46), [examples/custom_restraints/README.md](examples/custom_restraints/README.md#L1-L9)).

The input file uses a pipe-delimited, **one-based** record format parsed by `Sim.parse_custom_restraints`:

| Field | Position | Content | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Endpoint i | before first `\|` | `name copy bead` (space-separated) | `hnRNPA1S 1 4` |
| Endpoint j | between pipes | `name copy bead` | `hnRNPA1S 1 10` |
| Parameters | after second `\|` | `r k` (distance, force constant) | `1.0 700.0` |

Because component placement order is not user-stable (`reorder_components` moves solutes before lipids and crowders), the file references **logical** addresses that `map_custom_restraints` translates into absolute OpenMM particle indices: it first computes each component's `start_bead` as the cumulative sum of `nmol * nbeads`, then resolves `x_abs = start_bead + (copy-1)*nbeads + (bead-1)` ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L589-L624)). The regression test pins this down exactly — components A (2×3), B (1×4), C (2×5) yield `start_bead` values `[0, 6, 10]`, and a restraint from B copy 1 bead 4 to C copy 2 bead 1 maps to absolute pair `[9, 15]` ([tests/test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L29-L58)).

Mapping is deliberately strict. Every endpoint is validated, and violations raise `ValueError` with precise messages — unknown component names, and out-of-range copy or bead indices — as verified parametrically in the test suite ([tests/test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L60-L90)):

| Invalid endpoint | Raised message |
|---|---|
| `["missing", 1, 1]` | component 'missing' is not in the system |
| `["A", 3, 1]` (nmol=2) | copy 3 is outside the valid range 1-2 |
| `["A", 1, 4]` (nbeads=3) | bead 4 is outside the valid range 1-3 |
| `["A", 0, 1]` / `["A", 1, 0]` | copy/bead 0 is outside the valid range |

Population happens **after every molecule is placed**, at the end of `build_system`: `map_custom_restraints()` followed by `add_custom_restraints()` ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L291-L293)). `add_custom_restraints` instantiates the force via `interactions.init_restraints(self.config.custom_restraint_type)`, adds each bond through `interactions.add_single_restraint`, and — critically — collects the pair list into an `exclusion_map` that `add_exclusions` turns into exclusions on **every** nonbonded force (`ah`, `yu`, plus lipid `cos`/`cn` when present), mirroring how component-level restrained pairs are excluded from AH/YU ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L481-L501)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["cres.txt<br/>(1-based, logical)"] --> B["parse_custom_restraints<br/>split on '|'"]
    B --> C["map_custom_restraints<br/>start_bead offsets + range checks"]
    C --> D["custom_restr_abs<br/>(absolute indices, r, k)"]
    D --> E["init_restraints(type)"]
    D --> F["add_single_restraint per pair"]
    F --> G["add_exclusions on AH/YU/cos/cn"]
    E --> H["system forces at add_forces_to_system"]
    G --> H
```

> [!TIP]
> The exclusion step is not optional hygiene — a restrained pair that stays inside the AH/YU neighbor lists double-counts interactions and distorts the restrained potential. When writing any custom restraint pathway, follow the `exclusion_map → add_exclusions` convention so restrained beads are visible **only** through your force.

Sources: [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L175-L177), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L589-L644), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L291-L293), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L481-L501), [tests/test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L29-L90)

## Restraint Type Semantics: Harmonic vs Go

Because `custom_restraint_type` reuses the same `RestType` vocabulary as component restraints, both pathways share identical force semantics. The choice determines the OpenMM force class, the parameter payload, and the unit conventions applied in `add_single_restraint` ([interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L161-L176), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L245-L256)):

| Aspect | `harmonic` | `go` |
|---|---|---|
| Force class | `HarmonicBondForce` | `CustomBondForce` |
| Energy form | OpenMM built-in k(r−r₀)² | `k*(5*(s/r)^12-6*(s/r)^10)` |
| Bond parameters | `(r0, k)` positional | per-bond `s`, `k` |
| Units for `r`, `k` in file | nm, kJ·mol⁻¹·nm⁻² | nm, kJ/mol |
| Typical constant | `k_harmonic = 700.0` | `k_go = 15.0` |

Both forces call `setUsesPeriodicBoundaryConditions(True)`, keeping restraint geometry consistent with the periodic box ([interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L175-L176)). The default constants `k_harmonic` and `k_go` are defined at the component level ([inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L65-L66)), and the custom-restraints integration test uses `700.0` in its restraint file — the same scale as component-level harmonic restraints ([tests/test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L121-L127)).

Sources: [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L13-L13), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L161-L176), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L245-L258), [inputmodels.py](calvados/inputmodels.py#L60-L70)

## Writing Your Own Force: A Recipe

When the two declarative pathways are insufficient, extend programmatically by **reusing the factory conventions** rather than inventing new plumbing. The codebase itself demonstrates the canonical sequence, and any custom force should reproduce it:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    S1["1. Build the force object<br/>(energy expr + parameters + units)"] -->
    S2["2. Populate particles/bonds<br/>with system-level offsets"] -->
    S3["3. Add exclusions on AH/YU<br/>for any restrained pair"] -->
    S4["4. Register via system.addForce<br/>before Context creation"]
```

For an external one-body potential, replicate the `rcent` pattern: construct `openmm.CustomExternalForce(expr)`, add a global parameter (e.g., `k` in `kJ/mol/nm`), then loop `addParticle(i+offset)` using the same offset arithmetic as `add_ext_restraints` (`offset = nparticles - comp.nbeads`) ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L550-L555), [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L503-L535)). For new pair potentials, wrap your expression in a factory returning `CustomNonbondedForce` with `CutoffPeriodic` and an explicit force group, exactly as `init_ah_interactions` and `init_yu_interactions` do ([interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L63-L115)).

Verification is a first-class part of the extension workflow, and the test suite is your template. The end-to-end `test_cres` builds a minimal 8 nm box system with `custom_restraints=True`, runs `sim.run`, deserializes the produced `sysname.xml` with `openmm.XmlSerializer`, and asserts the restraint force exists with exactly one bond between absolute beads `i == 0` and `j == 9` — closing the loop from user file to OpenMM system ([tests/test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L92-L182)). It also proves the checkpoint contract: the run must produce `custom-restart.chk` and no plain `restart.chk` ([tests/test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L174-L179)).

| Step | Standard system | System with custom forces | Verified by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Force inventory | AH, YU (+ bonded per component) | + `cres` bond force / external force | XML deserialization, `getForces()` |
| Nonbonded exclusions | bonded neighbors only | + restrained pairs on AH/YU/cos/cn | `getNumExclusions()` |
| Output artifacts | `restart.chk` | `custom-restart.chk` when configured | file existence asserts |

Sources: [sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L503-L555), [interactions.py](calvados/interactions.py#L63-L115), [tests/test_custom_restraints.py](tests/test_custom_restraints.py#L92-L182)

## Boundaries and Related Pages

This page deliberately excludes two adjacent topics. **Component-internal restraint machinery** — `init_restraint_force`, `init_scaled_nonbonded`, Go-type scaled AH/YU activation inside `make_components` ([sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L96-L107)) — is documented in [Structure-Based Restraints & AlphaFold Guidance](11-structure-based-restraints-and-alphafold-guidance), and the physical content of AH/YU expressions belongs to [Ashbaugh-Hatch Hydrophobic Interactions](6-ashbaugh-hatch-hydrophobic-interactions) and [Debye-Hückel Electrostatics](7-debye-huckel-electrostatics). For the validation layer that guards all extension flags (`extra="forbid"` Pydantic models rejecting misspelled keys), continue with [Declarative Configuration & Validation](12-declarative-configuration-and-validation); for how the assembled force set is executed, checkpointed, and resumed, see [Simulation Engine & Checkpointing](14-simulation-engine-and-checkpointing). To validate the energetics of a custom force against reference kernels, the energy-conservation harnesses are covered in [Testing & Energy Validation](19-testing-and-energy-validation).


# Testing & Energy Validation



This page documents how the CALVADOS repository guarantees physical correctness of its coarse-grained force field through a three-tier test strategy: **analytical energy validation** (does the simulated potential energy match closed-form physics?), **structural force verification** (are the OpenMM force definitions exactly as intended?), and **end-to-end integration testing** (do full simulations produce structurally valid systems?). The crown jewel is `tests/test_potentials.py`, which treats simulation output as a measurable quantity and confronts it against independently written reference equations — the strongest possible guarantee that the force field implementation is free of sign, factor, and unit errors.

Sources: [pytest.ini](pytest.ini#L1-L15), [tests/test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L1-L124)

## Test Suite Architecture & Execution Model

The test suite follows a deliberate **layered validation pyramid**, where each tier answers a different question about the codebase. Unit tests verify invariants of isolated functions (pure verification), definition tests pin the exact structure of generated OpenMM forces (regression locks), and integration tests execute real simulations through the `sim.run()` entry point and inspect the serialized artifacts. This mirrors the Diátaxis principle that a test should fail with a diagnosis, not just a symptom.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph T1["Tier 1 — Analytical Validation"]
        TP["test_potentials.py<br/>E_sim vs E_analytical"]
    end
    subgraph T2["Tier 2 — Structural Verification"]
        TI["test_interactions.py<br/>force expressions & params"]
        TC["test_cfg.py / test_sequence.py<br/>golden values & validation rules"]
    end
    subgraph T3["Tier 3 — Integration"]
        TS["test_sim.py<br/>barostat dispatch, step batching"]
        TB["test_rna_bonds.py<br/>XML system topology"]
        TR["test_custom_restraints.py<br/>restraint index mapping"]
    end
    T2 -->|"forces pinned"| T1
    T3 -->|"systems built correctly"| T1
    TP -.->|"validates physics of"| TI
```

Execution is governed by `pytest.ini`, which encodes several non-obvious policies. `--doctest-modules` means every module's docstrings are collected as tests alongside the `tests/` directory, `--import-mode=importlib` avoids package import collisions, and — critically — `filterwarnings` is set to `error`, so any unexpected warning (e.g., a NumPy overflow or OpenMM deprecation) fails the suite immediately. Only `PendingDeprecationWarning`, `UserWarning`, and `DeprecationWarning` are explicitly tolerated. This "strict warnings" policy acts as a tripwire for silent numerical issues in scientific code.

| Setting | Value | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `testpaths` | `tests` | Discovery root |
| `addopts` | `--doctest-modules --import-mode=importlib -r a -v` | Docstring tests, no path conflicts, full report |
| `filterwarnings` | `error` + 3 ignores | Warnings fail tests unless explicitly whitelisted |
| `norecursedirs` | `dist build .tox scripts` | Skip packaging artifacts |

Sources: [pytest.ini](pytest.ini#L1-L15), [calvados/sim.py](calvados/sim.py#L871-L887)

The nine test modules partition cleanly by subsystem. The inventory below maps each module to its tier and testing style — note that four modules (`test_potentials`, `test_rna_bonds`, `test_custom_restraints`, and parts of `test_sim`) run **actual OpenMM simulations** on the CPU platform, making the suite a genuine physics regression harness rather than a mock-based one.

| Module | Tier | Focus | Style |
|---|---|---|---|
| `test_potentials.py` | Analytical | AH+DH energy vs closed form | End-to-end sim + `np.allclose` |
| `test_interactions.py` | Structural | Force expressions, parameters, force groups | Exact string/param assertions |
| `test_cfg.py` | Unit | Pydantic validation, YAML round-trip | Schema contract tests |
| `test_sequence.py` | Unit | Charges, sequence statistics | Golden numeric values |
| `test_sim.py` | Unit/Integration | Step batching, barostat selection | `Sim.__new__` surgery |
| `test_components.py` | Unit | Registry dispatch, numerical stability | Registry + edge-case floats |
| `test_rna_bonds.py` | Integration | RNA bond topology in serialized system | Full sim + XML introspection |
| `test_custom_restraints.py` | Integration | Restraint index mapping, custom checkpoints | Full sim + file assertions |
| `test_analysis.py` | Unit | Contact maps, slab binning, COM trajectories | monkeypatch + real mdtraj files |

Sources: [tests/](tests), [pytest.ini](pytest.ini#L1-L15)

## Closed-Form Energy Validation: The Physics Oracle

The heart of this page is `tests/test_potentials.py`, which answers the question every force-field developer must eventually face: *does OpenMM compute the energy I think it does?* The strategy is to write the reference Ashbaugh-Hatch and Debye-Hückel potentials **from scratch as NumPy lambdas** — never importing production code — so a bug shared between implementation and test is impossible. This mirrors the reference-vs-oracle pattern from numerical libraries.

Sources: [tests/test_potentials.py](tests/test_potentials.py#L13-L21)
